subtopic_detail: Acute severe colitis initial inpatient management
stem:
You are the admitting medical registrar for a 23-year-old woman with a two year history of ulcerative colitis maintained on mesalazine. Over eight days she has had up to nine bloody stools daily including two overnight, with cramping that wakes her.

She has taken no anti-inflammatory drugs and has not travelled or taken antibiotics recently. Stool testing for Clostridioides difficile and for enteric pathogens is negative and cytomegalovirus serology is pending. Abdominal radiograph shows no colonic dilatation and no free gas.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 108/66, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.9
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with generalised tenderness, bowel sounds present, no rebound
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-155); white cells 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5); albumin 28 g/L (35-50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 40 mg daily with an increase in the mesalazine dose
Intravenous infliximab as a single induction dose with oral mesalazine continued
Intravenous ciprofloxacin and metronidazole with intravenous fluid resuscitation
Urgent surgical referral for consideration of subtotal colectomy within 24 hours
Intravenous hydrocortisone with prophylactic enoxaparin and fluid resuscitation

subtopic_detail: Ascitic fluid analysis and infection management in cirrhosis
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 58-year-old man with alcohol related cirrhosis and a two day history of increasing abdominal distension and diffuse discomfort. He stopped drinking eleven months ago and takes spironolactone and furosemide.

He is alert and orientated with no asterixis. A diagnostic paracentesis is performed on arrival before any antibiotic is given. Blood cultures are collected at the same time and his usual diuretics are withheld pending review.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98, BP 102/58, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 37.8
data_table.Examination: Tense ascites, generalised abdominal tenderness without guarding, no encephalopathy
data_table.Investigations: Ascitic neutrophils 480 x10^6/L; ascitic Gram stain negative; serum creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110); bilirubin 46 micromol/L (less than 20); international normalised ratio 1.5 (0.8-1.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral norfloxacin and repeat the paracentesis in 48 hours for cell count
Start intravenous ceftriaxone and give intravenous albumin on days one and three
Await ascitic fluid culture results before committing to any antibiotic therapy
Perform large volume paracentesis with albumin cover and restart both diuretics
Start intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam and add oral metronidazole cover

subtopic_detail: Albuminuric chronic kidney disease pharmacotherapy
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 61-year-old man in the renal clinic. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension and takes perindopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily and metformin 1 g twice daily.

His blood pressure has been consistently below 130/80 at home and his glycaemic control has been stable for two years. Repeat urine testing over six months confirms persistent albuminuria and his estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 52 to 43 mL/min/1.73 m2 over eighteen months. Renal ultrasound shows two normal sized kidneys with no obstruction and his immunology screen is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 126/74, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: No peripheral oedema, no bruits, jugular venous pressure not elevated
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 43 mL/min/1.73 m2; urine albumin to creatinine ratio 48 mg/mmol (less than 2.5); potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); HbA1c 52 mmol/mol (less than 42)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next addition to his treatment?

options.text: Add candesartan to the perindopril and recheck the potassium in one week
Add a thiazide diuretic and set a lower home blood pressure target of 120/70
Stop metformin because of the falling filtration rate and start basal insulin
Add dapagliflozin and continue the current perindopril dose unchanged
Add a low protein diet of 0.6 g/kg daily and review the ratio in six months

subtopic_detail: Treatment selection after minimal trauma vertebral fracture
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 72-year-old woman four weeks after admission with sudden mid-back pain that began while she was hanging washing. Imaging showed a wedge compression fracture at T8 with no other cause identified.

She takes no glucocorticoids and has never smoked. Her bone mineral density scan shows a lumbar spine T-score of minus 2.1 and a femoral neck T-score of minus 2.3. She swallows tablets easily and can remain upright for half an hour after taking them.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Localised thoracic tenderness, no neurological deficit, height loss of 4 cm since age 60
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.60); 25-hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (more than 50); estimated glomerular filtration rate 74 mL/min/1.73 m2; thyroid function and serum protein electrophoresis within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment recommendation?

options.text: Advise calcium and vitamin D supplements with a supervised weight bearing program
Start weekly oral alendronate with calcium and vitamin D intake reviewed
Defer drug treatment and repeat the density scan in two years to guide therapy
Start daily teriparatide injections as the initial agent for eighteen months
Start six monthly denosumab injections and cease all other bone directed therapy

subtopic_detail: National bowel screening pathway after a positive immunochemical test
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a general medicine clinic seeing a 59-year-old man who has brought in a letter reporting a positive result on his national bowel screening kit. He completed the kit six weeks ago after ignoring the previous two rounds.

He reports no change in bowel habit or rectal bleeding, and he feels entirely well. His father had a colonic polyp removed at age 70. He takes no regular medicines and has not previously been investigated.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no mass, rectal examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 146 g/L (130-175); ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30-300)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the immunochemical faecal test now and refer only if it is positive again
Reassure him that a normal haemoglobin makes significant pathology very unlikely
Request computed tomography colonography as the initial diagnostic investigation
Refer for colonoscopy aiming for the procedure within 30 days of the result
Arrange carcinoembryonic antigen testing and refer if the level is above normal

subtopic_detail: Anticipatory prescribing for breathlessness at the end of life
stem:
You are the medical registrar caring for a 76-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer who has chosen to die at home with community palliative care support. Disease directed treatment was stopped three weeks ago and she is now bed bound and drowsy for much of the day.

She describes distressing breathlessness at rest that is worst when she is repositioned. Oxygen saturation is 94 per cent on room air and a trial of a handheld fan gave only partial relief. She has no history of opioid use, her renal function is preserved and the family asks what they should have at home for the coming days.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 106/64, RR 26, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Reduced air entry at the right base, no wheeze, no peripheral oedema, chest wall not tender
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL/min/1.73 m2; haemoglobin 112 g/L (115-155)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prescription for her breathlessness?

options.text: Low dose immediate release oral morphine regularly with breakthrough doses available
Continuous home oxygen by nasal prongs titrated to comfort during repositioning
Regular oral diazepam with additional doses available for episodic distress
Regular nebulised salbutamol four times daily with saline nebulisers in between
Regular oral dexamethasone with a proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection

subtopic_detail: Obstructive sleep apnoea and fitness to drive
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 48-year-old man who drives a semi-trailer interstate and holds a commercial licence. His partner reports loud snoring with witnessed pauses, and he describes falling asleep at traffic lights twice in the past month.

His body mass index is 36 kg/m2 and his Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 17 out of 24. A laboratory sleep study performed last week reports an apnoea hypopnoea index of 42 events per hour with oxygen desaturation to 84 per cent. His thyroid function and morning cortisol are within normal limits and he takes no sedating medicines.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 148/88, RR 14, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Neck circumference 46 cm, Mallampati class 4, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Apnoea hypopnoea index 42 events per hour; nadir oxygen saturation 84 per cent; HbA1c 44 mmol/mol (less than 42)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Start continuous positive airway pressure and clear him to keep driving meanwhile
Recommend a six month supervised weight loss program before any device therapy
Advise him not to drive, notify the licensing authority, and start airway pressure therapy
Fit a mandibular advancement splint and repeat the sleep study in three months
Prescribe modafinil for daytime sleepiness and review his symptoms in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Severe cutaneous adverse reaction discrimination
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 63-year-old man with a widespread rash and fever. He began allopurinol 24 days ago after two attacks of gout and takes perindopril unchanged for six years.

He has a confluent red rash over more than half his body surface with marked swelling of his face and eyelids. There is no mucosal ulceration, no blistering and Nikolsky sign is negative. He has palpable cervical lymph nodes and mild right upper quadrant discomfort.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106, BP 128/74, RR 20, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform eruption with facial oedema, cervical lymphadenopathy, mucosae intact
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 1.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5); alanine aminotransferase 216 U/L (less than 40); creatinine 132 micromol/L (60-110); atypical lymphocytes on film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Transfer to a burns unit for management of extensive epidermal detachment
Continue allopurinol, give oral antihistamines, and review the rash in 48 hours
Cease perindopril as the likely culprit and observe on antihistamines overnight
Start intravenous immunoglobulin and admit for continuous cardiac monitoring
Cease allopurinol immediately and start systemic corticosteroid with organ monitoring

subtopic_detail: Parkinsonism with hallucinations and antipsychotic selection
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 74-year-old man admitted with a fall. His wife reports that for eight months he has seen small animals in the lounge room in the late afternoon, and that on some days he is sharp and on others barely rouses from his chair.

He was started on metoclopramide seven weeks ago for reflux. Cognitive testing shows impaired attention and visuospatial function with relatively preserved recall. Examination shows symmetric bradykinesia with mild rigidity and no tremor, and his wife adds that for several years he has shouted and thrashed during dreams. He has had no urinary symptoms and postural blood pressures show no significant drop.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70, BP 132/78, RR 14, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Examination: Symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity, no resting tremor, gait short stepped, no cerebellar signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function, calcium, thyroid function and B12 within normal limits; computed tomography brain shows mild generalised atrophy only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his hallucinations?

options.text: Start risperidone 0.5 mg at night and review his symptoms in one week
Start levodopa with carbidopa and continue the metoclopramide for his reflux
Start donepezil and add regular oxazepam at night for behavioural disturbance
Start quetiapine 25 mg at night and continue the metoclopramide for his reflux
Cease metoclopramide, treat reversible contributors, and start a cholinesterase inhibitor

subtopic_detail: Deteriorating myasthenia gravis and respiratory assessment
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 38-year-old woman with acetylcholine receptor antibody positive myasthenia gravis, admitted with four days of worsening weakness after a urinary tract infection treated with nitrofurantoin. She takes pyridostigmine 60 mg five times daily and prednisolone 15 mg daily.

She can no longer lift her head from the pillow and her speech becomes unintelligible after two sentences. She has no muscarinic features such as cramps or excess salivation, and her pupils are 3 mm and reactive. Forced vital capacity measured at the bedside is 1.1 L, having been 2.2 L on admission, and her single breath count is 12.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 138/82, RR 24, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.2
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis, weak neck flexion, nasal speech, paradoxical abdominal movement when supine
data_table.Investigations: Arterial blood gas on room air pH 7.42, PaCO2 41 mmHg (35-45), PaO2 84 mmHg (80-100), bicarbonate 25 mmol/L (22-32)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase pyridostigmine to 90 mg five times daily and reassess in four hours
Withhold pyridostigmine and give intravenous atropine for cholinergic excess
Arrange critical care review for airway support and start immunoglobulin or plasma exchange
Start high flow nasal oxygen and repeat the arterial blood gas in two hours
Increase prednisolone to 50 mg daily and continue current ward level observation

subtopic_detail: Early Guillain-Barre spectrum with non-diagnostic cerebrospinal fluid
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 29-year-old man with three days of unsteadiness and double vision. Ten days ago he had a diarrhoeal illness after a barbecue that settled without treatment.

He walks with a broad based gait and cannot tandem walk. He has bilateral partial external ophthalmoplegia, absent ankle and knee reflexes, and normal power in all limbs. Sensation to pinprick and vibration is intact, with no sensory level and no back pain. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and whole spine is normal, and the cerebrospinal fluid taken today shows protein 0.38 g/L with one white cell.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 126/76, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ophthalmoplegia, areflexia, ataxic gait, power 5/5 throughout, no sensory level
data_table.Investigations: Cerebrospinal fluid protein 0.38 g/L (0.15-0.45); cerebrospinal fluid white cells 1 x10^6/L (less than 5); forced vital capacity 3.6 L; glucose and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat the lumbar puncture in seven days and withhold treatment until protein rises
Start intravenous immunoglobulin and monitor vital capacity and swallowing
Give intravenous methylprednisolone for three days and arrange neurology review
Give intravenous thiamine and treat for a nutritional brainstem syndrome
Arrange urgent computed tomography angiography of the posterior circulation

subtopic_detail: Acute kidney injury in decompensated cirrhosis
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 54-year-old woman with hepatitis C related cirrhosis and diuretic controlled ascites, admitted five days ago with peritonitis that is now improving on ceftriaxone. Her diuretics were stopped on admission.

Her creatinine has risen from a baseline of 74 micromol/L to 196 micromol/L despite 48 hours of intravenous albumin at 1 g/kg daily. She has passed 380 mL of urine in the last 24 hours. She has received no contrast and no nephrotoxic drug, and renal ultrasound shows normal sized unobstructed kidneys.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 92/54, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Moderate ascites, warm peripheries, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no asterixis
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 196 micromol/L (45-90); sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145); urinary sodium 8 mmol/L; urine microscopy shows no casts and no protein; ascitic neutrophils now 90 x10^6/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Give a 1 litre crystalloid bolus and repeat the creatinine in six hours
Restart furosemide and spironolactone to control the ascites and improve output
Change ceftriaxone to meropenem and continue supportive care unchanged
Start terlipressin with continued albumin and refer for transplantation assessment
Arrange urgent renal biopsy to distinguish tubular necrosis from glomerular disease

subtopic_detail: Effusion classification in a diuretic treated patient
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 79-year-old woman with known heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, admitted three days ago with breathlessness and treated with intravenous furosemide. She has lost 4 kg and her breathlessness has improved, but a right sided effusion persists on chest radiograph.

She has never smoked and reports no chest pain or fever, with no occupational asbestos exposure. A diagnostic pleural aspiration is performed today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80, BP 118/70, RR 18, SpO2 95% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Stony dull percussion to mid zone on the right, jugular venous pressure 3 cm, trace ankle oedema
data_table.Investigations: Pleural protein 32 g/L; serum protein 68 g/L; pleural lactate dehydrogenase 168 U/L; serum lactate dehydrogenase 250 U/L; pleural albumin 21 g/L; serum albumin 36 g/L; pleural glucose and pH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: Treat as a transudate given the albumin gradient and continue heart failure therapy
Treat as an exudate by the protein ratio and arrange contrast computed tomography
Insert an intercostal catheter for drainage and send fluid for cytological analysis
Refer for thoracoscopy with pleural biopsy to exclude malignant pleural disease
Start empirical antibiotics for parapneumonic infection and repeat the aspiration

subtopic_detail: Major bleeding on a factor Xa inhibitor
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department for a 77-year-old man with atrial fibrillation on apixaban 5 mg twice daily who has vomited fresh blood twice in the past hour. His last apixaban dose was six hours ago.

He is pale and clammy with ongoing haematemesis in the department. He takes no antiplatelet agent and has had no previous ulcer. Two units of red cells have been started and the gastroenterology on call has been contacted for urgent endoscopy. His renal function is preserved and there is no prior history of thrombosis beyond the atrial fibrillation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 84/52, RR 24, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.2
data_table.Examination: Cool peripheries, epigastric tenderness, melaena on rectal examination
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 71 g/L (130-175); platelets 210 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110); international normalised ratio 1.3 (0.8-1.2); fibrinogen 2.4 g/L (2.0-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate haemostatic intervention?

options.text: Give prothrombin complex concentrate alongside resuscitation and urgent endoscopy
Give intravenous vitamin K 10 mg and fresh frozen plasma while awaiting endoscopy
Give intravenous protamine sulfate and repeat the coagulation profile in one hour
Give idarucizumab as a 5 g intravenous dose and proceed to urgent endoscopy
Give activated charcoal by nasogastric tube and withhold further anticoagulation

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulant choice in cancer associated thrombosis
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to advise on anticoagulation for a 66-year-old woman with a newly diagnosed locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma who has a confirmed segmental pulmonary embolism on computed tomography. She is haemodynamically stable and is due to start chemotherapy next week.

She describes intermittent nausea with reduced oral intake and has had two episodes of small volume coffee ground vomiting in the past fortnight. Her endoscopy report describes a friable ulcerated tumour at the gastro-oesophageal junction. Renal function is preserved and she takes no antiplatelet drug.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 118/72, RR 20, SpO2 95% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: No leg swelling, chest clear, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155); platelets 240 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 76 micromol/L (45-90); right ventricular size normal on computed tomography

lead_in: Which anticoagulation strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Oral rivaroxaban at treatment dose continued for at least six months
Warfarin bridged with enoxaparin, targeting an international normalised ratio of 2 to 3
Retrievable inferior vena cava filter with no systemic anticoagulation started
Prophylactic dose enoxaparin daily with weekly review through chemotherapy
Therapeutic dose enoxaparin daily, reviewed as treatment and bleeding risk evolve

subtopic_detail: Sequence of investigation for a thyroid nodule with suppressed thyrotropin
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 48-year-old woman who had a carotid ultrasound arranged after a transient episode of dizziness, and the report incidentally describes a 2.5 cm nodule in the right thyroid lobe with smooth margins and no microcalcification.

She has noticed no lump herself and has no difficulty swallowing, no voice change and no neck pain. She had no radiation exposure in childhood and no family history of thyroid cancer or endocrine tumours. She mentions she has felt warmer than others recently and her resting heart rate has been higher on her fitness watch. Her thyroid function has come back today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 128/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Smooth mobile 2.5 cm right thyroid nodule, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no proptosis or lid lag
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 0.08 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); free thyroxine 19.4 pmol/L (10-20); ultrasound shows a 2.5 cm solid isoechoic nodule with smooth margins and no microcalcification

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Perform ultrasound guided fine needle aspiration of the thyroid nodule
Arrange thyroid scintigraphy before considering any biopsy of the nodule
Measure thyroglobulin and calcitonin to stratify her risk of malignancy
Repeat the neck ultrasound in twelve months without any biopsy now
Refer for hemithyroidectomy given the size of the nodule on imaging

subtopic_detail: Second line eradication after failed first line therapy for Helicobacter pylori
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 45-year-old man with eight months of epigastric burning that wakes him at night. A urea breath test six months ago was positive and you prescribed esomeprazole with amoxicillin and clarithromycin for seven days.

He brought the empty packets to his review and confirms he took every dose. He stopped the proton pump inhibitor two weeks before the follow up breath test and had taken no antibiotics in that period. That repeat breath test, done six weeks after finishing treatment, is again positive. He has no dysphagia, no vomiting, no weight loss and no anaemia, and he has no allergy to penicillin.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness, no mass, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Repeat urea breath test positive six weeks after completing therapy; haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180); iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the same triple therapy for a further fourteen days of treatment
Refer for gastroscopy with biopsy for culture before any further therapy
Give a proton pump inhibitor alone and retest him again in three months
Give a levofloxacin based triple regimen for seven days starting now
Give a bismuth based quadruple regimen for fourteen days starting now

subtopic_detail: Disposition after computed tomography confirms a distal ureteric stone
stem:
You are the emergency department resident caring for a 41-year-old man who arrived four hours ago with sudden severe right sided back pain that came in waves and made him unable to sit still. He has vomited twice and says his urine looked pink this morning.

His pain settled well after intravenous ketorolac and he is now comfortable and eating. He has no fever, no rigors and no dysuria. His urinalysis shows blood without nitrites or leucocytes, and his creatinine is normal. Computed tomography of the kidneys, ureters and bladder shows a 4 mm calculus at the right vesicoureteric junction with mild proximal hydronephrosis and no perinephric stranding, and both kidneys are of normal size.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 132/80, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Right renal angle tenderness only, abdomen soft, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 84 micromol/L (60-110); white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); urinalysis shows blood without nitrites or leucocytes; computed tomography shows a 4 mm right vesicoureteric junction calculus with mild hydronephrosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit him for intravenous fluids to help flush the stone through
Arrange urgent ureteric stenting by the urology registrar on call today
Book extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy for him within 24 hours
Discharge with analgesia and tamsulosin with urology review arranged
Start empirical oral antibiotics and repeat the imaging in a week

subtopic_detail: Synpharyngitic haematuria with normal complement in a young adult
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24-year-old man who noticed his urine turned the colour of cola yesterday morning. He developed a sore throat the day before that and still has one.

He has had two similar episodes over the past three years, each lasting a couple of days and each starting within a day of a cold, and on both occasions he was told it was a urinary infection although no organism was ever grown. He has no rash, no joint swelling and no abdominal pain. His urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts, and his complement C3 and C4 levels are both within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1
data_table.Examination: Pharyngeal erythema without exudate, no rash, no oedema, no joint swelling
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110); urine protein creatinine ratio 60 mg/mmol (less than 30); urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts; complement C3 and C4 within normal limits; antistreptolysin O titre not raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Treat him with penicillin and repeat the urine test in six weeks' time
Arrange computed tomography urography to find a bleeding source now
Refer to nephrology for consideration of a renal biopsy for him
Start oral prednisolone now and review the proteinuria later
Reassure him that this is benign haematuria and no action is needed

subtopic_detail: Crystals in synovial fluid do not exclude coexisting septic arthritis
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 78-year-old woman admitted overnight with a hot swollen right knee that became painful over two days. She has osteoarthritis and hypertension, has never had a joint replacement and has had one similar episode in the same knee three years ago that settled with tablets.

She has been shivery at home and her family say she has been more confused than usual. The knee is warm with a moderate effusion and she resists any movement. You have aspirated the joint and the fluid is turbid yellow. Polarised light microscopy shows positively birefringent rhomboid crystals and the Gram stain shows no organisms, with culture pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104, blood pressure 124/70, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 37.9
data_table.Examination: Warm swollen right knee with moderate effusion, resists all passive movement, no overlying break in the skin
data_table.Investigations: Synovial white cell count 42 x10^9/L with 88 per cent neutrophils; positively birefringent rhomboid crystals present; synovial Gram stain negative with culture pending; blood white cell count 13.5 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 140 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Start oral colchicine and review the knee again in 48 hours
Start intravenous antibiotics while awaiting the synovial fluid culture
Give an intra-articular corticosteroid injection into the affected knee
Start oral prednisolone 25 mg daily for five days and review her then
Start regular naproxen with proton pump inhibitor cover for her now

subtopic_detail: Drug induced acute interstitial nephritis in a euvolaemic patient
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 68-year-old man whose routine bloods show a creatinine that has climbed from 78 micromol/L six months ago to 236 micromol/L today. He feels reasonably well and has noticed only some tiredness.

He has taken ramipril for five years at an unchanged dose and started pantoprazole eight weeks ago for reflux. He has had no vomiting or diarrhoea, drinks normally and his weight is unchanged. He has no rash, no joint pain and no fever. He is euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes and no postural drop, and his renal ultrasound reports normal sized kidneys with no obstruction and no asymmetry.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76, blood pressure 132/78 with no postural drop, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no rash, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 236 micromol/L (60-110) risen from 78 six months ago; urine protein creatinine ratio 40 mg/mmol (less than 30); urine microscopy shows white cells and white cell casts with no growth on culture; eosinophils 0.7 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5); renal ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the ramipril and recheck his creatinine again in one week
Give a two litre intravenous fluid challenge to him over four hours
Start oral prednisolone before any of his medications are stopped
Refer him for urgent haemodialysis given the level of his creatinine
Stop the proton pump inhibitor and monitor his renal function closely

subtopic_detail: Pancytopenia with macrocytosis and a low reticulocyte count
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 66-year-old man referred with three months of fatigue and bruises appearing on his shins and forearms without injury. He has needed to stop halfway up his driveway to catch his breath.

He drinks two beers a week, takes no regular medication and has had no recent infection or travel. He has no lymphadenopathy and no splenomegaly, and there is no jaundice. His blood film is reported as showing occasional hypogranular neutrophils with no blasts seen. His vitamin B12, folate, thyroid function and liver function are all within normal limits, and his reticulocyte count is low.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 128/74, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Pallor of the conjunctivae, scattered ecchymoses over the shins and forearms, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (130-180); mean cell volume 106 fL (80-100); platelets 42 x10^9/L (150-400); neutrophils 1.1 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5); reticulocytes 12 x10^9/L (20-100); vitamin B12, folate, thyroid and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin and repeat the count in a month
Transfuse red cells and platelets and review him in the outpatient clinic
Start prednisolone for presumed immune mediated platelet destruction
Refer for urgent bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy for him
Repeat the full blood count in three months before making any referral

subtopic_detail: Corticosteroid timing and eye protection in acute unilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 38-year-old man woke 30 hours ago unable to move the left side of his face. He noticed his coffee dribbling out of the left corner of his mouth and that his left eye waters constantly and feels gritty.

He cannot raise the left eyebrow or bury the left eyelashes, and the left eye rolls upwards when he attempts to close it. Taste is reduced on the left front of the tongue and sounds seem uncomfortably loud in the left ear. Limb power, coordination and reflexes are normal, the other cranial nerves are intact, and there is no rash or vesicle on the pinna, in the canal or on the palate. The tympanic membranes are normal and there is no parotid mass.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 15, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Complete left upper and lower facial weakness with positive Bell phenomenon, normal tympanic membranes, no vesicles, no parotid mass, no other cranial nerve deficit
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 5.6 mmol/L (4.0-7.8); no imaging performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral prednisolone now with lubricating drops by day and ointment plus taping at night
Start oral valaciclovir alone with lubricating drops and review the weakness in one week
Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before starting any treatment for him
Arrange urgent computed tomography of the brain to exclude a stroke as the cause of this
Refer for facial nerve decompression surgery and start lubricating drops while he waits

subtopic_detail: Bedside positional testing to separate peripheral positional vertigo from continuous vestibular loss
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 58-year-old woman describes the room spinning when she rolls over in bed or tips her head back to hang washing. Each attack lasts under a minute and settles completely if she keeps still, and she is entirely well between attacks.

This has happened many times over the last three weeks. She has no hearing loss, tinnitus or ear fullness, and no headache, diplopia, dysarthria or limb symptoms. On the Dix Hallpike manoeuvre to the right there is a two second latency then upbeating torsional nystagmus lasting about 20 seconds with reproduction of her vertigo, and the manoeuvre to the left is negative. Gait is steady, the head impulse test is normal in both directions and there is no nystagmus at rest.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72, blood pressure 132/80 lying and 128/78 standing, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Right Dix Hallpike positive with latency, upbeating torsional nystagmus and fatigability; normal head impulse test; no spontaneous nystagmus; normal cerebellar examination
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed in the practice

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe prochlorperazine regularly for two weeks and review her symptoms afterwards
Perform an Epley repositioning manoeuvre on the right side at this consultation today
Start a course of oral prednisolone and refer her for vestibular rehabilitation therapy
Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the posterior fossa before treating her at all
Advise a low salt diet with betahistine and review the frequency of her attacks in six weeks

subtopic_detail: Sequencing conservative treatment and nerve conduction testing in nocturnal hand paraesthesia
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 47-year-old woman who works as a hairdresser describes tingling and burning in her right hand that wakes her most nights and that she relieves by hanging the hand over the side of the bed and shaking it. It has been going on for five months.

The symptoms involve the thumb, index and middle fingers and spare the little finger, and she has begun dropping her scissors. Tapping over the front of the wrist reproduces the tingling and holding both wrists flexed for a minute brings it on within 30 seconds. There is no wasting of the thenar eminence and thumb abduction power is normal. Neck movements are full and painless and do not reproduce the symptoms, and reflexes in both arms are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Reduced light touch over the radial three and a half digits, positive Tinel and Phalen signs at the right wrist, no thenar wasting, normal abductor pollicis brevis power, full painless cervical movements
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone and glycated haemoglobin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for surgical decompression of the affected nerve at the wrist within the next month
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine to look for nerve root compression
Fit a neutral position night splint and arrange nerve conduction studies to confirm severity
Prescribe a two week course of oral corticosteroid and review her symptoms after that time
Prescribe amitriptyline at a neuropathic pain dose and review her symptoms in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Positive diagnosis of a functional bowel disorder versus reflex endoscopy in a young adult
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 27-year-old woman has had lower abdominal cramping for two years that comes and goes, is relieved by opening her bowels, and alternates between loose stools three times a morning and two days without a motion. She feels bloated by the evening and better in the morning.

She has not lost weight, has never seen blood in the toilet or on the paper, and has no nocturnal symptoms that wake her from sleep. There is no family history of bowel cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. Examination reveals mild left iliac fossa tenderness with no mass and a normal perianal inspection. Full blood count, C-reactive protein, coeliac serology on a gluten containing diet and faecal calprotectin are all normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, mild left iliac fossa tenderness without guarding, no palpable mass, normal perianal and rectal examination
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 138 g/L (115-165); C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5); tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A negative with normal total immunoglobulin A; faecal calprotectin 22 mcg/g (less than 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for colonoscopy to exclude inflammatory bowel disease before offering any treatment
Make a positive diagnosis, explain the condition and trial dietary and symptom directed therapy
Advise a strict gluten free diet for three months and repeat the coeliac serology afterwards
Arrange a computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis with oral and intravenous contrast
Prescribe a proton pump inhibitor and an antispasmodic and review her symptoms in six weeks

subtopic_detail: Recognition of an emergent spinal syndrome in a patient with a long history of mechanical back pain
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 44-year-old warehouse worker with ten years of intermittent mechanical low back pain presents at 11 pm with three days of much worse pain radiating down both legs after lifting a pallet.

He has passed no urine since the morning and says he does not feel any urge, although he has not felt his bladder full either. He mentions in passing that the toilet seat felt strange against his skin this evening. Straight leg raise is limited to 40 degrees bilaterally, ankle jerks are absent on both sides and there is reduced sensation to light touch across both buttocks and the inner thighs. Power is 4 out of 5 in ankle plantarflexion bilaterally. He is afebrile, has never been diagnosed with cancer and does not inject drugs. A bladder scan shows a residual volume of 780 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 138/82, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Bilateral reduced perineal sensation, absent ankle jerks, plantarflexion power 4 of 5 bilaterally, reduced anal tone on rectal examination
data_table.Investigations: Bladder ultrasound post-void residual 780 mL; C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5); white cell count 7.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Insert a urinary catheter and arrange emergency magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine tonight
Give opioid analgesia with diazepam and arrange an outpatient magnetic resonance scan this week
Start high dose intravenous dexamethasone and arrange a computed tomography scan of the spine
Arrange plain lumbar spine radiographs and refer him to the physiotherapy clinic tomorrow
Start empirical intravenous antibiotics and take blood cultures to cover a spinal infection

subtopic_detail: Antiviral window and neuralgia risk assessment in a dermatomal vesicular eruption
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 71-year-old woman describes two days of deep burning pain across the right side of her chest that she initially thought was muscular, and since yesterday morning a rash has appeared over the same area.

There are grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a band from the right side of the spine around to the sternum, stopping abruptly at the midline. She rates the pain at 8 out of 10 and it is stopping her sleeping. She takes ramipril and atorvastatin, has an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 68 mL/min/1.73m2, and is not immunosuppressed. There are no lesions on the face, no eye symptoms and no lesions crossing the midline.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 138/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 37.2
data_table.Examination: Grouped vesicles in a unilateral thoracic dermatomal band, marked allodynia over the affected skin, no ocular or facial involvement
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL/min/1.73m2 (greater than 60); no viral swab taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe topical aciclovir cream with simple analgesia and review her again in one week
Withhold antiviral treatment because the rash has already been present for over 24 hours
Prescribe oral valaciclovir with analgesia and defer any vaccination until she has recovered
Prescribe oral prednisolone alone for the pain and arrange review in the clinic in 48 hours
Give the recombinant zoster vaccine today and prescribe oral analgesia for the acute pain

subtopic_detail: Serological workup of an occupationally acquired zoonosis and pre vaccination screening requirements
stem:
You are the emergency registrar in a regional Queensland hospital. A 32-year-old man who has worked in an abattoir for six weeks presents with ten days of high fevers with drenching sweats, severe frontal headache and aching muscles. He has no cough, rash, joint swelling or diarrhoea.

He has not travelled overseas and has no tick bite or freshwater exposure. He drinks little alcohol and takes no medication. Blood cultures taken on arrival are negative at 48 hours and a chest radiograph is normal. His employer runs a vaccination program for new staff but he had not yet been assessed for it.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96, blood pressure 118/70, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 39.1
data_table.Examination: No rash, no lymphadenopathy, chest clear, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, no splenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400); alanine aminotransferase 142 U/L (less than 40); C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5); blood cultures negative at 48 hours; chest radiograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start intravenous benzylpenicillin for presumed leptospirosis and repeat blood cultures now
Give the vaccine now to protect him and start doxycycline empirically at the same time
Send acute serology with a convalescent sample planned, and start empirical doxycycline
Arrange a bone marrow aspirate to investigate the fever with thrombocytopenia and hepatitis
Discharge with paracetamol and advise review only if the fevers persist beyond a fortnight

subtopic_detail: Mandatory arterial assessment before applying compression to a chronic lower limb ulcer
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 68-year-old woman has had a shallow ulcer above the right medial malleolus for four months. It weeps a lot, is only mildly uncomfortable and improves when she puts her feet up in the evening.

The surrounding skin is brown stained and firm with a bottle shaped lower leg, and there is pitting oedema to mid calf. She has type 2 diabetes for twelve years and smokes 15 cigarettes a day. She has no rest pain and no night pain. The dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are difficult to feel through the oedema. A district nurse has asked you to authorise four layer compression bandaging.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 142/84, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Shallow irregular ulcer with a granulating base above the right medial malleolus, haemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis, pitting oedema to mid calf, foot warm with capillary refill under 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 68 mmol/mol (less than 53); ulcer swab shows mixed skin flora; no vascular studies performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply four layer compression bandaging now and review the ulcer size again in two weeks
Take a deep wound swab and start oral flucloxacillin for two weeks before dressing it
Measure the ankle brachial pressure index before deciding on the compression regimen
Refer for punch biopsy of the ulcer edge to exclude a malignant cause of the ulceration
Refer urgently to vascular surgery for angiography and consideration of arterial bypass

subtopic_detail: Treatment route decision for cobalamin deficiency with neurological involvement in a metformin user
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for nine years describes six months of numbness and pins and needles in both feet that has crept up to mid calf, and says he has become unsteady in the dark and in the shower with his eyes shut.

He has taken metformin 2 g daily throughout and has no other regular medication and no proton pump inhibitor. He eats meat and dairy and drinks two standard drinks a week. Vibration sense is absent at both ankles and reduced at both knees, joint position sense is impaired at both great toes and the Romberg test is positive. Ankle reflexes are absent but both plantar responses are extensor.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Absent vibration at ankles, impaired proprioception at both great toes, positive Romberg, absent ankle jerks with extensor plantar responses, no pallor
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 121 g/L (130-180); mean cell volume 104 fL (80-100); serum vitamin B12 118 pmol/L (150-700); folate normal; glycated haemoglobin 58 mmol/mol (less than 53); thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop metformin, start insulin and recheck the vitamin B12 concentration in three months
Start high dose oral vitamin B12 replacement and review his neurological signs in three months
Start a neuropathic pain agent and refer him to the diabetes education service for review
Start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin loading, check intrinsic factor antibodies and review metformin
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine before starting any replacement therapy

subtopic_detail: Investigation of dysphagia to solids and liquids after a failed empirical acid suppression trial
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar. A 41-year-old woman has had 18 months of food sticking behind the sternum. She says it happens with bread and with water equally, that she has learnt to stand up and arch her back to make it go down, and that she brings up undigested food from earlier in the day, particularly at night onto her pillow.

She has lost 6 kg. Four months of a proton pump inhibitor at double dose made no difference to the symptoms. Gastroscopy last month showed retained food in the oesophagus with a puckered but easily traversed gastro oesophageal junction and no mucosal abnormality, and oesophageal biopsies showed fewer than 5 eosinophils per high power field. She has never smoked and drinks minimally.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 20 kg/m2, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, chest clear, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy with retained food, patent puckered gastro oesophageal junction, normal mucosa; oesophageal biopsies fewer than 5 eosinophils per high power field; haemoglobin 129 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat gastroscopy with careful biopsy of the gastro oesophageal junction under sedation
Arrange 24 hour ambulatory oesophageal pH monitoring off acid suppressing medication
Arrange a computed tomography scan of the chest and abdomen with intravenous contrast
Arrange a barium swallow and proceed to balloon dilatation of the sphincter if it is abnormal
Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry to characterise the motility abnormality

subtopic_detail: Treatment threshold and target in genetically confirmed iron overload with normal organ function
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 48-year-old man whose brother was recently diagnosed with an inherited iron overload disorder. He feels well, and specifically denies joint pain, skin darkening or loss of libido.

He drinks four standard drinks a week and takes no supplements or iron tablets. Genetic testing confirms he carries two copies of the C282Y variant. His transferrin saturation is 68 per cent and his ferritin is 890 mcg/L. His liver enzymes, fasting glucose and echocardiogram are all normal, and hepatitis B and C serology are negative. He asks whether he needs treatment when he has no symptoms at all.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No hepatomegaly, no skin pigmentation, no joint swelling, no signs of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: Transferrin saturation 68 per cent (15-45); ferritin 890 mcg/L (30-300); alanine aminotransferase 28 U/L (less than 40); fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.5); haemoglobin 152 g/L (130-180); hepatitis B and C serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise a low iron diet with avoidance of red meat and recheck his ferritin in twelve months
Arrange liver biopsy to stage fibrosis before deciding whether to start any treatment at all
Start oral iron chelation therapy and monitor his ferritin and organ function every three months
Reassure him that he is asymptomatic and repeat his iron studies again in twelve months' time
Begin weekly venesection to reduce ferritin below 50 mcg/L, then move to maintenance

subtopic_detail: Recognising a microangiopathy that requires plasma exchange rather than platelet transfusion
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the ward at 2 am. A 39-year-old woman admitted this evening with confusion and bruising has become more agitated and is now intermittently disoriented to place. She has no fever source, no diarrhoea and takes no regular medication.

Her platelet count is 12 x10^9/L and her haemoglobin has fallen from 118 to 78 g/L over 24 hours. The blood film shows numerous red cell fragments and marked thrombocytopenia. Her international normalised ratio is 1.1, activated partial thromboplastin time is 32 seconds and fibrinogen is 3.6 g/L. Her creatinine is 118 micromol/L. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. The intern has already ordered a platelet transfusion for the bruising and low count.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108, blood pressure 124/76, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.4
data_table.Examination: Widespread petechiae and bruising, fluctuating disorientation, no focal neurology, no organomegaly, no rash of purpura fulminans
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 12 x10^9/L (150-400); haemoglobin 78 g/L (115-165); red cell fragments on film; international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.8-1.2); fibrinogen 3.6 g/L (2.0-4.0); lactate dehydrogenase 1180 U/L (120-250); bilirubin 46 micromol/L (less than 20); creatinine 118 micromol/L (45-90); direct antiglobulin test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Proceed with the platelet transfusion and reassess her conscious state after it has run
Start intravenous immunoglobulin and high dose corticosteroid for immune thrombocytopenia
Cancel the platelets, request urgent plasma exchange and send a sample for ADAMTS13 activity
Give fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate to correct the consumptive coagulopathy present
Arrange urgent computed tomography of the brain before any haematological intervention

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic selection for severe community acquired sepsis in tropical northern Australia
stem:
You are the emergency registrar in Darwin in February. A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and a glycated haemoglobin of 91 mmol/mol presents with four days of fever, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain, and has become confused in the last six hours. He is a heavy drinker and works clearing drains, and there has been heavy rain for a fortnight.

He has not travelled outside the Northern Territory. His chest radiograph shows bilateral upper lobe consolidation with a small cavity on the right. Blood cultures and sputum have been sent. He has had no recent hospital admission and takes no immunosuppressive medication. He is being prepared for the intensive care unit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128, blood pressure 82/48, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 88 per cent on 6 L/min oxygen, temperature 39.4
data_table.Examination: Confused and peripherally shut down, bronchial breathing in both upper zones, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, no skin abscess
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 21.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); creatinine 186 micromol/L (60-110); lactate 4.6 mmol/L (less than 2.0); glycated haemoglobin 91 mmol/mol (less than 53); chest radiograph with bilateral upper lobe consolidation and right sided cavitation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin with oral doxycycline and admission to the intensive care unit
Intravenous ceftriaxone with azithromycin and a single dose of intravenous gentamicin
Intravenous vancomycin with piperacillin tazobactam and oral oseltamivir for influenza cover
Intravenous meropenem with azithromycin and rifampicin added for atypical organism cover
Intravenous ceftazidime with azithromycin added to cover atypical community pathogens

subtopic_detail: Progressive breathlessness on long term antiarrhythmic therapy with an ambiguous cardiac history
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a general clinic. A 72-year-old man with persistent atrial fibrillation has had four months of progressive breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough. He has taken amiodarone 200 mg daily for three years for rhythm control.

He has lost 4 kg and has been febrile at home twice. He has no orthopnoea and no paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, his jugular venous pressure is not elevated and there is no peripheral oedema. Fine inspiratory crackles are audible at both bases and do not clear with coughing. His echocardiogram last week showed preserved left ventricular systolic function with normal filling pressures. A chest radiograph shows bilateral reticular shadowing that was not present two years ago, and his N terminal pro B type natriuretic peptide is 96 ng/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 irregularly irregular, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 91 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Fine bibasal inspiratory crackles unchanged by coughing, no elevated jugular venous pressure, no peripheral oedema, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: N terminal pro B type natriuretic peptide 96 ng/L (less than 125); thyroid stimulating hormone 3.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); chest radiograph with new bilateral reticular shadowing; transfer factor 48 per cent predicted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase his diuretic dose and review his weight and breathlessness again in two weeks
Start a course of oral antibiotics for a chest infection and repeat the chest radiograph after it
Measure thyroid function and liver enzymes and continue his current dose while monitoring
Refer for right heart catheterisation to assess for pulmonary hypertension as the cause
Cease the amiodarone in discussion with cardiology and arrange high resolution chest tomography

subtopic_detail: Vomiting of retained food in long standing diabetes and the investigation that must precede prokinetics
stem:
You are the medical registrar. A 44-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes for 26 years describes six months of fullness after a few mouthfuls, nausea most afternoons and vomiting of food she recognises from the previous evening. Her weight is down 5 kg.

Her glucose readings have become erratic with unexplained hypoglycaemia one to two hours after meals followed by later hyperglycaemia. She has background retinopathy and albuminuria and takes no opioid, anticholinergic or glucagon like peptide 1 agonist. Her abdomen is soft with a succussion splash four hours after a meal and no palpable mass, and there is no jaundice or lymphadenopathy. Her thyroid function and electrolytes are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 with reduced beat to beat variation, blood pressure 128/76 lying and 106/64 standing, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Succussion splash four hours postprandially, soft abdomen with no mass or organomegaly, absent ankle jerks, reduced vibration sense to both ankles
data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 74 mmol/mol (less than 53); thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits; urea, electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits; haemoglobin 126 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start regular metoclopramide and review her symptoms and glucose readings in four weeks
Refer for insertion of a percutaneous jejunostomy tube for enteral feeding and hydration
Increase her basal insulin dose and refer her to the diabetes educator for review of technique
Arrange a computed tomography scan of the abdomen with oral and intravenous contrast
Arrange gastroscopy to exclude mechanical obstruction, then a gastric emptying study

subtopic_detail: Inflammatory back pain in a young adult with normal plain radiographs
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 28-year-old man with 10 months of low back and buttock pain. It is worst when he has been still, wakes him in the second half of the night, and eases after he has been moving for half an hour.

He describes about 90 minutes of stiffness each morning. Ibuprofen helps substantially. He has had one episode of a painful red eye treated by an optometrist and his sister has ulcerative colitis. On examination lumbar flexion is reduced with a modified Schober measurement of 3.5 cm and chest expansion is 4 cm, with no neurological deficit and negative straight leg raise. Anteroposterior pelvis and lumbar spine radiographs are reported as normal with no sacroiliac erosion or sclerosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Modified Schober 3.5 cm, chest expansion 4 cm, tenderness over both sacroiliac joints, no neurological deficit, negative straight leg raise
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5); erythrocyte sedimentation rate 28 mm/h (less than 15); pelvis and lumbar spine radiographs reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Request human leucocyte antigen B27 testing and manage on that result
Repeat the pelvic radiographs in 12 months to look for interval change
Request magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints with a rheumatology referral
Request computed tomography of the lumbar spine to assess the facet joints
Refer for a structured physiotherapy program without further imaging

subtopic_detail: Separating true iron overload from a raised ferritin caused by inflammation or metabolic disease
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 45-year-old man of northern European ancestry who came in about tiredness and stiff painful hands. He has had a raised ferritin noted twice over the past year.

He has a body mass index of 32 kg per square metre, treated hypertension and impaired fasting glucose, so the previous doctor attributed the ferritin to fatty liver. He drinks four standard drinks on a Friday night and none otherwise. His father died at 58 of liver disease that the family attributed to drinking. On examination he has tenderness and bony swelling of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands, no jaundice or spider naevi, and a liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74, blood pressure 138/84, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Bony swelling and tenderness of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally, liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin, no jaundice, ascites or spider naevi
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 1450 mcg/L (30-300); transferrin saturation 68 per cent (15-45); alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 45); C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5); glycated haemoglobin 45 mmol/mol (less than 48)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Attribute the ferritin to fatty liver and repeat the iron studies in six months
Begin weekly venesection now and monitor the ferritin every four weeks
Arrange liver biopsy to quantify hepatic iron and assess the degree of fibrosis
Advise complete alcohol abstinence and recheck the liver enzymes in three months
Request HFE genotyping and assess the liver for fibrosis non invasively

subtopic_detail: Who should be screened for intracranial aneurysm in polycystic kidney disease
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 38-year-old woman with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease diagnosed at 30. Her blood pressure is well controlled on an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor and her estimated glomerular filtration rate has been stable.

She has no headache today and no neurological symptoms. She has come because her mother, who had the same kidney disease, died at 52 of a bleed on the brain, and her maternal uncle had a brain aneurysm clipped in his forties. She works as a school teacher, has never smoked, and asks you directly whether she should be having a scan of her head. Her neurological examination and fundoscopy are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70, blood pressure 124/76, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, no papilloedema, ballotable kidneys bilaterally, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90); estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL/min/1.73m2; urine protein creatinine ratio 8 mg/mmol (less than 15)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Screening is not indicated because she has no neurological symptoms today
Arrange magnetic resonance angiography of the cerebral circulation now
Arrange computed tomography angiography and repeat it every year thereafter
Screening should be offered to every patient with this kidney disease routinely
Good blood pressure control removes the need for any imaging of her head

subtopic_detail: Sequencing the biochemical workup when growth hormone excess is suspected
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 46-year-old man who has come about numb hands that wake him at night. Over the past three years he has gone up two shoe sizes and has had his wedding ring cut off and enlarged twice.

His wife says he sweats through his shirt at rest and that his snoring has become much worse. He was diagnosed with hypertension last year and with impaired glucose tolerance six months ago. On examination his hands are broad with doughy soft tissue, Tinel sign is positive at both wrists, his brow and jaw are prominent, and there is a wide gap between his lower incisors. Visual field testing to confrontation is normal. He has brought photographs from a decade ago that show a strikingly different face.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 148/92, respiratory rate 15, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Broad doughy hands, prominent supraorbital ridge and mandible, interdental separation, bilateral positive Tinel sign, normal confrontation visual fields
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.6 mmol/L (3.0-5.4); glycated haemoglobin 47 mmol/mol (less than 48); calcium and phosphate within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: Measure serum insulin like growth factor 1 with an age matched reference range
Measure a random serum growth hormone level in the morning while fasting
Request magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary with gadolinium contrast
Arrange an oral glucose tolerance test with paired growth hormone sampling
Arrange overnight polysomnography to investigate his worsening snoring first

subtopic_detail: Drug treatment that must accompany resuscitation in bleeding from oesophageal varices
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department. A 54-year-old man with cirrhosis from hepatitis C has vomited a bowl of fresh blood twice in the past hour and passed a black tarry stool.

He has known oesophageal varices seen at endoscopy last year and takes propranolol. He is drowsy but rousable, with spider naevi, palmar erythema and shifting dullness. Two large bore cannulas are in, blood has gone for crossmatch, and a fluid bolus is running. The gastroenterologist has been called and says she can bring him to the endoscopy suite within the hour. His haemoglobin is 78 g/L and his international normalised ratio is 1.6.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, spider naevi, palmar erythema, shifting dullness, no asterixis, melaena on rectal examination
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L (130-180); platelets 68 x10^9/L (150-400); international normalised ratio 1.6; bilirubin 46 micromol/L (less than 20); albumin 28 g/L (35-50); creatinine 108 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: In addition to ongoing resuscitation, what is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Transfuse red cells to a target haemoglobin above 100 g/L before endoscopy
Give fresh frozen plasma to correct the international normalised ratio to below 1.5
Insert a balloon tamponade tube now to control bleeding before endoscopy
Start terlipressin and intravenous ceftriaxone before he goes for endoscopy
Start a high dose proton pump inhibitor infusion as the definitive drug treatment

subtopic_detail: Visible haematuria coinciding with an upper respiratory infection in a young adult
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24-year-old man whose urine turned the colour of cola yesterday. He had a sore throat the day before it started and has had two similar episodes in the past three years, each settling within a few days.

He has no dysuria, no flank pain, no rash and no joint symptoms, and he has never smoked. He takes no medication and there is no family history of kidney disease or deafness. His blood pressure today is 142 over 90 on two readings, and he has no oedema. His throat is mildly injected with no exudate and no cervical lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74, blood pressure 142/90, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: No rash, no peripheral oedema, no joint swelling, mildly injected pharynx without exudate
data_table.Investigations: Urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts; urine protein creatinine ratio 82 mg/mmol (less than 15); creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110); complement C3 and C4 within normal limits; antistreptolysin O titre not raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Treat the throat with oral phenoxymethylpenicillin and repeat the urine later
Refer to nephrology for renal biopsy and formal glomerular assessment
Arrange computed tomography urography and cystoscopy to exclude a tumour
Reassure him that this follows infection and recheck the urine in six weeks
Start perindopril for the blood pressure and review the urine in three months

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic sparing management of uncomplicated acute diverticulitis
stem:
You are the emergency department resident seeing a 58-year-old woman with two days of steady left iliac fossa pain and a change to looser stool. She has no vomiting and is eating and drinking normally.

She has no diabetes, takes no immunosuppressant or corticosteroid, and has had one similar episode four years ago that settled. On examination her abdomen is soft with localised tenderness in the left iliac fossa, no guarding, no rebound and no palpable mass. Computed tomography of the abdomen reports sigmoid diverticula with pericolic fat stranding and mural thickening, with no abscess, no free gas and no free fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 128/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.5
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with localised left iliac fossa tenderness, no guarding or rebound, no mass, bowel sounds present
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 32 mg/L (less than 5); computed tomography shows uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis with no abscess, perforation or obstruction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge with analgesia, oral fluids and review in 48 to 72 hours
Prescribe oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for five days and review her then
Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole with bowel rest
Arrange colonoscopy during this admission to inspect the sigmoid segment
Refer for elective sigmoid colectomy after this second documented episode

subtopic_detail: Antiviral window and adjunctive decisions in acute herpes zoster
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68-year-old man who noticed a painful band of blisters across the right side of his back and flank yesterday morning. A deep burning pain in the same area preceded the rash by three days and is now severe enough to keep him awake.

He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, and he takes no immunosuppressant. On examination there are grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a single band on the right, extending from the spine to the midline of the abdomen and stopping abruptly at the midline. No lesions are present elsewhere, his face and eyes are unaffected, and he is systemically well with clear lungs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 138/82, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Grouped vesicles on erythematous base in a single unilateral band stopping at the midline, no facial or ocular involvement, no disseminated lesions
data_table.Investigations: Random glucose 8.4 mmol/L (3.0-7.7); glycated haemoglobin 52 mmol/mol (less than 48)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply topical aciclovir cream five times daily with simple oral analgesia
Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days to cover secondary bacterial infection
Give oral prednisolone for seven days alongside regular simple analgesia
Start oral valaciclovir for seven days with regular analgesia and review
Withhold antiviral treatment because he is immunocompetent and review him

subtopic_detail: Making a positive diagnosis of a functional bowel disorder rather than a diagnosis of exclusion
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 27-year-old woman with eight months of cramping lower abdominal pain that eases after she opens her bowels. Her stools alternate between loose and pellet like, and the pain is worse in the week before her period.

She has no weight loss, no rectal bleeding, and she never wakes at night with pain or to open her bowels. She has no family history of bowel cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. Her abdomen is soft with mild tenderness in the left iliac fossa and no mass, and rectal examination is normal. She has been avoiding whole food groups on the advice of an online quiz and is frightened that she has something serious.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with mild left iliac fossa tenderness, no mass or organomegaly, normal rectal examination, body mass index 22 kg per square metre
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 134 g/L (115-165); C-reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5); ferritin 52 mcg/L (30-200); thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for colonoscopy to exclude inflammatory bowel disease and cancer
Prescribe a course of rifaximin for probable small intestinal overgrowth
Start a proton pump inhibitor and reassess her symptoms in eight weeks
Request faecal occult blood testing and repeat it again in twelve months
Check coeliac serology, then give a positive diagnosis and dietary advice

subtopic_detail: Anticipating and treating constipation caused by opioid analgesia
stem:
You are the doctor on a community palliative care visit to a 72-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer in bone. His pain is well controlled on modified release morphine 30 mg twice daily, started three weeks ago, with immediate release morphine used twice a week.

He has not opened his bowels for five days and is straining without result. He feels bloated and has lost his appetite but is not vomiting. He drinks about a litre of fluid a day and is mostly in a chair. His abdomen is soft and distended with palpable faecal loading in the left colon and active bowel sounds, and rectal examination shows a rectum loaded with soft stool and no impaction or obstruction. He was not given any aperient when the morphine was started.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 80, blood pressure 122/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Soft distended abdomen with left sided faecal loading, active bowel sounds, rectum loaded with soft stool, no impaction, anal tone normal
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.20-2.60); potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); thyroid stimulating hormone 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start a bulk forming fibre supplement and encourage a high fibre diet
Prescribe docusate alone twice daily and review his bowels in one week
Start a regular osmotic plus stimulant laxative and titrate to response
Give subcutaneous methylnaltrexone now and continue it every second day
Reduce the morphine dose by half and accept a higher level of background pain

subtopic_detail: Treating an acute crystal arthritis when renal function and anticoagulation restrict the usual options
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68-year-old man who woke at 3 am with an exquisitely painful right great toe. He cannot bear the weight of a bed sheet on it and has had two similar attacks in the past two years.

He has atrial fibrillation and takes warfarin with an international normalised ratio of 2.6 last week, and he takes furosemide for heart failure. On examination the first metatarsophalangeal joint is red, hot and swollen with the skin shiny over it, and there is a firm painless nodule on the right helix. He is afebrile and there is no break in the skin, no ascending erythema and no lymphangitis. His serum urate is 0.42 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 134/80, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Red hot swollen right first metatarsophalangeal joint with shiny overlying skin, firm nodule on the right helix, no skin breach or ascending erythema
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110); estimated glomerular filtration rate 35 mL/min/1.73m2; urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.15-0.45); C-reactive protein 48 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for this attack?

options.text: Prescribe indometacin 25 mg three times daily for five days with a proton pump inhibitor
Prescribe oral prednisolone 30 mg daily for five days and review him after that
Prescribe colchicine 1 mg then 0.5 mg three times daily until symptoms settle
Start allopurinol 300 mg daily today to bring the serum urate level down quickly
Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin after taking blood cultures from both arms

subtopic_detail: Choosing the biopsy site in suspected autoimmune blistering disease
stem:
