You are the general medicine registrar asked to see a 76-year-old woman with a six week history of intensely itchy red plaques on her trunk and limbs, which for the past week have developed blisters.

The blisters are tense and up to 3 cm across, some are blood stained, and they sit on inflamed skin in the flexures, the inner thighs and the lower abdomen. Rubbing adjacent normal looking skin does not produce a new blister. Her mouth, eyes and genital mucosa are unaffected and she is eating normally. She takes perindopril and metformin, both for over a decade, and started no new drug this year. She is systemically well.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Tense bullae up to 3 cm on urticarial plaques over flexures, inner thighs and lower abdomen, negative Nikolsky sign, no oral or conjunctival lesions
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5); white cell count 9.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); creatinine 82 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic step?

options.text: Biopsy a fresh blister edge for histology and adjacent skin for immunofluorescence
Send a bacterial swab from a deroofed blister and start oral flucloxacillin
Take the immunofluorescence sample from the centre of the largest blister roof
Start oral prednisolone 50 mg daily now and biopsy only if she fails to respond
Arrange patch testing to identify a contact allergen responsible for the eruption

subtopic_detail: Severe cutaneous adverse reaction with organ involvement several weeks after a new drug
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department seeing a 52-year-old man with fever and a rash. He started allopurinol five weeks ago after two attacks of gout and takes no other new medication.

The rash began on his trunk four days ago and has spread to cover most of his body. He describes his face as puffy and his wife says his eyelids are swollen. On examination there is a confluent morbilliform eruption covering an estimated 70 per cent of his body surface, marked facial oedema, and tender lymph nodes in both axillae and the neck. There is no mucosal ulceration, no skin detachment and no target lesions, and rubbing the skin does not shear the epidermis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104, blood pressure 124/76, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.7
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform eruption over about 70 per cent body surface area, facial oedema, cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, no mucosal involvement, negative Nikolsky sign
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 2.1 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5); white cell count 14.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); alanine aminotransferase 268 U/L (less than 35); creatinine 132 micromol/L (60-110); atypical lymphocytes present on film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue the allopurinol and give a non sedating oral antihistamine daily
Transfer him urgently to a burns unit for management of epidermal detachment
Start broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics for presumed bacterial sepsis
Stop the allopurinol, admit him, and start systemic corticosteroid therapy
Give intravenous immunoglobulin as the first line treatment for the reaction

subtopic_detail: Separating hungry bone syndrome from surgical hypoparathyroidism after parathyroidectomy
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the surgical ward on the second day after a 58-year-old man had a total parathyroidectomy for tertiary hyperparathyroidism on long term haemodialysis. He tells you his lips and fingertips have been tingling since the morning and that his hands keep cramping when he holds his cup.

He is alert and comfortable at rest. Tapping over the facial nerve produces twitching of the ipsilateral upper lip. His dialysis access is functioning and his last session was yesterday. He is taking no calcium or vitamin D supplement.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 1.68 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), phosphate 0.54 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), alkaline phosphatase 512 U/L (30-110), magnesium 0.86 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 490 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral colecalciferol 1000 units daily and repeat the calcium
Commence cinacalcet and repeat the parathyroid hormone in 24 hours
Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 30 minutes
Give intravenous calcium gluconate with oral calcitriol and calcium
Arrange urgent neck imaging and withhold calcium until it is done

subtopic_detail: Post infectious polyarthritis in regional Australia and the decision not to start a disease modifying drug
stem:
You are the general practice registrar in a regional New South Wales town seeing a 34-year-old woman who has had sore, puffy wrists, ankles and knuckles for three weeks. She works on a river property and had a blotchy rash over her trunk and arms in the first week that faded on its own. She is exhausted by mid afternoon.

Her joints are stiff for about 40 minutes each morning. There is soft tissue swelling and tenderness of both wrists and the metacarpophalangeal joints without deformity, and no nail or skin changes. She takes no regular medication and has never had joint symptoms before.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 24 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 38 mm/h (less than 20), rheumatoid factor negative, anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody negative, antinuclear antibody negative, full blood count and creatinine within normal limits
data_table.Serology: Ross River virus IgM positive and IgG positive, Barmah Forest virus IgM negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily and review in eight weeks
Advise simple analgesia and graded activity with review in four weeks
Start methotrexate 10 mg weekly with folic acid supplementation
Start doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for two weeks and review
Repeat the viral serology in two weeks before any treatment

subtopic_detail: Choosing antidote over standard hyperkalaemia therapy in cardiac glycoside poisoning
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 78-year-old woman brought in by her daughter, who says her mother has been off her food for four days, has vomited several times, and keeps saying that everything in the room looks like it has a yellow tinge. She takes digoxin for atrial fibrillation and was started on a fluid tablet by her general practitioner a fortnight ago.

She is drowsy but rousable and orientated to person only. Her chest is clear and she is not oedematous. The cardiac monitor shows a regular narrow complex rhythm at 38 beats per minute.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 38 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 186 micromol/L (45-90), urea 18.4 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), serum digoxin 4.1 micrograms/L (0.5-2.0), corrected calcium and magnesium within normal limits
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Regularised narrow complex bradycardia with downsloping ST depression in the lateral leads

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Give digoxin specific antibody fragments intravenously now
Give intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 per cent
Give intravenous insulin with dextrose and repeat the potassium
Insert a temporary transvenous pacing wire for the bradycardia
Arrange urgent haemodialysis to clear digoxin and potassium

subtopic_detail: Recognising overwhelming infection risk in asplenia after an animal bite
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 46-year-old man who had a splenectomy six years ago after a motorcycle crash. Two days ago the family dog caught his left hand while they were playing and left two small punctures over the thenar eminence. He tells you he shook and could not get warm through the night.

He has not filled a prescription for preventive antibiotics since the year of his operation. The puncture wounds are clean with only 5 mm of surrounding redness and no discharge or fluctuance. There are scattered non blanching purple spots over both shins that were not there yesterday.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 94/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 22.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), platelets 68 x10^9/L (150-400), lactate 3.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0), creatinine 132 micromol/L (60-110), international normalised ratio 1.6
data_table.Examination: Two puncture wounds over the left thenar eminence with 5 mm of surrounding erythema, purpuric lesions on both shins

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Take a wound swab and withhold antibiotics until cultures return
Give oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and review in 24 hours
Give intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam after blood cultures
Give intravenous flucloxacillin and arrange surgical debridement
Give intravenous vancomycin with gentamicin and admit for observation

subtopic_detail: Recognising monogenic hypercholesterolaemia and acting on the family as well as the patient
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 32-year-old accountant who had a lipid profile done for a life insurance application. He is well, does not smoke, and runs three times a week. His father had a heart attack at 44 years of age and his older sister has been told she has high cholesterol.

His body mass index is 23 kg per square metre. There is a firm nodular thickening of both Achilles tendons and a pale ring at the corneal margin of each eye. Thyroid function, liver function, fasting glucose and urine albumin to creatinine ratio are all within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Total cholesterol 9.4 mmol/L (less than 5.5), low density lipoprotein cholesterol 6.9 mmol/L (less than 3.4), high density lipoprotein cholesterol 1.3 mmol/L (greater than 1.0), triglycerides 1.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0)
data_table.Examination: Bilateral Achilles tendon thickening, bilateral corneal arcus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange genetic testing before starting any lipid lowering therapy
Start ezetimibe 10 mg daily and repeat the lipid profile in three months
Start rosuvastatin 5 mg daily and refer for coronary calcium scoring
Advise a six month trial of dietary change and reassess the lipids
Start atorvastatin 40 mg daily and offer his relatives lipid testing

subtopic_detail: Separating destructive from iodine loaded thyrotoxicosis during amiodarone therapy
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 64-year-old man who has taken amiodarone 200 mg daily for 18 months for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Over the past two months he has lost 6 kg without trying, his hands shake when he holds the newspaper, and he feels his heart racing in the evenings.

He has no eye discomfort, no lid retraction and no proptosis. His thyroid is not enlarged and there is no bruit over it. He has never had thyroid disease and there is none in his family.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute and irregular, blood pressure 142/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 44 pmol/L (9-25), free triiodothyronine 9.2 pmol/L (3.5-6.5), thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibody negative
data_table.Imaging: Thyroid ultrasound shows a normal sized gland with no nodules and absent flow on colour Doppler

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence carbimazole 30 mg daily and repeat thyroid function tests
Commence prednisolone 40 mg daily and repeat thyroid function tests
Commence potassium perchlorate with carbimazole and monitor weekly
Refer for radioactive iodine ablation once amiodarone is stopped
Stop amiodarone alone and repeat thyroid function tests in six weeks

subtopic_detail: Managing drug induced hyponatraemia where removing the cause outranks fluid restriction
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 76-year-old woman whose daughter says she has been sleepy and wobbly on her feet for the past week and is not her usual self. Her blood pressure tablet was changed to hydrochlorothiazide six weeks ago and nothing else has altered.

She is orientated to place and person but slow to answer. Her mucous membranes are moist, her jugular venous pressure is visible 2 cm above the sternal angle and there is no peripheral oedema or postural drop. She has not vomited, has had no diarrhoea and drinks about six cups of tea a day.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 134/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 121 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), serum osmolality 252 mmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 430 mmol/kg, urine sodium 58 mmol/L, creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Additional tests: Thyroid stimulating hormone and 9 am cortisol within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease hydrochlorothiazide and recheck the serum sodium in 24 hours
Continue hydrochlorothiazide and restrict fluid to 1000 mL daily
Commence tolvaptan and continue the current antihypertensive drugs
Infuse hypertonic 3 per cent sodium chloride 100 mL over 10 minutes
Infuse 1 litre of 0.9 per cent sodium chloride over four hours

subtopic_detail: Perioperative handling of a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor before elective surgery
stem:
You are the medical officer running the preadmission clinic and reviewing a 58-year-old man booked for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy in five days. He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin 1 g twice daily and empagliflozin 25 mg daily, and his diabetes has been stable for two years.

He eats normally, has never had a hospital admission for his diabetes and has no symptoms of infection. He asks you which of his tablets he should keep taking in the days before the operation.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 7.2 per cent (53 mmol/mol), estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 90 mL/min/1.73m2, sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), bicarbonate 25 mmol/L (22-32)
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 25 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily

lead_in: What advice should you give about the empagliflozin?

options.text: Continue empagliflozin and omit only the dose on the day of surgery
Continue empagliflozin and measure blood ketones on the morning of surgery
Withhold empagliflozin for seven days and restart it after discharge
Withhold empagliflozin for the two days before surgery and on the day
Replace empagliflozin with gliclazide for the week before the surgery

subtopic_detail: Reading dorsal column signs in a patient whose neuropathy has an assumed cause
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who has taken metformin 1 g twice daily for nine years. He says his feet have felt numb for about six months and that he now has to hold the wall when he walks to the bathroom in the dark.

His ankle reflexes are absent and vibration sense is reduced to the knees, and he sways and steps sideways when he closes his eyes with his feet together. His tongue is smooth and beefy. He takes no other regular medication, drinks two standard drinks a week and eats meat most days.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 116 g/L (130-180), mean cell volume 104 fL (80-100), vitamin B12 128 pmol/L (150-700), red cell folate within normal limits, glycated haemoglobin 6.9 per cent (52 mmol/mol)
data_table.Additional tests: Thyroid stimulating hormone and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Attribute the signs to diabetic neuropathy and commence pregabalin
Commence oral folic acid 5 mg daily and repeat the blood film
Commence intramuscular hydroxocobalamin and review the metformin
Cease metformin and recheck the vitamin B12 level in three months
Refer for nerve conduction studies before commencing any treatment

subtopic_detail: Preventing rebound vertebral fracture when a monoclonal antibody for osteoporosis is stopped
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68-year-old woman who has had six monthly denosumab injections for five years after a wrist fracture. She is moving to a rural property with no local pathology service, dislikes injections and tells you she would like to stop treatment altogether.

She has had no further fractures and takes colecalciferol 1000 units daily with a dairy rich diet. Her most recent bone densitometry shows a femoral neck T score of minus 1.9, improved from minus 2.9 at the start of treatment. Renal function and corrected calcium are within normal limits and she has had no dental problems.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (greater than 50), estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 60 mL/min/1.73m2
data_table.Bone densitometry: Femoral neck T score minus 1.9, lumbar spine T score minus 1.7

lead_in: What should you recommend?

options.text: Stop denosumab and arrange bone densitometry in twelve months
Switch to raloxifene 60 mg daily and continue calcium and vitamin D
Switch to teriparatide and review the fracture risk after two years
Stop denosumab and continue only calcium and colecalciferol daily
Give zoledronic acid within six months of the last denosumab dose

subtopic_detail: Choosing between live and recombinant zoster vaccine in a patient on immunosuppression
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis in remission on methotrexate 20 mg weekly by subcutaneous injection and prednisolone 5 mg daily. Her neighbour has just had a painful rash across one side of the chest and she asks whether she can be protected against the same thing.

She has never had shingles and has no history of chickenpox vaccination. She has no active infection, her arthritis has been quiet for two years and she has no plans to change her treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and creatinine within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Methotrexate 20 mg weekly subcutaneously, folic acid 5 mg weekly, prednisolone 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to shingles prevention?

options.text: Give the live attenuated zoster vaccine at today's consultation
Give the recombinant zoster vaccine as two doses two months apart
Give the live attenuated vaccine four weeks after stopping methotrexate
Advise that no zoster vaccine can be given while she is immunosuppressed
Prescribe valaciclovir 500 mg daily as long term shingles prophylaxis

subtopic_detail: Applying direct oral anticoagulant dose reduction criteria in a small older patient
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing an 84-year-old woman admitted with a chest infection in whom an irregularly irregular pulse was noted. Her electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation at 88 beats per minute with no acute ischaemic change, which she had not noticed herself.

She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes and takes aspirin 100 mg daily, which was started years ago after a fall. She has had no bleeding and no falls in the past year, and she manages her own medicines with a dose administration aid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute and irregular, blood pressure 138/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 121 micromol/L (45-90), calculated creatinine clearance 28 mL/min, haemoglobin 124 g/L (120-160), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antithrombotic regimen?

options.text: Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily with six monthly renal function testing
Apixaban 5 mg twice daily with six monthly renal function testing
Rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily with six monthly renal function testing
Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily with six monthly renal function testing
Aspirin 100 mg daily with six monthly cardiovascular risk assessment

subtopic_detail: Acting on out of office blood pressure when clinic readings disagree
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 47-year-old teacher whose blood pressure has been recorded above target at three separate visits over the past two months. He feels well, exercises twice a week, drinks four standard drinks a week and has never smoked.

He tells you he gets tense in medical rooms and that a machine at the pharmacy gave him much lower numbers. He has no headaches, no snoring, no palpitations and no family history of early cardiovascular disease. His fundi show no arteriolar narrowing or haemorrhage.

data_table.Vital signs: Clinic blood pressure readings of 156/96, 152/94 and 158/98 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 92 mL/min/1.73m2, urine albumin to creatinine ratio 1.4 mg/mmol (less than 2.5), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), fasting lipids and glucose within normal limits
data_table.Ambulatory monitoring: Daytime average 128/78 mmHg, night time average 110/66 mmHg, 24 hour average 124/74 mmHg
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm with no left ventricular hypertrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start perindopril 5 mg daily and review the blood pressure in six weeks
Start amlodipine 5 mg daily and review the blood pressure in six weeks
Refer for investigation of a secondary cause of the raised readings
Give lifestyle advice and repeat ambulatory monitoring in twelve months
Treat according to the clinic readings and add a second agent if needed

subtopic_detail: Recognising dopaminergic augmentation rather than disease progression in restless legs syndrome
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 62-year-old man who has taken pramipexole for restless legs syndrome for three years. The dose has been increased twice because his symptoms kept breaking through, and each increase helped for a few months.

He now says the crawling feeling starts in the middle of the afternoon rather than at bedtime, and that in the past six months it has begun to affect his arms as well as his legs. He has no numbness, his ankle reflexes are present and his pedal pulses are normal. He takes no antihistamine, antidepressant or antiemetic.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 190 micrograms/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 32 per cent (15-45), creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate within normal limits, haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180)
data_table.Medications: Pramipexole 0.75 mg at night, increased from 0.25 mg over three years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase pramipexole and add a bedtime dose to cover the afternoon
Add oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily and reassess in three months
Taper and cease pramipexole and commence gabapentin at night
Change to a rotigotine patch and continue the current evening dose
Add clonazepam 0.5 mg at night and continue pramipexole unchanged

subtopic_detail: Treating spontaneous bacterial peritonitis on the ascitic neutrophil count with albumin cover
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 61-year-old man with alcohol related cirrhosis. His partner says his tummy has been swelling over the past fortnight and that he has been muddled since yesterday, sleeping through the day and awake at night.

He stopped drinking alcohol six weeks ago and has never had a gastrointestinal bleed. He takes spironolactone and furosemide. On examination he has shifting dullness and mild generalised abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound. You perform a diagnostic paracentesis on the ward before prescribing anything.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Ascitic fluid: Polymorphonuclear cell count 480 x10^6/L, total protein 9 g/L, Gram stain shows no organisms
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110), bilirubin 46 micromol/L (2-24), international normalised ratio 1.6 (0.8-1.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Large volume paracentesis with albumin cover and no antibiotic therapy
Intravenous cefotaxime together with an intravenous albumin infusion
Oral norfloxacin alone with a repeat diagnostic paracentesis at 48 hours
Await the ascitic culture result before committing to any antibiotic
Intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam and an urgent surgical review

subtopic_detail: Recognising heparin induced thrombocytopenia and choosing a non heparin anticoagulant rather than warfarin or platelets
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to review a 68-year-old woman on the orthopaedic ward on the sixth day after an elective total knee replacement. She has been on prophylactic enoxaparin since surgery.

The nurse reports that her left calf has become swollen and tender overnight, and the morning bloods show a fall in platelets. She has had no bleeding, no bruising and no transfusion. Her operative leg is the right one, and the swelling is on the left. A compression ultrasound of the left leg shows an occlusive popliteal vein thrombus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 68 x10^9/L (150-400), preoperative platelets 244 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 106 g/L (115-165), fibrinogen 4.2 g/L (2.0-4.0), international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.8-1.2)
data_table.Medications: Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily, paracetamol, oxycodone as required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue enoxaparin and start intravenous immunoglobulin therapy
Cease enoxaparin and start intravenous unfractionated heparin
Cease enoxaparin and start a therapeutic dose of danaparoid
Cease enoxaparin and start warfarin with a five day overlap
Continue enoxaparin and transfuse a pooled platelet concentrate

subtopic_detail: Vasoactive drug plus antibiotic prophylaxis before endoscopy in suspected variceal haemorrhage
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department seeing a 64-year-old man with hepatitis C related cirrhosis who has vomited what his wife describes as a bowl of dark red blood twice in the past hour.

He is drowsy but rousable and orientated. He has spider naevi and moderate ascites. Two large bore cannulas are in and he has received one litre of compound sodium lactate. The gastroenterology team can bring him to endoscopy in about three hours once the theatre list is cleared.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 84 g/L (130-180), platelets 74 x10^9/L (150-400), international normalised ratio 1.8 (0.8-1.2), creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), bilirubin 52 micromol/L (2-24)

lead_in: Which combination is the most appropriate to start now?

options.text: Intravenous terlipressin together with a non selective beta blocker
Intravenous tranexamic acid together with fresh frozen plasma
Intravenous pantoprazole together with red cell transfusion to 100 g/L
Intravenous terlipressin together with intravenous ceftriaxone
Intravenous vitamin K together with intravenous ceftriaxone therapy

subtopic_detail: Risk stratifying a monoclonal gammopathy and choosing modern imaging over a plain radiograph skeletal survey
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 72-year-old man in clinic who was investigated by his general practitioner for six months of tiredness. Serum electrophoresis found an IgG kappa paraprotein.

He has no bone pain, no infections and no weight loss, and he walks his dog daily without difficulty. Examination is unremarkable. His serum free light chain ratio is abnormal and the paraprotein concentration is above 15 g/L, while his calcium, creatinine and haemoglobin are all within the reference range.

data_table.Investigations: IgG kappa paraprotein 22 g/L, serum free light chain kappa to lambda ratio 9.4 (0.26-1.65), haemoglobin 132 g/L (130-180), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110), albumin 39 g/L (35-50)
data_table.Examination: No bone tenderness, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a plain radiograph skeletal survey and review in one month
Commence lenalidomide with dexamethasone after a renal ultrasound
Repeat the paraprotein and full blood count again in six months
Refer for a bone marrow biopsy and whole body low dose imaging
Start a bisphosphonate and repeat the paraprotein in three months

subtopic_detail: Recognising malignant spinal cord compression and imaging the whole spine rather than the painful level
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 58-year-old woman in the emergency department. She finished treatment for breast cancer four years ago and has had two weeks of mid back pain that is worse when she lies flat and wakes her in the early hours.

Over the past three days her legs have felt heavy climbing the stairs and she has had to pull herself up on the rail. She has not noticed any change in bladder or bowel control. Knee and ankle reflexes are brisk with sustained ankle clonus on the right, and there is a band of reduced pinprick sensation below the level of the umbilicus.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Power 4 out of 5 in hip flexion bilaterally, brisk lower limb reflexes with right sided ankle clonus, sensory level at the umbilicus, normal anal tone
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.42 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), alkaline phosphatase 168 U/L (30-110), haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange a thoracic spine radiograph and review the result tomorrow
Give dexamethasone and arrange a bone scan within the next 48 hours
Arrange lumbar puncture with cytology and start regular oral opioids
Refer for outpatient physiotherapy and review in the fracture clinic
Give dexamethasone and arrange whole spine magnetic resonance imaging

subtopic_detail: Volume expansion with albumin before committing to a diagnosis of hepatorenal syndrome
stem:
You are the medical registrar looking after a 55-year-old woman with alcohol related cirrhosis and diuretic responsive ascites, admitted five days ago for symptom control. Her creatinine has climbed steadily since admission.

She has passed less urine than usual but has no urinary symptoms and no rash. Her spironolactone and furosemide were withheld 48 hours ago and she has had no contrast, no non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs and no aminoglycosides. A diagnostic paracentesis on admission showed a polymorphonuclear count of 60 x10^6/L. Renal tract ultrasound shows normal sized unobstructed kidneys.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 94/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 186 micromol/L (45-90), admission creatinine 88 micromol/L, sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), bilirubin 78 micromol/L (2-24), international normalised ratio 1.9 (0.8-1.2)
data_table.Urine: Urinary sodium 8 mmol/L, no protein on dipstick, microscopy shows no casts and no red cells

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Give intravenous albumin daily for two days with diuretics withheld
Start terlipressin with noradrenaline in the intensive care unit
Give a two litre bolus of 0.9 per cent sodium chloride over four hours
Start low dose dopamine and repeat the creatinine in 24 hours
Arrange urgent renal biopsy before any volume expansion is given

subtopic_detail: Choosing manometry after a normal endoscopy in progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar seeing a 42-year-old man in clinic. For eight months food has felt like it sticks behind his breastbone, and he now has the same trouble with water. He has taken to standing up and arching his back to get things down.

He wakes at night coughing and finds bits of the previous evening's meal on the pillow, still tasting of the meal rather than sour. He has lost 6 kg. A gastroscopy last week showed retained saliva and food residue in the oesophagus with normal mucosa, and the endoscope passed into the stomach with slight resistance at the junction. Biopsies from the mid and distal oesophagus showed no eosinophils and no inflammation.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180), albumin 38 g/L (35-50), C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange a therapeutic trial of high dose proton pump inhibitor
Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry to define motility
Arrange a barium swallow with a timed five minute upright film
Arrange 24 hour ambulatory oesophageal pH and impedance monitoring
Arrange computed tomography of the chest and upper abdomen

subtopic_detail: Malignancy screening at diagnosis of an inflammatory myopathy with characteristic skin disease
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 54-year-old woman referred with three months of difficulty lifting her arms above her head to hang out washing and trouble rising from a low chair without pushing up on her thighs.

She has noticed a purple discolouration around both eyelids that she first blamed on a new eye cream, and scaly raised patches over the backs of her knuckles. There is no ptosis, no double vision and no fatigability on sustained upgaze. Muscle power is 3 out of 5 at the shoulder and hip girdles with normal distal power, and reflexes are preserved throughout. She takes no statin and no other regular medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 1840 U/L (30-150), alanine aminotransferase 84 U/L (5-35), C reactive protein 9 mg/L (less than 5), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), antinuclear antibody positive at 1 in 320

lead_in: In addition to starting oral prednisolone, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of both thighs with muscle biopsy
Electromyography of the proximal limbs with nerve conduction study
Serum thyroid stimulating hormone with a vitamin D concentration
Skin biopsy of the knuckle plaques with direct immunofluorescence
Computed tomography of chest, abdomen and pelvis with mammography

subtopic_detail: Securing histology before treatment in superior vena caval obstruction without airway compromise
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 66-year-old man who has smoked 30 cigarettes a day since his twenties. For three weeks his face has felt puffy, worst when he first wakes, and his shirt collar no longer does up.

He has no stridor, speaks in full sentences and lies flat without distress. There are distended veins across the upper chest and neck that do not pulsate, and his face is plethoric. He has had no previous cancer and no biopsy of any kind. A computed tomography scan shows a right hilar mass compressing the superior vena cava with collateral filling, mediastinal nodes, and no cerebral oedema.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-180), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), lactate dehydrogenase 310 U/L (120-250)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent biopsy of the mediastinal mass for tissue diagnosis
Start high dose dexamethasone and arrange biopsy in one week
Refer for endovascular stenting of the superior vena cava today
Start empirical mediastinal radiotherapy while awaiting the histology
Commence therapeutic enoxaparin and repeat imaging in seven days

subtopic_detail: Separating cold agglutinin disease from warm autoimmune haemolysis on the direct antiglobulin pattern
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 74-year-old woman with six weeks of increasing tiredness. She tells you her fingers and the tip of her nose go a dusky blue and ache when she walks to the shops on a cold morning, and that the colour settles once she is back inside.

After one such walk last week she passed urine the colour of cola for a day. She has no joint pain, no rash and no recent infection. There is mild scleral icterus and no splenomegaly. The laboratory telephones to say the sample needed warming before the full blood count would run because the cells were clumping in the analyser.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 82 g/L (115-165), reticulocytes 145 x10^9/L (20-100), bilirubin 46 micromol/L (2-24), lactate dehydrogenase 480 U/L (120-250), haptoglobin less than 0.1 g/L (0.3-2.0)
data_table.Immunohaematology: Direct antiglobulin test positive for complement C3d, negative for immunoglobulin G

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: High dose prednisolone with a proton pump inhibitor and referral
Elective splenectomy with pre operative vaccination and referral
Intravenous immunoglobulin over two days with haematology referral
Therapeutic plasma exchange over five days with haematology referral
Thermal protection with warmed transfusion and haematology referral

subtopic_detail: Treating exocrine pancreatic insufficiency once faecal elastase and calcification confirm chronic pancreatitis
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man in clinic. He drank heavily for two decades and has been abstinent for two years, and he has had several admissions with upper abdominal pain in that time.

Over the past nine months his motions have become pale and bulky, float in the bowl and are hard to flush away, and he has lost 8 kg without trying. He has no diarrhoea in the sense of urgency or frequency, and no blood. His coeliac serology is negative with a normal total immunoglobulin A, and a computed tomography scan shows diffuse pancreatic calcification with a dilated main duct and no mass.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Faecal elastase 42 mcg/g (greater than 200), haemoglobin 126 g/L (130-180), albumin 33 g/L (35-50), glycated haemoglobin 48 mmol/mol (less than 42), international normalised ratio 1.4 (0.8-1.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start a proton pump inhibitor and arrange coeliac serology testing
Arrange endoscopic ultrasound with fine needle aspiration of the head
Start pancreatic enzyme replacement and check fat soluble vitamins
Start a low fat diet and repeat the faecal elastase in three months
Start loperamide before meals and refer to the dietitian for review

subtopic_detail: Choosing decompression over conservative therapy in median neuropathy with motor signs
stem:
You are the general medical registrar reviewing a 52-year-old cleaner in the ambulatory clinic. For nine months she has been waking two or three times a night with both hands feeling dead, and she now says the numbness in her right hand never fully goes away and she keeps dropping her keys.

Neck rotation and extension are full and pain free, and the triceps and biceps reflexes are symmetrical. On the right there is visible flattening of the muscle bulk at the base of the thumb and thumb abduction against resistance is weak. Sensation is reduced over the pulps of the right thumb, index and middle fingers but preserved over the skin of the thenar eminence itself.

data_table.Examination: Right abductor pollicis brevis power 3 out of 5, left grip and thumb abduction normal, no wasting of the first dorsal interosseous
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function within normal limits, fasting glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine
Trial a nocturnal wrist splint held in neutral for six weeks
Inject corticosteroid into the carpal tunnel under ultrasound
Refer for surgical decompression of the carpal tunnel
Prescribe a two week tapering course of oral prednisolone

subtopic_detail: Imaging choice in inflammatory back pain when plain radiographs of the sacroiliac joints are normal
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 26-year-old carpenter referred with fourteen months of low back pain. He tells you the pain wakes him in the early hours and that he has to get up and walk about, and that he feels loosest after a shift rather than after a rest day. Stiffness on waking lasts about an hour.

He had a painful red right eye treated with steroid drops last year. Lumbar flexion is reduced with a modified Schober of 3.5 cm and chest expansion is 4 cm. Plain radiographs of the sacroiliac joints reported today are normal, and straight leg raise is negative bilaterally with normal ankle and knee reflexes.

data_table.Examination: Modified Schober 3.5 cm, chest expansion 4 cm, sacroiliac joints tender to direct pressure
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 32 mm/h (1-20), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Computed tomography of the sacroiliac joints without intravenous contrast
Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints with fluid sensitive sequences
Human leucocyte antigen B27 typing on a peripheral venous blood sample
Repeat plain radiographs of the sacroiliac joints in twelve months
Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine with gadolinium contrast

subtopic_detail: Selecting the first agent to withdraw after recurrent falls in a resident on multiple medicines
stem:
You are the visiting medical officer at a residential aged care facility reviewing an 84-year-old woman after her third fall in ten weeks. Staff say she is unsteady when she gets up to the toilet before dawn and that she seems foggy until mid morning.

She has been taking nitrazepam 10 mg at night for three years, started for insomnia during a hospital admission. Lying and standing blood pressures are 138/78 mmHg and 134/76 mmHg. Her gait is wide based and slow but she has no tremor, no cogwheeling and normal ankle jerks, and the timed up and go is 21 seconds. Vitamin B12, calcium and thyroid function are within normal limits, and she has been on colecalciferol for two years.

data_table.Medications: Nitrazepam 10 mg nocte, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nocte, sertraline 50 mg daily, pantoprazole 20 mg daily, colecalciferol 1000 units daily
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 58 mL/min/1.73m2, sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), haemoglobin 126 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: Which medication change would you make first?

options.text: Halve the perindopril dose and review the blood pressure in a fortnight
Cease the atorvastatin given her age and limited life expectancy
Taper and cease the nitrazepam over eight to twelve weeks
Cease the sertraline because of the fall risk in older women
Cease the pantoprazole and review reflux symptoms after four weeks

subtopic_detail: Recognising a delayed multiorgan drug hypersensitivity and committing to systemic corticosteroid
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 58-year-old man with five days of fever and a spreading itchy red rash that began on his trunk. His wife says his face has puffed up so much that he looks like a different man.

He started allopurinol thirty four days ago after two attacks of gout and takes nothing else new. The rash is a confluent morbilliform eruption over more than 60 per cent of his body surface with marked facial oedema. There are no target lesions, no mucosal erosions and Nikolsky sign is negative. He has tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 1.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), white cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), alanine aminotransferase 340 U/L (less than 41), creatinine 142 micromol/L (60-110), blood cultures collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue allopurinol and add oral cetirizine with topical betamethasone
Cease allopurinol and observe on supportive care without systemic therapy
Cease allopurinol and commence oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg daily
Cease allopurinol and commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kg
Commence intravenous flucloxacillin and await the blood culture result

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a modestly raised prolactin alongside a large pituitary mass
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar seeing a 34-year-old woman referred with fifteen months of absent periods and milky discharge from both breasts. She has not been pregnant, has never breastfed, and takes no antipsychotic, antiemetic or antidepressant medication.

Confrontation testing shows loss of the outer half of each visual field. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary reports a 3.4 cm sellar mass with suprasellar extension compressing the optic chiasm. Her serum prolactin, taken as a single unstressed sample, is 1750 mIU/L. Thyroid function and morning cortisol are within normal limits and her renal function is normal.

data_table.Examination: Bitemporal field loss on confrontation, no acral enlargement, no proximal weakness, no striae
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1750 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, creatinine within normal limits, beta human chorionic gonadotrophin not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for urgent transsphenoidal decompression of the sellar mass
Commence cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly and repeat imaging at three months
Request measurement of macroprolactin on the stored serum sample
Measure insulin like growth factor 1 and an overnight dexamethasone suppression test
Request repeat prolactin measurement performed on serially diluted serum

subtopic_detail: Acting on a single raised prostate specific antigen result in an asymptomatic man
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 58-year-old accountant who asked for a prostate check at his last visit after a colleague was diagnosed with prostate cancer. He has no urinary symptoms and no first degree relative with prostate cancer.

He has not cycled, ejaculated or had a urinary catheter in the week before the blood test, and he takes no finasteride or dutasteride. Digital rectal examination performed today finds a smooth, symmetrical gland without nodularity. A midstream urine was collected at the same visit as the blood test.

data_table.Examination: Smooth symmetrical prostate without nodules, abdomen soft, no bony tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Prostate specific antigen 5.2 mcg/L, midstream urine no growth and no pyuria, creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the prostate specific antigen within one to three months
Refer to urology now for transperineal prostate biopsy
Arrange multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging of the prostate
Reassure him and repeat the blood test in two years
Prescribe four weeks of ciprofloxacin then repeat the blood test

subtopic_detail: Reversing warfarin in the presence of clinically significant bleeding
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department for a 78-year-old woman who has passed three black tarry stools since last night and feels faint on standing. She takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation and finished a course of trimethoprim for a urinary infection four days ago.

She is alert and orientated. There is no external bleeding and no neurological deficit. Two large bore cannulas are in place, group and hold has been sent and the gastroenterology team has been contacted about endoscopy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 6.2 (0.8-1.2), haemoglobin 76 g/L (115-165), platelets 214 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 104 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate reversal strategy?

options.text: Withhold warfarin and recheck the international normalised ratio in six hours
Give intravenous vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate
Give intravenous vitamin K alone and repeat it after twelve hours
Transfuse four units of fresh frozen plasma without other agents
Give intravenous tranexamic acid and transfuse two units of red cells

subtopic_detail: Separating an inflammatory arthritis with dactylitis from a post infective arthritis
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the rheumatology clinic seeing a 38-year-old plumber with eight weeks of joint pain. Six weeks before the joints began he had four days of bloody diarrhoea after a work barbecue, which settled without treatment.

The right second toe and the left third finger are swollen along their whole length rather than at the joint lines, and the right knee and left ankle are swollen and warm. The distal interphalangeal joints of both hands are tender. Several fingernails show pinpoint depressions in the nail plate and there is thickened scaling behind both ears and at the umbilicus. Eye examination is normal and there is no urethral discharge.

data_table.Examination: Sausage swelling of the right second toe and left third finger, warm effusions in the right knee and left ankle, pitting of four fingernails
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 38 mg/L (less than 5), rheumatoid factor not detected, anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody not detected, serum urate 0.34 mmol/L (0.20-0.42), stool culture no growth

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Reactive arthritis triggered by the recent enteric infection
Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis with early joint swelling
Psoriatic arthritis with dactylitis and nail involvement
Polyarticular gout with a chronic tophaceous component
Disseminated gonococcal infection with tenosynovitis

subtopic_detail: Choosing the screening test for suspected growth hormone excess
stem:
You are the general medical registrar assessing a 46-year-old man referred with hypertension that has needed three agents over two years. His wife brought old photographs to the consultation and you can see that his jaw and brow have coarsened.

He volunteers that his wedding ring had to be cut off last year and that he has gone up three shoe sizes since his thirties. He sweats through two shirts a day and snores heavily with witnessed pauses. On examination there is spacing between the lower incisors and the tongue is enlarged. Fasting glucose is 7.4 mmol/L and thyroid function is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 158/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 7.4 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, calcium corrected 2.44 mmol/L (2.10-2.60)

lead_in: Which initial investigation would best establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Random serum growth hormone measured on a single morning sample
Oral glucose tolerance test with paired growth hormone sampling
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with contrast
Serum insulin like growth factor 1 interpreted against age matched values
Overnight dexamethasone suppression test with morning serum cortisol

subtopic_detail: Next test after raised ferritin with a high transferrin saturation in a middle aged man
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 44-year-old man in clinic with eighteen months of tiredness and aching in the knuckles of both hands. He tells you his older brother was told he had too much iron and now gives blood regularly at the hospital.

He drinks four standard drinks a week and takes no supplements, no iron tablets and no over the counter tonics. The second and third metacarpophalangeal joints are tender with bony swelling. There is no palpable liver edge, no spider naevi and no ascites. Hepatitis B and C serology is negative and his C reactive protein is 3 mg/L.

data_table.Examination: Tender bony swelling of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints, no hepatomegaly, no stigmata of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 1480 mcg/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 71 per cent (16-45), alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L (less than 41), C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Percutaneous liver biopsy to quantify the hepatic iron concentration
Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver to estimate iron concentration
Repeat fasting iron studies with inflammatory markers in three months
Commence weekly venesection and reassess the ferritin after ten weeks
HFE genotyping for the C282Y and H63D variants on peripheral blood

subtopic_detail: Withholding biopsy and corticosteroid in an acute presentation with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 31-year-old childcare worker with ten days of fever and painful lumps on both shins that she says look like bruises that will not fade. Both ankles are swollen and she can only walk a few steps.

She has no cough, no breathlessness and no weight loss, has never smoked, and has not travelled outside Australia or had contact with anyone known to have tuberculosis. Examination shows tender raised red nodules over both shins and warm swollen ankles. Chest radiograph reports symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields. Spirometry is normal, corrected calcium is normal and an interferon gamma release assay is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields, corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), C reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5), interferon gamma release assay negative, spirometry within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Symptomatic treatment with naproxen and repeat chest imaging in three months
Endobronchial ultrasound guided needle aspiration of the hilar nodes
Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg per kg daily with a taper over six months
Empirical rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol therapy
Weekly oral methotrexate with folic acid cover and monthly bloods

subtopic_detail: Recognising opioid neurotoxicity as renal function falls and choosing the substitute agent
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 69-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer in the palliative care unit. Her daughter says her mother has started twitching in her sleep, plucking at the bedsheets, and talking to people who are not there, and that she jumped when a nurse touched her arm this morning.

Her chest wall pain has been controlled for six weeks on modified release morphine 90 mg twice daily with immediate release morphine for breakthrough, and the dose has not changed. She has vomited twice today and drunk little for three days. She is rousable and orientated to person only. Pupils are 3 mm and equal, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute and there are multifocal jerks of both arms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 218 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 21 mL/min/1.73m2, sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), corrected calcium 2.42 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the modified release morphine and add regular oral haloperidol
Add regular subcutaneous midazolam for the involuntary muscle jerking
Administer intravenous naloxone in titrated doses and observe closely
Rotate to subcutaneous fentanyl at a reduced equianalgesic dose with fluids
Continue morphine unchanged and treat for hypercalcaemia of malignancy

subtopic_detail: Sequencing replacement when both cobalamin and folate are low with neurological signs
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 63-year-old woman referred with four months of tiredness and a feeling that she is walking on cotton wool. She has had autoimmune thyroid disease for a decade and takes levothyroxine only.

She is unsteady when she closes her eyes while standing with her feet together, and vibration sense is absent at both medial malleoli with reduced joint position sense in both great toes. Ankle jerks are absent but both plantar responses are upgoing. Her tongue is smooth and beefy red. She is not a vegetarian and drinks no alcohol.

data_table.Examination: Romberg positive, vibration sense absent at both medial malleoli, absent ankle jerks with upgoing plantars, atrophic glossitis
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-165), mean cell volume 112 fL (80-100), serum cobalamin 74 pmol/L (150-700), serum folate 4 nmol/L (greater than 7), reticulocytes 24 x10^9/L (20-100), thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start oral folic acid 5 mg daily and review the blood film in four weeks
Transfuse two units of red cells and repeat the full blood count after
Start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin, adding folic acid once it is underway
Start oral cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg daily and reassess at three months
Await intrinsic factor antibody and gastric parietal cell antibody results

subtopic_detail: Daily headache in a woman whose episodic migraine has become continuous while she takes a combination analgesic
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34-year-old woman who says her head has hurt on most days for the past six months. Two years ago she had one or two bad headaches a month with nausea and light sensitivity, each settling with a tablet. Now the pain is present when she wakes and is dull and pressing on both sides, with a severe throbbing attack roughly weekly.

She buys a combination tablet containing paracetamol, codeine and doxylamine over the counter and takes between fifteen and twenty doses a week, mostly because she is afraid a bad attack will start at work. She has tried no preventive medication. Her neurological examination including fundoscopy is normal and there is no neck stiffness, no new focal symptom and no headache that peaks within seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fundoscopy normal, cranial nerves intact, no papilloedema, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Medication history: Paracetamol with codeine and doxylamine combination tablets, 15 to 20 doses per week for at least 6 months, no preventive agent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Add a sumatriptan tablet to be taken at the onset of every headache day she experiences
Arrange computed tomography of the brain and defer any treatment change until it reports
Cease the codeine containing analgesic and start regular propranolol as daily prevention
Continue her current analgesia and begin amitriptyline at ten milligrams each night
Refer her for greater occipital nerve blocks before altering her regular analgesic intake

subtopic_detail: Fourth episode of lower limb cellulitis in a year in a man with chronic lymphoedema
stem:
You are the registrar in a general medical clinic reviewing a 55-year-old man two weeks after discharge from his fourth admission with right leg cellulitis in twelve months. Each episode has begun with rigors and a spreading red leg and each has settled on intravenous then oral flucloxacillin, and the current episode has fully resolved.

He has had chronic swelling of that leg since an inguinal lymph node dissection for melanoma six years ago and wears a compression garment inconsistently because it is uncomfortable in summer. Today the leg is swollen and firm but not red, warm or tender. Between his toes the skin is macerated and fissured with fine scaling. He has no ulcer, no diabetes and no injecting drug use, and his body mass index is 34 kg/m2.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 per minute, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Non pitting oedema of the right leg with skin thickening, no erythema or tenderness, interdigital maceration and fissuring of the fourth web space, no ulceration
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 7.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to reduce further episodes?

options.text: Give a single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin now and repeat it if he relapses
Start twice daily oral phenoxymethylpenicillin as continuing prophylaxis with review at twelve months
Treat the interdigital skin with a topical antifungal cream and take no other preventive measure
Refer for supervised compression bandaging and lymphoedema therapy as the only ongoing measure
Prescribe a rotating cycle of oral doxycycline for one week in every month over the coming year

subtopic_detail: Positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test returned through the national screening program
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62-year-old woman who has brought in a letter reporting a positive result from the bowel screening kit she posted six weeks ago. She feels entirely well, her bowel habit is unchanged, and she has seen no blood in the toilet.

She has never had a colonoscopy. No first degree relative has had bowel cancer. She takes perindopril for hypertension and no antiplatelet or anticoagulant. On examination her abdomen is soft and non-tender, and rectal examination reveals small external haemorrhoids that are not bleeding and no palpable mass. Her full blood examination shows haemoglobin 138 g/L (115-155) with mean cell volume 88 fL (80-100), and her ferritin is 96 micrograms/L (30-200).

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no mass, small non bleeding external haemorrhoids on rectal examination
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 138 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 88 fL (80-100), ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30-200), immunochemical faecal occult blood test positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the immunochemical faecal occult blood test in three months and act only if it is positive again
Attribute the result to her haemorrhoids and review her again if she reports any rectal bleeding
Refer her for colonoscopy with the aim of the procedure occurring within thirty days of the result
Order computed tomography colonography first and reserve colonoscopy for any abnormality it detects
Send a faecal calprotectin level and base the decision to refer her on whether it is elevated

subtopic_detail: Deciding the duration of anticoagulation three months after a first unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis
stem:
You are the registrar in a thrombosis clinic reviewing a 48-year-old man three months after a first deep vein thrombosis involving the right femoral and popliteal veins. He has taken apixaban at treatment dose throughout and has had no bleeding, and his leg swelling has settled.

In the three months before it he had no surgery, immobilisation, plaster cast or long haul travel, and he has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis at diagnosis and an age-appropriate screening history revealed no malignancy. He is otherwise well, works as a plumber, drinks minimally, and takes no antiplatelet agent. His full blood examination, renal function and liver function are normal today, and his repeat ultrasound shows partial recanalisation with residual non occlusive thrombus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68 per minute, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-175), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 90 mL/min/1.73m2, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L (less than 40)
data_table.Imaging: Repeat compression ultrasound shows partial recanalisation with residual non occlusive thrombus in the femoral vein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan from here?

options.text: Stop anticoagulation now on the basis that three months of treatment has been completed
Continue apixaban indefinitely at the lower prophylactic dose with annual review of risk and bleeding
Change to low dose aspirin daily as ongoing secondary prevention against further clot
Perform an inherited thrombophilia screen and let those results determine the treatment duration
Switch to warfarin with a target range of 2.0 to 3.0 and plan to stop after six further months

subtopic_detail: Influenza confirmed on day two of illness in a frail aged care resident during a facility outbreak
stem:
You are the doctor attending a residential aged care facility where three residents have tested positive for influenza A in the past two days. You are asked to see an 82-year-old woman who developed fever, a dry cough and aching limbs yesterday morning.

She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with two exacerbations in the past year, uses tiotropium and a combination inhaler, and had her influenza vaccination four months ago. She is alert and orientated, her chest is quiet with a prolonged expiratory phase and no focal crackles, and her chest radiograph shows hyperinflation without consolidation. A point-of-care polymerase chain reaction swab taken this morning is positive for influenza A. Her creatinine is 96 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 48 mL/min/1.73m2.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 per minute, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 93 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Influenza A detected on polymerase chain reaction, C reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 48 mL/min/1.73m2
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph shows hyperinflation with no consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start oral oseltamivir now at a dose reduced for her renal function and continue it for five days
Provide supportive care only because antiviral therapy has no benefit once fever is established
Give oral amoxicillin for seven days on the basis of her fever and raised C reactive protein
Prescribe inhaled zanamivir twice daily for five days as her preferred antiviral treatment option
Await the formal laboratory confirmation of the subtype before committing her to any antiviral drug

subtopic_detail: Nodular acne with early scarring that has not responded to four months of oral tetracycline and topical therapy
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 19-year-old woman who has been using adapalene with benzoyl peroxide each night and taking doxycycline 100 mg daily for the past four months. She has taken the tablets consistently and has not missed applications.

Her face and upper back carry deep tender nodules that last several weeks, and she has developed several small depressed scars on both cheeks since her last visit. She has stopped going to her university tutorials and describes feeling flat about her appearance, though she denies any thoughts of self-harm. Her periods are regular, she is not sexually active, and she takes no other medication. There is no hirsutism, no acanthosis nigricans and no galactorrhoea, and her body mass index is 22 kg/m2.

data_table.Examination: Deep inflammatory nodules over both cheeks, jawline and upper back, several atrophic scars on the cheeks, no comedonal predominance, no hirsutism
data_table.Treatment history: Adapalene with benzoyl peroxide nightly and doxycycline 100 mg daily for 4 months with good adherence

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Continue the current doxycycline and topical regimen for a further six months before any change
Substitute minocycline for the doxycycline while keeping the topical treatment unchanged
Add a combined oral contraceptive pill and reassess her skin again in a further three months
Refer her to a dermatologist for assessment for a course of oral isotretinoin treatment
Intensify the topical regimen with the addition of a topical clindamycin preparation twice daily

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of blood streaked sputum in a heavy smoker whose chest radiograph is reported as normal
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old man who has coughed up streaks of blood in his morning phlegm on most days for three weeks. He describes the amount as a teaspoon at most and says the phlegm is otherwise clear.

He has smoked 25 cigarettes a day since he was 18 and has no diagnosis of chronic lung disease. He has had no fever or purulent sputum at any stage, and his weight and exercise tolerance are unchanged. Examination of his chest is normal with equal breath sounds and a normal voice. A chest radiograph performed yesterday was reported as showing clear lung fields with no mass, effusion or collapse. His full blood examination and coagulation profile are normal and he takes no anticoagulant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 per minute, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Chest clear with equal air entry, no clubbing, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination and coagulation profile normal, chest radiograph reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat the chest radiograph in six weeks and investigate further only if a new abnormality appears
Prescribe a course of amoxicillin with clavulanate and reassess him once the treatment is finished
Send three early morning sputum specimens for cytology and base further imaging on those results
Attribute the blood to airway irritation from smoking and review him after a cessation attempt
Arrange contrast enhanced computed tomography of the chest and refer him for respiratory assessment

subtopic_detail: Thyrotoxicosis emerging after eighteen months of amiodarone with an avascular gland on Doppler
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 68-year-old man referred by his cardiologist. He has taken amiodarone for eighteen months to maintain sinus rhythm after two failed ablations, and over the past six weeks he has lost 7 kg, become heat intolerant and had two documented episodes of rapid atrial fibrillation.

He has no eye signs, no neck pain and no tenderness over the thyroid, and the gland is not enlarged or nodular. He has never lived in an iodine deficient region and has no family history of thyroid disease. His thyroid stimulating hormone is less than 0.01 mIU/L with a free thyroxine of 42 pmol/L. Thyroid receptor antibodies are negative, and colour flow Doppler of the thyroid shows markedly reduced vascularity throughout the gland.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 per minute and irregular, blood pressure 142/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 42 pmol/L (10-20), free triiodothyronine 9.8 pmol/L (3.5-6.0), thyroid receptor antibodies negative, C reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5)
data_table.Imaging: Colour flow Doppler shows markedly reduced thyroidal vascularity with a normal sized gland

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for his thyroid disorder?

options.text: Commence carbimazole at high dose and continue it until the free thyroxine has normalised
Cease the amiodarone alone and recheck his thyroid function in six to eight weeks' time
Arrange radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid gland once his heart rate is controlled
Start oral prednisolone at an anti inflammatory dose and taper it as thyroid function improves
Refer him for urgent total thyroidectomy as the definitive management of his thyrotoxicosis

subtopic_detail: Screening for primary aldosteronism in a patient whose general practitioner has already started a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
stem:
You are the registrar in a hypertension clinic seeing a 52-year-old woman referred for investigation of blood pressure that has stayed above target on three agents. Her general practitioner added spironolactone 25 mg daily eight weeks ago as a fourth agent and her readings have improved since.

She also takes perindopril, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. Home readings average 148/92 mmHg. She has never been pregnant, has no snoring or witnessed apnoeas, and her body mass index is 27 kg/m2. She takes no liquorice, no non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs and no decongestants. Renal ultrasound performed by her general practitioner showed two normal sized kidneys with no asymmetry. Her potassium today is 4.2 mmol/L and her creatinine is 74 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74 per minute, blood pressure 152/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), bicarbonate 27 mmol/L (22-32)
data_table.Medication history: Perindopril, amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, and spironolactone 25 mg daily started 8 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Measure the aldosterone to renin ratio at the next visit while she continues her current medications
Proceed directly to adrenal vein sampling to establish whether her excess is unilateral or bilateral
Request computed tomography of the adrenal glands to look for an adenoma before any blood testing
Arrange a seated saline suppression test on her current regimen to confirm autonomous secretion
Cease the spironolactone for six weeks, control her pressure with verapamil or prazosin, then screen

subtopic_detail: Ophthalmoplegia with ataxia and areflexia after gastroenteritis when the early cerebrospinal fluid protein is normal
stem: A 46-year-old man has four days of double vision and an unsteady walk, ten days after five days of watery diarrhoea.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral partial ptosis with restricted eye movements in all directions, wide based ataxic gait, generalised areflexia, limb power 5 out of 5
data_table.Investigations: Cerebrospinal fluid protein 0.38 g/L (0.15-0.45) with 1 white cell, forced vital capacity 3.6 L, contrast MRI brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin with regular vital capacity monitoring
Repeat the lumbar puncture in one week before treating
High dose intravenous methylprednisolone for three days
High dose parenteral thiamine before any glucose load
Urgent thrombolysis assessment for brainstem ischaemia

subtopic_detail: Prosthetic valve endocarditis with new regurgitation and pulmonary oedema after antibiotics were started in the community
stem: A 62-year-old man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve replaced fourteen months ago has three weeks of fever, treated with oral amoxicillin before admission and vancomycin and gentamicin since. Overnight he became breathless lying flat.

data_table.Examination: Bibasal crackles, new early diastolic murmur, SpO2 91 per cent on 6 L oxygen
data_table.Investigations: Three blood culture sets sterile at 48 hours, CRP 186 mg/L
data_table.Imaging: Echocardiography shows a 12 mm vegetation, severe aortic regurgitation and a root abscess

lead_in: What is the most important next step?

options.text: Continue antimicrobials for six weeks
Stop antibiotics 48 hours and reculture
Add rifampicin to the current regimen
Immediate referral for surgical valve replacement
Therapeutic heparin to reduce embolic risk

subtopic_detail: Timing of antiretroviral therapy in a newly diagnosed patient being treated for cryptococcal meningitis
stem:
You are the infectious diseases registrar looking after a 38-year-old man diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus infection nine days ago after presenting with headache and confusion. His CD4 count is 28 cells per microlitre and his viral load is 420 000 copies per mL.

Cerebrospinal fluid on admission grew Cryptococcus neoformans with an opening pressure of 34 cmH2O, and he has had daily therapeutic lumbar punctures. He is on day five of liposomal amphotericin B with flucytosine and his headache and conscious state have improved markedly. He has no tuberculosis symptoms, a normal chest radiograph and a negative urinary lipoarabinomannan test.
