His renal function and potassium are being replaced and remain stable, and he is keen to begin treatment for the virus as soon as possible.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: CD4 count 28 cells per microlitre, HIV viral load 420 000 copies per mL, cerebrospinal fluid culture positive for Cryptococcus neoformans, opening pressure 34 cmH2O at diagnosis, creatinine 92 micromol/L (60-110), potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph normal, computed tomography of the brain shows no focal lesion or hydrocephalus

lead_in: When should antiretroviral therapy be started?

options.text: Today, because a CD4 count below 50 cells per microlitre makes any delay in treatment unsafe
Once the induction antifungal course finishes at two weeks, provided the repeat culture is sterile
Only after the full twelve month course of maintenance fluconazole has been successfully completed
Immediately, but with a corticosteroid started alongside it to prevent an inflammatory reaction
After four to six weeks of antifungal therapy, once his intracranial pressure has been controlled

subtopic_detail: Painful desquamating rash with mucosal ulceration three weeks after an anticonvulsant was introduced
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 34-year-old woman brought in by her partner with two days of fever and a spreading rash that she describes as feeling like scalding. She started lamotrigine three weeks ago for bipolar disorder and the dose was increased last week.

Her lips are crusted and bleeding, her conjunctivae are injected with adhesions forming at the lid margin, and there are erosions on the buccal mucosa that stop her drinking. Dusky macules with central blistering cover her trunk and proximal arms, and gentle lateral pressure on apparently normal skin at the shoulder shears the epidermis away. You estimate detached and detachable skin at about 12 per cent of body surface area. She has no facial oedema, no lymphadenopathy and no eosinophilia, and her liver enzymes are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 122 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Dusky targetoid macules with blistering over 12 per cent body surface area, positive skin shear sign, haemorrhagic crusting of the lips, ocular and buccal erosions, no facial oedema or lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 0.1 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L (less than 40), creatinine 104 micromol/L (45-90), bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22-32)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease the lamotrigine and arrange urgent transfer to a burns unit with ophthalmology review
Reduce the lamotrigine to the previous lower dose and observe her on the medical ward overnight
Commence intravenous aciclovir and swab the mucosal lesions for herpes simplex virus testing
Start intravenous flucloxacillin for presumed staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and admit her
Give a three day course of pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone before any change to her medication

subtopic_detail: Symmetrical parkinsonism with early falls and syncope that responds poorly to a full levodopa trial
stem:
You are the general physician reviewing a 66-year-old man diagnosed with Parkinson disease eighteen months ago by his general practitioner. He now takes levodopa with carbidopa four times daily at a total daily levodopa dose of 1000 mg, taken reliably.

His wife reports he has fallen backwards eleven times in the past six months and has blacked out three times while standing at the kitchen bench. He has needed a urinary catheter twice for retention and wakes at night with loud snoring and shouting. His movements are stiff and slow on both sides to an equal degree, and there is no tremor at rest. Standing blood pressure falls from 138/82 to 92/58 mmHg after three minutes with no rise in pulse rate. His wife says the medication made no appreciable difference at any dose.

data_table.Vital signs: Supine pulse rate 76 per minute, supine blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, standing blood pressure 92/58 mmHg at 3 minutes with pulse rate 78 per minute, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical rigidity and bradykinesia, no rest tremor, retropulsion on pull testing, normal eye movements in the vertical plane
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination, electrolytes, thyroid function and vitamin B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the total daily levodopa dose further and review his response again in eight weeks
Refer for neurology assessment with magnetic resonance imaging as the pattern suggests atypical disease
Add a dopamine agonist to his regimen and titrate it upwards over the following several weeks
Commence an anticholinergic agent to target his rigidity and reduce the frequency of his falls
Start a cholinesterase inhibitor on the basis that his falls and night time behaviour indicate dementia

subtopic_detail: Acute monoarthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint in a man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease
stem: A 68-year-old man woke with a hot swollen painful left great toe, the third such episode in two years. He has stage 4 chronic kidney disease and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and takes furosemide 80 mg daily.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73 m2, urate 0.52 mmol/L, CRP 28 mg/L, white cells 9.4 x10^9/L

lead_in: Which treatment is most appropriate for this episode?

options.text: Indometacin 50 mg orally three times daily for five days
Prednisolone 30 mg orally daily for a five day course
Colchicine 1 mg orally then 500 microgram one hour later
Allopurinol 300 mg orally daily with review in four weeks
Aspirate the joint and start intravenous flucloxacillin empirically

subtopic_detail: Escalating calf pain eight hours after a closed tibial fracture with a palpable pulse and a warm foot
stem: A 24-year-old man with a closed tibial fracture in a below knee backslab has escalating pain eight hours after injury despite 18 mg of intravenous morphine. The calf is tense and firm, passive toe extension reproduces severe calf pain, and first web space sensation is reduced. The dorsalis pedis pulse is palpable and the foot is warm.

data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 3200 U/L (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Split the cast and refer for emergency fasciotomy
Elevate the limb and reassess in one hour
Arrange an urgent arterial duplex of the leg
Measure compartment pressures and act above 30 mmHg
Increase his analgesia and review in two hours

subtopic_detail: Eight months of inflammatory back pain in a young man whose sacroiliac radiographs and inflammatory markers are both normal
stem: A 26-year-old carpenter has eight months of low back and buttock pain that wakes him at night, with over an hour of morning stiffness that eases with movement. Ten months ago he had a painful red eye treated with steroid drops. His father has psoriasis. Modified Schober increase is 3.5 cm.

data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 4 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 9 mm/h; sacroiliac radiographs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: HLA-B27 testing, diagnosing him if positive
Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints
Computed tomography of the sacroiliac joints
A graded exercise program and review in six months
Lumbar spine magnetic resonance imaging for disc disease

subtopic_detail: Watery diarrhoea with a rising creatinine and a white cell count of 19 following a course of clindamycin
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 72-year-old woman with six days of watery diarrhoea, opening her bowels around eight times a day with lower abdominal cramping. She finished a ten day course of clindamycin for a dental infection eleven days ago and has taken no other new medication.

She looks dry with reduced skin turgor and her abdomen is soft with generalised mild tenderness and no guarding or rigidity. Her white cell count is 19.2 x10^9/L, her creatinine has risen from a baseline of 68 micromol/L three months ago to 145 micromol/L, and her albumin is 26 g/L. Her temperature is 38.2 degrees C. A stool sample is positive for the organism by nucleic acid amplification with a positive toxin enzyme immunoassay. An abdominal radiograph shows no colonic dilatation and there is no free gas.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 108/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 145 micromol/L (45-90, baseline 68), albumin 26 g/L (35-50), lactate 1.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0), stool nucleic acid amplification and toxin immunoassay both positive
data_table.Imaging: Supine abdominal radiograph with no colonic dilatation, normal haustral pattern, no free intraperitoneal gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start intravenous vancomycin 1 g twelve hourly for a ten day course
Start oral metronidazole 400 mg eight hourly for a ten day course
Start oral vancomycin 125 mg six hourly for a ten day course
Start loperamide with oral rehydration and repeat the toxin assay in 48 hours
Refer for urgent subtotal colectomy and start intravenous fluid resuscitation

subtopic_detail: Six weeks of shoulder and hip girdle pain with an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 68 and no cranial symptoms
stem: A 71-year-old woman has six weeks of shoulder and hip girdle pain with 90 minutes of morning stiffness. She cannot lift her arms to wash her hair. She has no headache, jaw claudication or visual disturbance.

data_table.Examination: Painful restriction with full passive range, power 5/5, no synovitis
data_table.Investigations: ESR 68 mm/h, CRP 42 mg/L, creatine kinase 92 U/L, rheumatoid factor negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Prednisolone 50 mg daily with temporal artery biopsy
Prednisolone 15 mg daily with review within one week
Methotrexate 10 mg weekly with folic acid supplementation
Naproxen 500 mg twice daily with review in four weeks
MRI of both shoulders before starting any treatment

subtopic_detail: Dark urine and severe thigh pain three days after a first high intensity gym session with a dipstick positive for blood and no red cells
stem: A 21-year-old man has three days of severe pain and swelling in both thighs after his first high intensity gym class, with two days of dark tea coloured urine passed in reduced volume.

data_table.Examination: Thighs swollen and tender, compartments soft, no pain on passive knee extension
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 48200 U/L (30-200), creatinine 138 micromol/L, potassium 5.4 mmol/L, corrected calcium 1.98 mmol/L, dipstick strongly positive for blood with no red cells

lead_in: What is the most important initial treatment?

options.text: Intravenous furosemide to maintain urine output
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise urine
Intravenous calcium gluconate for the hypocalcaemia
Urgent haemodialysis to clear circulating myoglobin
High volume intravenous sodium chloride titrated to output

subtopic_detail: Nausea, confusion and yellow tinged vision in an elderly woman whose diuretic dose was increased after a heart failure admission
stem: An 81-year-old woman has nausea and confusion. She takes digoxin 125 microgram daily for atrial fibrillation. Her furosemide was increased from 40 mg to 80 mg three weeks ago, and lights now look yellow with halos.

data_table.Investigations: Digoxin 3.4 nmol/L (1.0-2.6), potassium 3.1 mmol/L, creatinine 155 micromol/L, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Atrial fibrillation at 44 /min, no ventricular ectopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold digoxin and correct her potassium and magnesium
Give digoxin specific antibody fragments as an intravenous infusion
Insert a temporary transvenous pacing wire for the bradycardia
Give intravenous calcium chloride to stabilise the cardiac membrane
Halve the digoxin dose and recheck the level in one week

subtopic_detail: Three days of headache and nausea that improve at work in a couple using an unflued gas heater, with normal oxygen saturation
stem: A 34-year-old man has three days of headache and poor concentration that clear at work. This morning his partner found him unrousable for 30 seconds. They run an unflued gas heater at home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 /min, SpO2 99 per cent in air
data_table.Investigations: Carboxyhaemoglobin 22 per cent (less than 3), arterial oxygen 96 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oxygen by nasal prongs at 4 L per minute for six hours
High flow oxygen, discharging him once symptoms settle
Computed tomography of the brain before any specific treatment
Titrate oxygen to 94 per cent saturation and admit for observation
High flow oxygen and urgent referral for hyperbaric treatment

subtopic_detail: Shock and bradycardia two hours after a deliberate overdose, with a low blood glucose and a narrow QRS complex
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar managing a 58-year-old woman brought in by ambulance two hours after telling her daughter she had taken all of her tablets. The empty packet is metoprolol 100 mg and about forty tablets are unaccounted for, and she drank two glasses of wine at the same time.

She is drowsy but rousable with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14, cool peripheries and a capillary refill of four seconds. She has received 1.2 mg of atropine in divided doses and a litre of sodium chloride with no improvement in her heart rate or blood pressure. Her capillary glucose is 3.1 mmol/L. Her twelve lead electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia at 38 per minute with a QRS duration of 88 milliseconds and a corrected QT interval of 420 milliseconds. Her chest is clear and her serum lactate is 4.2 mmol/L. Her paracetamol level is undetectable and she takes no other regular medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 38 per minute, blood pressure 72/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.1 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), lactate 4.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine within normal limits, paracetamol undetectable, ethanol 0.06 per cent
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus bradycardia at 38 per minute, QRS duration 88 milliseconds, corrected QT interval 420 milliseconds, no ventricular ectopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate to narrow the QRS complex
Give intravenous calcium gluconate followed by a calcium infusion
Give intravenous lipid emulsion as a bolus followed by an infusion
Start an adrenaline infusion and titrate it against her blood pressure
Start high dose insulin with dextrose titrated against her blood pressure

subtopic_detail: Five months of night time hand numbness relieved by shaking, with no wasting and normal thumb abduction strength
stem: A 52-year-old woman has five months of numbness and tingling in her right thumb, index and middle fingers, worst at night and relieved by shaking the hand. The little finger is never involved.

data_table.Examination: Reduced light touch over the first three finger pulps with preserved thenar eminence sensation, thumb abduction 5 out of 5, no thenar wasting

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies before starting any treatment
Refer her for urgent surgical decompression of the nerve
Fit a neutral night wrist splint and review in six weeks
Arrange an MRI of the cervical spine to look for radiculopathy
Give a corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel today

subtopic_detail: Acute vestibular syndrome and bedside oculomotor testing
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 58-year-old man who has had continuous spinning dizziness for six hours, with vomiting and inability to stand unaided. He has hypertension and smokes 20 cigarettes a day. He reports no headache and no change in his hearing.

On examination he has horizontal nystagmus beating to the right that does not change direction on left or right gaze. The head impulse test produces no corrective saccade when his head is turned to either side. Cover test reveals a vertical shift of the left eye on uncovering. Limb power, coordination and speech are normal. He cannot walk without two people supporting him.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 168/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT brain reported as no acute intracranial abnormality; blood glucose 6.1 mmol/L (4.0-7.8)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Prescribe prochlorperazine and discharge with written vestibular sedative advice
Refer for outpatient audiometry and formal vestibular function testing next week
Perform Dix-Hallpike testing and treat with an Epley repositioning manoeuvre
Commence oral prednisolone for presumed inflammation of the vestibular nerve
Arrange urgent MRI brain with diffusion weighted imaging and stroke unit admission

subtopic_detail: Acute unilateral facial weakness and corticosteroid timing
stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents to your general practice clinic with drooping of the left side of her face that she first noticed on waking 30 hours ago. She describes her eye watering and food collecting in her left cheek, and says sounds seem uncomfortably loud on that side.

On examination she cannot wrinkle her left forehead or bury her left eyelashes, and the left corner of her mouth does not move on smiling. There is no rash in or around the ear and the tympanic membranes are normal. Limb power, sensation and coordination are normal, and her speech is clear. She is not pregnant and has no history of diabetes.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Complete left facial weakness including the forehead; Bell phenomenon present; corneal reflex intact; no vesicles in the external auditory canal; no parotid mass

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Provide eye lubrication and review in one week to assess spontaneous recovery
Start oral aciclovir alone, with eye lubrication and overnight eye taping
Arrange urgent CT brain before any drug treatment is commenced
Arrange serology and defer treatment until the results are available
Start oral prednisolone now, with eye lubrication and overnight eye taping

subtopic_detail: Proximal weakness and bone pain with a low calcium and raised alkaline phosphatase
stem:
A 58-year-old woman is referred to you with eight months of aching in her hips, thighs and ribs, and increasing difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs without pulling on the handrail. She has fallen twice.

She moved to Australia from Afghanistan 11 years ago, wears concealing clothing outdoors and rarely leaves the house during daylight. She eats very little dairy. She takes no corticosteroids, anticonvulsants or antiretroviral medicines and has had no gastrointestinal surgery. On examination she has symmetrical proximal weakness with a waddling gait, and tenderness when firm pressure is applied over the ribs and pelvis. There is no rash, no synovitis and no scalp tenderness.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.06 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), phosphate 0.62 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), alkaline phosphatase 320 U/L (30-110), parathyroid hormone 14.8 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 12 nmol/L (sufficient above 50), creatinine 71 micromol/L (45-90), creatine kinase within normal limits, erythrocyte sedimentation rate within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone at 15 mg daily for probable polymyalgia rheumatica
Commence a weekly oral bisphosphonate with calcium and review her in three months
Refer for parathyroidectomy after parathyroid localisation imaging is completed
Arrange electromyography and muscle biopsy to characterise the proximal myopathy
Commence high dose colecalciferol with calcium and review the response in three months

subtopic_detail: Acute symmetrical polyarthritis after mosquito exposure
stem:
A 41-year-old woman presents to your clinic with three weeks of pain and swelling in both wrists, both knees and the small joints of her hands, with two hours of morning stiffness. She has also had marked fatigue and a fine rash over her trunk that has now faded. She camped along the Murray River six weeks ago and recalls many mosquito bites.

On examination there is synovitis of both wrists and several metacarpophalangeal joints, with symmetrical distribution. There are no nail changes, no scaly plaques and no oral or genital ulcers. Rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are negative, and hand radiographs show no erosions.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 28 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 44 mm/h (less than 20), full blood count within normal limits, antinuclear antibody negative, uric acid within normal limits

lead_in: Which investigation is most likely to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Ross River virus and Barmah Forest virus IgM and IgG serology
Repeat anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody testing in six weeks
Human leucocyte antigen B27 typing and sacroiliac joint imaging
Extractable nuclear antigen panel and complement C3 and C4 levels
Ultrasound guided aspiration of the right knee for crystals and culture

subtopic_detail: Severity scoring and corticosteroid decision in acute alcohol related hepatitis
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 47-year-old man admitted with three weeks of deepening jaundice and abdominal swelling. He drinks approximately 15 standard drinks daily and stopped four days ago. He is tender in the right upper quadrant with a smooth palpable liver edge and shifting dullness.

He was started on intravenous fluids and thiamine on admission. A liver ultrasound with Doppler shows a coarse echotexture, patent hepatic and portal veins and moderate ascites, with no biliary dilatation. Diagnostic paracentesis yields a neutrophil count of 90 x10^6/L. Blood cultures and a viral hepatitis screen are negative, and his paracetamol level is undetectable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 268 micromol/L (less than 20), prothrombin time 22 s (control 12 s), aspartate aminotransferase 186 U/L (less than 40), alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 40), albumin 26 g/L (35-50), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110), white cell count 13.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone and monitor the response at day seven
Commence intravenous ceftriaxone and reassess the ascites in 48 hours
Commence oral pentoxifylline as the preferred alternative to corticosteroids
Arrange transjugular liver biopsy before any specific therapy is started
Refer for liver transplantation assessment after six months of abstinence

subtopic_detail: Chronic hepatitis C assessment before direct acting antiviral therapy
stem:
A 38-year-old man attends your general practice after a positive hepatitis C antibody test arranged at a needle and syringe program. He injected heroin between the ages of 19 and 27 and has not injected for 11 years. He drinks four standard drinks each week and takes no regular medicines.

He feels well and works full time. Abdominal examination is unremarkable with no palpable spleen, no ascites and no stigmata of chronic liver disease. He is anxious about the cost of treatment and asks whether he needs to see a specialist before anything can start. His hepatitis B surface antigen is negative and he is immune to hepatitis A.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis C RNA detected, genotype not performed; alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L (less than 40); bilirubin within normal limits; albumin 41 g/L (35-50); platelets 212 x10^9/L (150-400); international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.8-1.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a hepatologist for genotyping before any antiviral therapy is considered
Repeat the hepatitis C antibody test in three months to confirm true infection
Assess for cirrhosis, then prescribe a pangenotypic direct acting antiviral course
Advise six months of alcohol abstinence and reassess his liver enzymes after that
Arrange liver biopsy to stage fibrosis before deciding on antiviral treatment

subtopic_detail: Risk stratification of incidental hepatic steatosis on ultrasound
stem:
A 56-year-old woman is referred to you after an abdominal ultrasound performed for right sided abdominal discomfort reported a bright liver consistent with fatty infiltration and no gallstones. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin, a body mass index of 34 kg/m2 and treated hypertension.

She drinks two standard drinks per month. Hepatitis B and C serology, iron studies, antinuclear antibody and coeliac serology have all returned negative or within normal limits. She has no palpable spleen, no ascites and no spider naevi. She asks whether the fatty liver matters and what should happen next.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 46 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 39 U/L (less than 40), platelets 168 x10^9/L (150-400), albumin 40 g/L (35-50), HbA1c 7.6 per cent (less than 6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Repeat the liver ultrasound in 12 months to see whether the steatosis has progressed
Calculate a FIB-4 score and arrange transient elastography if it is not low risk
Reassure her that near normal transaminases exclude significant liver fibrosis
Cease metformin because of the risk of drug related hepatic injury in fatty liver
Refer directly for liver biopsy to determine whether steatohepatitis is present

subtopic_detail: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a well young adult
stem:
A 22-year-old university student is referred to you after a pre-employment medical showed a raised bilirubin. He recalls being told he looked slightly yellow during a bout of gastroenteritis two years ago, when he had eaten little for two days. He feels well, takes no medicines and has never injected drugs.

He has no abdominal pain, no dark urine and no pale stools. Examination shows mild scleral icterus, no hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly and no lymphadenopathy. A blood film is reported as normal with no spherocytes, no fragments and no polychromasia.

data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 58 micromol/L (less than 20) with conjugated fraction 6 micromol/L; alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase all within normal limits; haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-175), reticulocytes 62 x10^9/L (20-100), lactate dehydrogenase within normal limits, haptoglobin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Hereditary spherocytosis with chronic compensated extravascular haemolysis
Gilbert syndrome causing reduced hepatic bilirubin conjugation during fasting
Dubin-Johnson syndrome causing impaired biliary excretion of conjugated pigment
Primary sclerosing cholangitis producing early intrahepatic biliary obstruction
Chronic hepatitis B infection in the immune tolerant phase of the disease

subtopic_detail: Recognising serious drug induced liver injury and the decision to cease therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 63-year-old woman in clinic. She completed a two week course of amoxicillin with clavulanate for a dental infection five weeks ago and now describes two weeks of nausea, itch and dark coloured urine. She takes perindopril and atorvastatin, both unchanged for four years, and no herbal or over the counter preparations.

She drinks minimal alcohol. Examination shows jaundice and scratch marks over her forearms, with a soft non-tender abdomen and no ascites or hepatomegaly. Abdominal ultrasound shows a normal liver texture and no biliary dilatation, and viral hepatitis serology and autoimmune screen are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 96 micromol/L (less than 20), alanine aminotransferase 412 U/L (less than 40), alkaline phosphatase 310 U/L (30-110), international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.8-1.2), albumin 38 g/L (35-50), eosinophils 0.8 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5)

lead_in: Which action is most important in her management?

options.text: Cease atorvastatin and monitor her liver biochemistry weekly until it normalises
Record a permanent allergy alert for the implicated agent and monitor her recovery
Commence oral prednisolone to suppress the immune mediated hepatic inflammation
Arrange magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography to exclude a retained stone
Prescribe ursodeoxycholic acid to accelerate resolution of the cholestatic component

subtopic_detail: Fever during the neutrophil nadir after cytotoxic chemotherapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 61-year-old woman who received her second cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer nine days ago. She reports feeling shivery since this morning and has a mild sore throat but no cough, dysuria or diarrhoea.

Her tunnelled central line exit site looks clean and non-tender. Chest is clear on auscultation, the abdomen is soft and there are no skin lesions or mucosal ulcers. Intravenous access has been secured and peripheral and line blood cultures have just been drawn. She is alert and speaking in full sentences.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 0.3 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), white cell count 1.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-165), platelets 96 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), lactate 1.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.0); chest radiograph shows no focal consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam now, without waiting for culture results
Give intravenous vancomycin now as single agent empirical cover for line infection
Give oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and ciprofloxacin and discharge with review
Give a granulocyte colony stimulating factor injection and repeat the count in six hours
Give intravenous fluids and paracetamol and repeat the observations in two hours

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing acute transfusion reactions during a red cell transfusion
stem:
You are the hospital medical officer called urgently to a 74-year-old woman receiving her first unit of packed red cells for iron deficiency anaemia. Fifteen minutes into the transfusion, roughly 40 mL in, she becomes restless and complains of severe lower back pain and a burning sensation at the cannula site.

The nurse has stopped the transfusion and is running normal saline through a new giving set. The patient has no urticaria, no facial swelling, no wheeze and no stridor. Her chest is clear on auscultation and her jugular venous pressure is not elevated. Her urine in the catheter bag has turned dark red over the past few minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 126/min, BP 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Pre-transfusion haemoglobin 71 g/L (115-165); the unit and the patient wristband are being checked against the compatibility label

lead_in: Which complication is most likely to be occurring?

options.text: Transfusion associated circulatory overload from a rapid intravascular volume increase
Anaphylactic reaction to a plasma protein contained within the transfused component
Acute haemolytic reaction from an ABO incompatible unit reacting with recipient antibodies
Febrile non-haemolytic reaction caused by recipient antibodies against donor leucocytes
Transfusion related acute lung injury from donor antibodies directed against recipient neutrophils

subtopic_detail: Incidental paraprotein and the threshold for haematology referral
stem:
A 69-year-old man is referred to you after protein electrophoresis, requested during a work up for fatigue, showed an IgG kappa paraprotein of 11 g/L. He has osteoarthritis of both knees and takes no regular medicines other than occasional paracetamol.

He reports no bone pain, no weight loss, no night sweats and no recurrent infections. Examination reveals no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly and no bony tenderness over the spine, ribs or pelvis. A whole body low dose CT reports degenerative change only, with no lytic lesions. Serum free light chain ratio is mildly abnormal at 2.1 and a bone marrow aspirate shows 6 per cent clonal plasma cells.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 132 g/L (130-175), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), creatinine 79 micromol/L (60-110), albumin 39 g/L (35-50), beta-2 microglobulin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Commence bortezomib based induction chemotherapy with an autologous transplant plan
Discharge him from follow up because the investigations show no evidence of malignancy
Arrange urgent renal biopsy to identify occult light chain deposition within the kidney
Commence zoledronic acid infusions to reduce the risk of future skeletal events
Arrange periodic clinical and laboratory surveillance without commencing any therapy

subtopic_detail: Fever in a traveller returned from a malaria endemic region
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 29-year-old man with four days of fever to 39 degrees C, shaking chills, headache and generalised aching. He returned eight days ago from three weeks visiting family in Papua New Guinea, where he stayed in a village without bed nets.

He was prescribed doxycycline prophylaxis but admits he took it irregularly and stopped once he arrived home. He has no cough, no diarrhoea, no dysuria, no rash and no neck stiffness. On examination he has mild scleral icterus and a spleen tip palpable below the left costal margin. Chest is clear and there is no focal neurological deficit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, BP 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (130-175), platelets 84 x10^9/L (150-400), white cell count 6.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), bilirubin 38 micromol/L (less than 20), creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous ceftriaxone and admit for presumed bacterial sepsis
Arrange dengue and arboviral serology and manage supportively with oral fluids
Request urgent thick and thin blood films with a rapid antigen detection test
Review again in 48 hours, since his prophylaxis makes this diagnosis unlikely
Arrange CT brain and lumbar puncture before any antimicrobial therapy is given

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing primary from secondary causes of a raised haematocrit
stem:
You review a 58-year-old man in clinic after a raised haemoglobin was found on bloods taken for tiredness. He mentions intense itching after hot showers that has troubled him for a year, and describes burning discomfort in his fingers and toes.

He has never smoked, has no cough or breathlessness, and does not snore or wake unrefreshed. His partner has never noticed him stopping breathing overnight. He drinks four standard drinks weekly and takes no testosterone or diuretics. On examination the spleen is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin and there is facial plethora. Oxygen saturation is 98 per cent on room air.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 148/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 194 g/L (130-175), haematocrit 0.58 (0.40-0.52), white cell count 13.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), platelets 512 x10^9/L (150-400), serum erythropoietin 2.1 IU/L (3.7-29.5), ferritin 18 micrograms/L (30-300)

lead_in: Which investigation will most likely confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Overnight polysomnography to identify obstructive sleep apnoea driving the erythrocytosis
Arterial blood gas analysis to detect chronic hypoxaemia from unrecognised lung disease
Computed tomography of the abdomen to seek an erythropoietin secreting renal tumour
JAK2 V617F mutation testing on a peripheral blood sample from the same venepuncture
Repeat full blood count after two weeks of increased oral fluid intake and rest

subtopic_detail: Back pain with fever after a recent bacteraemia
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 66-year-old man with four weeks of worsening mid-thoracic back pain that now wakes him every night. He was treated six weeks ago for a Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia arising from an infected forearm wound and completed two weeks of intravenous antibiotics.

He has type 2 diabetes. The pain is not relieved by rest and he has lost 4 kg. On examination there is focal tenderness on percussion over the T8 and T9 spinous processes. Lower limb power, tone, reflexes and sensation are normal, and anal tone is preserved. Plain thoracic spine radiographs are reported as showing degenerative change only.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 12.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 78 mm/h (less than 20), HbA1c 8.9 per cent (less than 6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start empirical intravenous flucloxacillin and review the response after 48 hours
Refer for physiotherapy and prescribe regular analgesia with review in four weeks
Arrange MRI of the whole spine and take blood cultures before antibiotics are given
Arrange a bone scan to localise increased skeletal uptake before further imaging
Arrange CT of the chest and abdomen to look for a primary malignancy with metastases

subtopic_detail: Interpreting incidental pleural abnormality after occupational asbestos exposure
stem:
A 68-year-old retired carpenter attends your clinic with a chest CT performed after a fall, which reports bilateral calcified pleural plaques over the diaphragmatic surfaces and posterolateral chest wall, with no pleural effusion, no pleural thickening and normal lung parenchyma. He worked with fibre cement sheeting between 1976 and 1994.

He has no breathlessness, no chest pain and no weight loss. He has never smoked. Chest expansion is symmetrical, percussion note is resonant throughout and breath sounds are normal. Spirometry shows a forced vital capacity of 96 per cent predicted with a normal ratio. He asks whether he now has asbestosis and what monitoring he needs.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: CT chest: bilateral discrete calcified pleural plaques; no diffuse pleural thickening; no nodules; no effusion. Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in one second 94 per cent predicted, forced vital capacity 96 per cent predicted, ratio 0.78

lead_in: What should you tell him about these findings?

options.text: The plaques indicate established asbestosis and warrant referral for antifibrotic therapy
The plaques require surgical decortication to prevent progressive restriction of the lung
The plaques justify six monthly CT surveillance to detect early malignant transformation
The plaques exclude any future risk of mesothelioma because they are already calcified
The plaques are a marker of past exposure, and new breathlessness or chest pain needs review

subtopic_detail: Painful prosthetic joint with an equivocal inflammatory picture
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to see a 71-year-old man with a two week history of increasing pain and swelling in his left knee, four years after a total knee replacement. He has gout affecting both first metatarsophalangeal joints and takes allopurinol irregularly.

He describes the knee as constantly sore rather than intermittently flaring, and says it has ached at rest and at night since the replacement, never quite settling. There is a warm effusion with restricted flexion and no overlying wound or sinus. He has had no recent dental work and no skin infection. The orthopaedic team have been contacted and no aspiration has yet been performed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 138/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5), serum uric acid 0.44 mmol/L (0.20-0.42); knee radiograph shows a peri-prosthetic lucency at the tibial component

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone for a presumed crystal flare and review in one week
Commence empirical oral flucloxacillin and arrange orthopaedic review as an outpatient
Arrange a radionuclide bone scan to determine whether the prosthesis has loosened
Arrange arthroscopic washout of the knee before microbiological results become available
Arrange joint aspiration for cell count, crystals and culture before any antimicrobial therapy

subtopic_detail: Calf pain on walking with an abnormal ankle brachial index
stem:
A 64-year-old woman presents to your practice with six months of cramping pain in both calves that comes on after about 200 metres of walking and settles within three minutes of standing still. The pain does not come on when she stands still at the shops and is not relieved by leaning forward over a trolley.

She smokes 15 cigarettes daily and has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Femoral pulses are palpable, both popliteal pulses are weak and neither dorsalis pedis pulse is palpable. There is no ulceration, the feet are warm and capillary refill is under two seconds. Straight leg raise is negative and lower limb power and reflexes are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, BP 156/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Ankle brachial index 0.68 on the right and 0.71 on the left; HbA1c 7.9 per cent (less than 6.0); low density lipoprotein cholesterol 3.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0 for high risk)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for urgent vascular surgical assessment with a view to early revascularisation
Arrange lumbar spine MRI to assess for canal stenosis causing neurogenic claudication
Prescribe pentoxifylline for symptom relief and review her walking distance in three months
Start a statin and antiplatelet, provide smoking cessation support and a walking program
Advise rest from walking until symptoms settle and repeat the ankle brachial index annually

subtopic_detail: Accelerated occupational lung disease in an engineered stone worker
stem:
You are the respiratory registrar assessing a 34-year-old man with eight months of exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. For the past six years he has cut and polished engineered stone benchtops in a small workshop, often dry cutting indoors without respiratory protection.

He has never smoked and takes no medicines. He has no fevers, no night sweats and no weight loss, and an interferon gamma release assay is negative. On examination there are fine inspiratory crackles at both lung bases and no clubbing. A chest radiograph reports small rounded opacities in both upper zones with bilateral hilar enlargement.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in one second 72 per cent predicted, forced vital capacity 70 per cent predicted, ratio 0.84; diffusing capacity 61 per cent predicted; angiotensin converting enzyme within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most important next step?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone and arrange review of the response after eight weeks
Commence standard four drug antituberculous therapy pending sputum culture results
Arrange bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy to obtain a histological tissue diagnosis
Remove him from further silica exposure, notify the case and arrange high resolution CT
Prescribe inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting bronchodilator and review in three months

subtopic_detail: Conduction disease with syncope and the threshold for permanent pacing
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department assessing a 77-year-old man brought in after collapsing while queueing at the post office. Bystanders say he went pale and dropped to the ground without warning, was unresponsive for perhaps 20 seconds, then recovered fully within a minute with no confusion afterwards.

He reports two similar episodes over the past month and has felt occasionally lightheaded on standing still. He takes perindopril and atorvastatin, and no rate limiting agents. Postural blood pressures show no significant drop. His ECG shows sinus rhythm at 68/min with a PR interval of 180 ms, right bundle branch block, and intermittently non-conducted P waves with no preceding PR prolongation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, BP 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium within normal limits, creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, troponin not elevated on serial testing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange an outpatient 24 hour Holter monitor and review the recording in two weeks
Prescribe compression stockings and advise increased salt and fluid intake for presyncope
Arrange an implantable loop recorder insertion and discharge him with driving advice
Admit with cardiac monitoring and refer for permanent pacemaker implantation
Commence oral theophylline to improve conduction and arrange cardiology follow up

subtopic_detail: Matching antiemetic choice to the underlying emetic mechanism
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old woman on the ward with metastatic ovarian cancer who has vomited five times since yesterday. Her oral morphine was increased two days ago for worsening pelvic pain and the nausea began the following morning.

She describes constant queasiness that is worse when she moves her head and improves when she lies still. She is opening her bowels daily on regular macrogol and has no abdominal distension. The abdomen is soft with normal bowel sounds and no succussion splash. She has had no chemotherapy for six weeks and no headache or visual change.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), urea 5.1 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 71 micromol/L (45-90); abdominal radiograph shows no dilated bowel loops and no faecal loading

lead_in: Which antiemetic is most appropriate for her?

options.text: Hyoscine butylbromide, targeting muscarinic receptors in the gastrointestinal tract
Haloperidol, targeting dopamine receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone
Metoclopramide, targeting dopamine receptors and promoting gastric emptying
Ondansetron, targeting serotonin receptors in the gut and the chemoreceptor trigger zone
Dexamethasone, targeting peritumoural oedema and raised intracranial pressure

subtopic_detail: Dry eyes and dry mouth with bilateral parotid swelling
stem:
A 52-year-old woman presents to your clinic with 18 months of gritty, burning eyes and a persistently dry mouth that makes eating dry biscuits difficult without sipping water. She has needed three dental fillings in two years after a lifetime without caries.

She also reports fatigue and aching in her hands without swelling. On examination both parotid glands are mildly enlarged and non-tender, the oral mucosa appears dry with a lobulated tongue, and there is no lymphadenopathy. There is no rash, no Raynaud phenomenon and no sclerodactyly. Her only medicine is occasional ibuprofen, and she takes no anticholinergic or antihistamine preparations.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Antinuclear antibody positive at 1:640 speckled, rheumatoid factor positive, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 46 mm/h (less than 20), C-reactive protein within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, immunoglobulin G 21 g/L (7.0-16.0)

lead_in: Which investigation will best confirm the underlying diagnosis?

options.text: Anti-double stranded DNA antibody with complement C3 and C4 levels
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody with radiographs of both hands
Serum angiotensin converting enzyme with a chest radiograph for hilar adenopathy
Anti-Ro and anti-La antibody testing with objective measurement of tear production
Fine needle aspiration of the enlarged parotid gland for cytological assessment

subtopic_detail: Progressive exertional breathlessness with normal lung fields and spirometry
stem:
You review a 47-year-old woman in clinic with 14 months of progressive breathlessness, now limiting her to one flight of stairs. She has twice felt faint while climbing hills. Two courses of inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting bronchodilator produced no benefit.

She has never smoked. Her chest is clear on auscultation, and there is no wheeze and no crackles. Jugular venous pressure is elevated 5 cm with a prominent v wave, there is a left parasternal heave, and the pulmonary component of the second heart sound is loud. There is pitting oedema to both mid-calves. Chest radiograph shows clear lung fields with enlarged central pulmonary arteries, and full blood count and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 106/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in one second 88 per cent predicted, forced vital capacity 91 per cent predicted, ratio 0.79; diffusing capacity 48 per cent predicted; ECG shows right axis deviation with dominant R wave in V1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Transthoracic echocardiography to estimate right ventricular systolic pressure
High resolution CT of the chest to identify an occult interstitial lung process
Cardiopulmonary exercise testing to distinguish cardiac from ventilatory limitation
Right heart catheterisation to measure pulmonary artery and wedge pressures directly
Bronchial provocation testing to confirm variable airflow obstruction from asthma

subtopic_detail: Deciding whether antibiotic prophylaxis is required before a dental procedure
stem:
A 58-year-old man asks your advice before a dental extraction scheduled next week. He had mitral valve repair with an annuloplasty ring eight years ago for degenerative mitral regurgitation, and a recent echocardiogram showed trivial residual regurgitation with normal ventricular function.

He has no fever, no night sweats and no weight loss. He recalls being given antibiotics before dental visits in the years immediately after surgery and stopped when a previous doctor told him it was no longer needed. He has no penicillin allergy and takes only atorvastatin. Examination reveals a soft systolic murmur at the apex, no splinter haemorrhages and no clubbing.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiography: mitral annuloplasty ring in situ, trivial mitral regurgitation, left ventricular ejection fraction 58 per cent, no vegetations

lead_in: What advice should you give regarding antibiotic prophylaxis?

options.text: Prophylaxis is not required because the repair used his own valve rather than a prosthesis
Prophylaxis is required, with a single oral amoxicillin dose before the procedure
Prophylaxis is not required because the residual regurgitation is trivial on imaging
Prophylaxis is required, with a five day oral amoxicillin course after the procedure
Prophylaxis is not required because routine daily activities cause more bacteraemia overall

subtopic_detail: Separating primary from secondary Raynaud phenomenon at first presentation
stem:
A 44-year-old woman attends your clinic because her fingers turn white then blue in the cold, with pain on rewarming. This began 10 months ago and affects the index, middle and ring fingers of both hands, sparing the thumbs.

She has noticed the skin over her fingers feels tight and that she can no longer remove her wedding ring. There is a small pitted scar at the tip of the right index finger. She has heartburn most nights that has worsened over the same period. Nailfold capillaroscopy shows dilated and dropped out capillary loops. She takes no beta blockers or ergot preparations and does not use vibrating tools.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Antinuclear antibody positive at 1:1280 nucleolar pattern, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 32 mm/h (less than 20), full blood count within normal limits, creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), urinalysis shows no protein or blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that this is a benign vasospastic disorder and advise cold avoidance measures
Prescribe a calcium channel blocker and review her symptom diary in three months
Arrange arterial duplex ultrasound of both upper limbs to exclude proximal arterial disease
Request extractable nuclear antigen testing with pulmonary function tests and echocardiography
Commence a proton pump inhibitor and review the digital symptoms again in six months

subtopic_detail: Chronic watery diarrhoea with a macroscopically normal colonoscopy
stem:
A 63-year-old woman is referred to you with eight months of watery diarrhoea, opening her bowels six to nine times daily including twice most nights. She has lost 3 kg. She has coeliac serology that is negative on a gluten containing diet, and normal thyroid function.

She takes pantoprazole started 14 months ago and sertraline. Faecal calprotectin is mildly raised, and stool cultures and parasite testing are negative. Colonoscopy was performed by a colleague and reported normal mucosa throughout to the terminal ileum, with random biopsies taken. Abdominal examination is unremarkable with no mass and no tenderness.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-165), albumin 37 g/L (35-50), C-reactive protein within normal limits, faecal calprotectin 96 micrograms/g (less than 50), tissue transglutaminase antibody negative with normal immunoglobulin A

lead_in: What is the most likely explanation for her symptoms?

options.text: Irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea predominance triggered by her antidepressant
Microscopic colitis, in which inflammation is visible only on histological examination
Bile acid diarrhoea following occult terminal ileal disease or previous cholecystectomy
Early Crohn disease with patchy inflammation not yet visible at colonoscopic examination
Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth secondary to prolonged acid suppression therapy

subtopic_detail: wet season community acquired pneumonia in a diabetic gardener in the tropical north with rapid deterioration
stem:
You are the medical registrar in Darwin in February. A 54-year-old man is admitted with four days of fever, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain, having deteriorated over the past 12 hours.

He has type 2 diabetes with a glycated haemoglobin of 9.8 per cent, drinks heavily, and spent last weekend digging drainage channels in mud around his property after heavy rain. He has not travelled outside the Northern Territory. Chest radiograph shows a right upper lobe consolidation with a small cavity. Blood cultures taken on arrival are flagged at six hours as growing a Gram negative bacillus with bipolar staining described by the laboratory as having a safety pin appearance. He was started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin in the emergency department four hours ago and has since required 6 litres of oxygen by mask, with worsening tachypnoea and hypotension.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, SpO2 91% on 6 litres per minute, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-110), lactate 4.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0), glycated haemoglobin 9.8 per cent
data_table.Imaging: Right upper lobe consolidation with a small cavity
data_table.Microbiology: Blood cultures growing a Gram negative bacillus with bipolar safety pin staining at six hours

lead_in: What antibiotic change should you make now?

options.text: Add vancomycin to cover methicillin resistant staphylococcal cavitating pneumonia
Change to intravenous meropenem, with trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole considered for eradication
Continue ceftriaxone and azithromycin and add oseltamivir for possible influenza co-infection
Switch to intravenous benzylpenicillin with doxycycline for atypical and zoonotic pathogens
Add intravenous metronidazole for anaerobic cover given the cavitating upper lobe lesion

subtopic_detail: coagulopathy after a suspected snake bite with a normal bite site and no systemic symptoms
stem: A 41-year-old man presents 90 minutes after something struck his ankle. He did not see it. A pressure immobilisation bandage is in place. He feels well, with no ptosis or weakness, and there are two faint scratches without swelling or bruising.

data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio greater than 12, fibrinogen not detected, D-dimer elevated
data_table.Logistics: Antivenom on site; tertiary centre two hours away

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Remove the bandage and repeat coagulation studies in six hours
Give fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate now
Perform a venom detection kit test and withhold treatment
Give one vial of antivenom with adrenaline prepared
Arrange retrieval and defer antivenom until arrival

subtopic_detail: recurrent night time anaphylaxis several hours after meals in a bushwalker with frequent tick exposure
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 47-year-old man who has had three episodes in four months of generalised hives, lip swelling and wheeze, each waking him between 1 am and 3 am. Two required ambulance attendance and intramuscular adrenaline.

He lives on bushland on the New South Wales north coast and has had many tick bites, with several large local reactions. Each episode followed an evening meal by four to six hours. He has eaten fish, prawns and peanuts on other evenings with no problem at all. Reviewing the three meals with him, they were a beef stir fry, a lamb roast, and pork sausages, and he had no alcohol and took no medication in the hours before any episode, with no exercise beforehand. Skin prick testing to a standard food panel including peanut, shellfish, egg, milk and wheat is negative, and he has no history of asthma.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Episode pattern: Three nocturnal episodes of urticaria, angioedema and wheeze, each four to six hours after an evening meal, two treated with intramuscular adrenaline
data_table.Dietary review: Episodes followed beef, lamb and pork meals; fish, prawns and peanuts eaten uneventfully on other evenings
data_table.Exposure: Bushland residence with numerous tick bites and several large local reactions
data_table.Investigations: Skin prick testing to a standard food panel negative

lead_in: Which investigation will best confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Serum tryptase measured at baseline and again during a subsequent acute episode
A supervised oral food challenge with beef performed in a hospital day unit
A 24 hour urinary collection for methylhistamine and prostaglandin metabolites
Patch testing to a meat panel read at 48 and 96 hours after application to the back
Specific immunoglobulin E to the carbohydrate galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose in serum

subtopic_detail: progressive exertional breathlessness in a benchtop fabricator with upper zone nodularity on imaging
stem: A 36-year-old man has 10 months of progressive exertional breathlessness and dry cough. He dry cut engineered stone benchtops in an enclosed workshop for nine years wearing an ordinary dust mask, and has never smoked.

data_table.Examination: Fine upper zone crackles, SpO2 falls from 96 to 89 per cent on walking
data_table.Imaging: Upper zone predominant nodules with conglomerate masses, hilar nodes with peripheral calcification
data_table.Investigations: Interferon gamma release assay negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Remove from dust exposure, notify, screen for complications
Prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg daily, review in three months
Antifibrotic therapy with nintedanib for the restriction
Empirical four drug therapy for tuberculosis
Surgical lung biopsy for histological pattern

subtopic_detail: facial swelling and distended chest wall veins worse on bending forward with a right hilar mass
stem: A 62-year-old woman with a 40 pack year smoking history has three weeks of facial puffiness, worst on waking and on bending forward. Chest radiograph shows a right hilar mass with superior mediastinal widening.

data_table.Examination: Facial and bilateral arm swelling, distended non-pulsatile neck veins, dilated chest wall collateral veins, no stridor

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start high dose dexamethasone and arrange mediastinal radiotherapy before biopsy
Insert a femoral central line and start therapeutic anticoagulation
Arrange outpatient respiratory review in two weeks with bronchoscopy
Refer for immediate endovascular stenting before establishing the diagnosis
Perform contrast computed tomography of the chest and sample the mass

subtopic_detail: watery diarrhoea eight weeks into immunotherapy with negative stool studies and rectal bleeding
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 61-year-old man who has received four cycles of pembrolizumab for metastatic melanoma over eight weeks. He describes nine days of watery diarrhoea, now eight to ten times daily including twice overnight, with cramping and streaks of fresh blood in the stool.

He has lost 4 kg. He has not travelled, has taken no antibiotics and no new medications, and no one else at home is unwell. He has no fever and no vomiting. Stool microscopy and culture, a nucleic acid test for Clostridioides difficile toxin and a stool viral panel are all negative. Computed tomography of the abdomen shows diffuse colonic wall thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement and pericolic stranding, with no perforation, no abscess and no obstruction. His melanoma has responded, with reduction in the size of the liver and lung deposits on the same scan.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 78 mg/L (less than 5), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), stool cultures and Clostridioides difficile toxin negative
data_table.Imaging: Diffuse colonic wall thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement and pericolic stranding, no perforation or abscess
data_table.Treatment history: Four cycles of pembrolizumab over eight weeks with radiological response of metastatic disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start loperamide with oral rehydration and continue the next cycle of immunotherapy as scheduled
Withhold the immunotherapy and start high dose intravenous methylprednisolone with early gastroenterology review
Give empirical oral vancomycin for presumed Clostridioides difficile infection despite the negative test
Begin infliximab immediately as first line therapy, bypassing corticosteroids to prevent perforation
Cease the immunotherapy permanently and provide supportive care only with no immunosuppression

subtopic_detail: hot swollen midfoot with intact skin and normal inflammatory markers in long standing neuropathy
stem:
You are the doctor in a diabetes clinic. A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes of 19 years duration reports three weeks of a swollen, red, warm right foot. He has continued walking on it and working as a delivery driver throughout.

He has dense peripheral neuropathy and cannot feel the 10 g monofilament anywhere on either foot. He describes only a dull ache rather than pain. The right midfoot is swollen and about 4 degrees Celsius warmer than the left on infrared measurement, with intact skin, no ulcer, no break in the skin anywhere and no discharge. Foot pulses are easily palpable and his toe pressures are normal. He is systemically well and afebrile. Plain radiographs of the foot are reported as showing no fracture and no bone destruction, and blood tests taken today have returned. The swelling is reduced but not abolished when the foot is elevated for ten minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Swollen erythematous right midfoot 4 degrees Celsius warmer than the left, intact skin with no ulcer, palpable pedal pulses, absent monofilament sensation bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 7.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), glycated haemoglobin 8.1 per cent
data_table.Imaging: Plain radiographs reported as showing no fracture and no bone destruction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe oral flucloxacillin for two weeks and review the foot in the clinic afterwards
Start colchicine and check a serum urate level, treating this as an acute crystal arthropathy
Arrange compression stockings and diuretics for presumed dependent oedema of the lower limb
Refer urgently for vascular assessment and angiography given the unilateral erythema and swelling
Immobilise in a total contact cast with no weight bearing and arrange magnetic resonance imaging

subtopic_detail: sudden proximal limb paralysis on waking after a carbohydrate heavy meal with a suppressed thyrotropin
stem: A 28-year-old man woke unable to lift his legs after a large carbohydrate meal. Proximal power is 2 out of 5 in the legs and 3 out of 5 in the arms, with normal distal power and sensation. He has a fine tremor and a goitre.

data_table.Investigations: Potassium 2.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L, free thyroxine 38 pmol/L (10-20)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Rapid potassium replacement at 40 mmol per hour intravenously
Intravenous immunoglobulin for an acute polyradiculoneuropathy
Urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the spinal cord
Intravenous calcium gluconate, then insulin with dextrose
Cautious potassium replacement with a non-selective beta blocker

subtopic_detail: new jaundice with tender hepatomegaly after decades of heavy drinking and a markedly raised discriminant function
stem: A 51-year-old man has three weeks of deepening jaundice and anorexia. He drinks 20 standard drinks daily, last two days ago. He is afebrile, oriented without asterixis, with a smooth tender liver 4 cm below the costal margin.

data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 290 micromol/L, AST 186 U/L, ALT 78 U/L, INR 2.1 (control 1.0), white cell count 14.2 x10^9/L
data_table.Screening: Echogenic liver with patent veins; viral, autoimmune and metabolic screens normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment decision now?

options.text: Oral prednisolone with infection screening and day seven review
N-acetylcysteine infusion for paracetamol injury
Empirical piperacillin with tazobactam for 48 hours
Urgent transjugular liver biopsy before drug therapy
Thiamine, nutrition and withdrawal management alone

subtopic_detail: quotidian fevers with an evanescent salmon rash and sore throat in a young adult with extreme hyperferritinaemia
stem: A 27-year-old woman has a second admission in six weeks with fever to 39.5 degrees C each evening, settling by morning. A salmon coloured rash appears during the spikes and fades within hours. A sore throat and joint pain persist despite a week of ceftriaxone.

data_table.Investigations: White cells 21.6 x10^9/L, CRP 190 mg/L, ferritin 9800 micrograms/L (30-300)
data_table.Other: Blood cultures, antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor and viral serology negative; echocardiogram normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Culture negative endocarditis needing extended incubation
Systemic lupus erythematosus with fever and arthralgia
Lymphoma with B symptoms, splenomegaly and nodes
Acute rheumatic fever after streptococcal pharyngitis
Adult onset Still disease with systemic inflammation

subtopic_detail: sensory ataxia with brisk knee reflexes and absent ankle jerks in a young adult using recreational gas canisters
stem:
You are the neurology registrar. A 22-year-old man reports six weeks of numbness and tingling in his feet that has climbed to mid calf, with unsteadiness that is much worse in the dark and in the shower with his eyes closed.

He uses whipped cream chargers recreationally, inhaling up to 50 canisters on a weekend night for the past eight months. He does not drink alcohol, uses no other substances, eats a mixed diet including meat, and takes no medication. On examination vibration and joint position sense are markedly reduced to the knees, pinprick is reduced in a stocking distribution, knee reflexes are brisk with an extensor plantar response on the right, and ankle jerks are absent. Romberg test is positive. Power is 4 plus out of 5 in ankle dorsiflexion bilaterally, and there are no cranial nerve signs, no bladder symptoms and no cognitive change.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Reduced vibration and proprioception to the knees, brisk knee reflexes with absent ankle jerks, right extensor plantar, positive Romberg test
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (130-175), mean cell volume 104 fL (80-100), serum vitamin B12 210 pmol/L (150-700), homocysteine 42 micromol/L (less than 15), methylmalonic acid elevated
data_table.Substance use: Up to 50 nitrous oxide canisters per weekend night for eight months, no alcohol or other substances

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral thiamine and refer to a drug and alcohol service for assessment of alcohol use
Arrange nerve conduction studies before treatment to characterise the neuropathy fully
Prescribe pregabalin for neuropathic symptoms and review him in the clinic in six weeks
Give intravenous methylprednisolone for a presumed first demyelinating event of the spinal cord
Cease the inhalant use and start parenteral hydroxocobalamin with neurology follow up

subtopic_detail: unilateral neck pain with a small pupil and droopy lid days before focal weakness in a young adult
stem: A 38-year-old woman had 40 minutes of right arm weakness and slurred speech that has almost resolved. Five days ago she developed left neck and periorbital pain after overhead lifting.

data_table.Examination: Mild left ptosis with a small reactive left pupil, no facial anhidrosis, right pronator drift
data_table.Other: Brain computed tomography normal, electrocardiogram sinus rhythm, no vascular risk factors

lead_in: Which investigation should be requested now?

options.text: Transthoracic echocardiography with a bubble study for patent foramen ovale
Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage
Immediate computed tomography angiography of the neck and head vessels
Temporal artery ultrasound with an urgent erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Prolonged ambulatory cardiac monitoring for 14 days for atrial fibrillation

subtopic_detail: prolonged fever with hepatitis in an abattoir worker after calving season with negative routine cultures
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 44-year-old man with three weeks of daily fevers, drenching sweats, severe headache and profound fatigue. He has lost 6 kg and describes muscle aches across his shoulders and thighs.

He works at an abattoir in regional Queensland and also helps at a neighbouring property, where he assisted with several calvings six weeks ago and disposed of placental material. He has not travelled overseas, has no sick contacts, and has not been bitten by a tick or mosquito that he noticed. Examination shows a temperature of 38.9 degrees Celsius with a soft non-tender abdomen, no rash, no lymphadenopathy and no murmur. Two sets of blood cultures taken a week apart are negative. Chest radiograph is clear, and abdominal ultrasound shows a normal liver and spleen with no focal lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), platelets 132 x10^9/L (150-400), alanine aminotransferase 180 U/L (less than 35), alkaline phosphatase 160 U/L (30-110), C-reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5)
data_table.Microbiology: Two sets of blood cultures a week apart negative, chest radiograph clear
data_table.Exposure history: Abattoir work in regional Queensland, assisted with calvings and disposed of placental material six weeks ago

lead_in: Which test is most likely to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Thick and thin blood films examined for malarial parasites on three separate occasions
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to investigate a possible haematological malignancy
Positron emission tomography to localise a focus of occult infection or inflammation
Transoesophageal echocardiography to exclude culture negative infective endocarditis
Paired serology for Coxiella burnetii taken now and repeated two to three weeks later

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy - antibiotic selection
stem: A 28-year-old woman at 24+2 weeks gestation has 24 hours of right loin pain, rigors and vomiting, and 4 days of dysuria. She has no allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, temperature 39.0 degrees C, fetal heart rate 154 /min
data_table.Examination: Right renal angle tenderness, no contractions
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick 3+ nitrites and leukocytes; CTG reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for ten days
Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for seven days at home
Intravenous gentamicin and amoxicillin for seven days
Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily, then oral cefalexin
Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for five days

subtopic_detail: Migraine preventive selection in a patient with prior ischaemic stroke
stem: A 44-year-old woman has had migraine with aura since her teens, now six attacks a month relieved by sumatriptan. Two years ago she had a right occipital ischaemic stroke and percutaneous closure of a patent foramen ovale; she takes aspirin 100 mg daily. Blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg and she has no asthma.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line preventive?

options.text: A norethisterone-only regimen for cycle-linked prophylaxis
Amitriptyline 10 mg nightly, up-titrated to 75 mg nightly
Topiramate 25 mg nightly, titrated to 100 mg daily
Verapamil sustained release 240 mg daily as prevention
Propranolol 20 mg twice daily, up-titrated to 40 mg

subtopic_detail: IV iron indication after oral failure in inflammatory bowel disease
stem: A 32-year-old man with ulcerative colitis in remission on mesalazine stopped ferrous sulfate after eight weeks because of severe cramping and nausea. Repeat testing shows persistent microcytic anaemia and no overt bleeding.

data_table.Full blood count: Haemoglobin 102 g/L, mean cell volume 74 fL
data_table.Iron studies: Ferritin 8 microg/L, transferrin saturation 8 per cent, calprotectin 92 microg/g

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Alternate day ferrous fumarate for eight weeks, then repeat the count
Transfuse two units of red cells, then give intravenous iron
Four weekly intramuscular iron polymaltose 250 mg injections
Refer for elective total colectomy for ongoing occult blood loss
Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg intravenously as a single dose

subtopic_detail: Denosumab discontinuation and the rebound vertebral fracture window
stem: A 71-year-old woman has taken denosumab 60 mg six-monthly for four years for postmenopausal osteoporosis and now wishes to stop. Her next dose is due in three weeks. She had a wrist fracture ten years ago.

data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.36 mmol/L, eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m^2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate way to stop denosumab?

options.text: Continue denosumab indefinitely as the rebound risk is unavoidable
Skip the next dose with calcium and vitamin D cover
Give the next dose, then zoledronic acid 5 mg six months later
Switch now to teriparatide without any bisphosphonate cover
Continue calcium alone and repeat densitometry in 24 months

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in known primary adrenal insufficiency triggered by gastroenteritis
stem: A 38-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency on hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone has vomited and had diarrhoea for 24 hours, keeping nothing down since 6 am. She is drowsy and cool peripherally.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.8 mmol/L, glucose 3.9 mmol/L, creatinine 132 micromol/L (baseline 68)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Saline 20 mL/kg and increase oral hydrocortisone to 40 mg
Treat the hyperkalaemia first with calcium and insulin-dextrose
Dexamethasone 8 mg intravenously to preserve synacthen testing
Hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously with 1 L saline over an hour
3% saline for the hyponatraemia, delaying hydrocortisone

subtopic_detail: Clinically isolated syndrome and application of McDonald 2017 criteria
