stem: A 29-year-old woman has a first episode of right optic neuritis, improving over two weeks. The rest of the neurological examination is normal.

data_table.MRI: Two periventricular and one juxtacortical T2 lesions, one enhancing with gadolinium; spinal cord normal
data_table.CSF and serology: Two oligoclonal bands unique to CSF; aquaporin-4 IgG and MOG-IgG negative; mimic screen negative

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnose clinically isolated syndrome and re-image in three months
Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for five days as sole therapy
Treat empirically as neuromyelitis optica with monthly rituximab
Diagnose relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis and refer to neurology
Repeat MOG-IgG and JCV serology before making any diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion in the acute retroviral syndrome window
stem: A 24-year-old man has two weeks of fever, sore throat, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, a palatal ulcer and a truncal rash. He had condomless receptive anal sex four weeks ago without pre-exposure prophylaxis.

data_table.Investigations: Fourth generation HIV antigen-antibody test reactive, Western blot indeterminate; Epstein-Barr and cytomegalovirus IgM negative; platelets 118 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent same day HIV RNA with specialist referral for antiretrovirals
Discharge with safe sex advice and primary care review in four weeks
Start 28 days of post-exposure prophylaxis with tenofovir and raltegravir
Repeat the combination test in six weeks, treating as glandular fever
Start corticosteroids, deferring therapy until CD4 falls below 500

subtopic_detail: Direct oral anticoagulant reversal in life-threatening intracranial haemorrhage
stem: A 78-year-old woman on apixaban 5 mg twice daily fell 90 minutes ago with sudden headache and left hemiparesis. Last dose over 8 hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 202/118 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: CT brain 40 mL basal ganglia haemorrhage with 6 mm midline shift; INR 1.2; eGFR 34; anti-Xa pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal strategy?

options.text: Await the anti-Xa level; give tranexamic acid 1 g meanwhile
Prothrombin complex concentrate 50 IU/kg with vitamin K 10 mg
Idarucizumab 5 g intravenously with two units of fresh frozen plasma
Andexanet alfa 400 mg bolus then infusion; systolic below 140 mmHg
Protamine sulfate 50 mg and two units of packed red cells

subtopic_detail: Acute Stanford type A aortic dissection with malperfusion
stem: A 62-year-old man with hypertension developed sudden tearing interscapular pain 90 minutes ago. His left arm is cold and pulseless, the right femoral pulse absent and the right leg 2/5 weak.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 178/98 mmHg right arm, 82/54 mmHg left
data_table.Investigations: CT aortogram: Stanford type A dissection from the root beyond the left renal artery; small pericardial effusion, no tamponade

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Esmolol to heart rate 60, then nitroprusside; call surgeons
Nitroprusside alone to systolic 110 mmHg, admit to cardiology
Intravenous heparin infusion for the limb and renal ischaemia
Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg for the presumed arch-vessel stroke
Bedside pericardiocentesis before theatre transfer

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant adult woman
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 32-year-old woman with two days of dysuria and urinary frequency. She has had three previous urinary tract infections in her lifetime, most recently 18 months ago, all uncomplicated and community-acquired. She is not pregnant, is not immunocompromised, has no diabetes, and has no history of pyelonephritis or renal tract abnormality.

She denies fever, flank pain, nausea, and vomiting. There has been no recent overseas travel and no recent hospitalisation. She has no drug allergies.

On examination her observations are within normal limits; the abdomen is soft with mild suprapubic tenderness and no flank tenderness. Bedside urinalysis is nitrite positive with 3+ leukocyte esterase.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, mild suprapubic tenderness, no flank tenderness, no vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis nitrite positive, leukocytes 3+, urine microscopy and culture sent, urine hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic?

options.text: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally twice daily for 3 days as empirical first-line for uncomplicated cystitis
Amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for 5 days as empirical first-line for uncomplicated cystitis
Trimethoprim 300 mg orally at night for 3 days OR nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly for 5 days
Cefalexin 500 mg orally 12-hourly for 5 days as empirical first-line therapy for uncomplicated cystitis
Fosfomycin 3 g single oral dose as empirical first-line therapy for uncomplicated community cystitis

subtopic_detail: Disposition after emergency treatment of hyperkalaemia has worked
stem: A 64-year-old man was treated two hours ago in the emergency department for hyperkalaemia with electrocardiogram changes. His culprit medicines have been ceased. He feels well and asks to go home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 7.3 mmol/L on arrival, now 5.4 mmol/L; ECG now normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Admit for cardiac monitoring and repeat potassium testing
Discharge home with repeat potassium testing in one week
Discharge home with dietary potassium advice and review
Observe for one hour then discharge with resonium
Discharge with a cardiology outpatient appointment arranged

subtopic_detail: PE evaluation with age-adjusted D-dimer
stem:
An 82-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 1 day of right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild breathlessness. Apart from hypertension she is well, with no previous venous thromboembolism, cancer, recent surgery or immobilisation. She has not coughed up blood. Her medicines are amlodipine 5 mg and atorvastatin 20 mg daily.

After examining her and reviewing the chest X-ray and ECG, you judge PE to be the most likely diagnosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.9°C
data_table.Examination: Chest clear; no calf swelling or tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Chest X-ray normal; ECG sinus rhythm 88 /min; D-dimer 0.64 mg/L FEU (<0.50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange CT pulmonary angiography now, as the D-dimer is above the laboratory cut-off
Arrange a ventilation-perfusion scan instead of CTPA, to avoid contrast at her age
Do no imaging for PE, as the D-dimer is below the threshold adjusted for her age
Start therapeutic enoxaparin and arrange CT pulmonary angiography for tomorrow
Apply the PERC rule and discharge her without testing if all 8 criteria are met

subtopic_detail: Infective endocarditis empirical therapy by valve type
stem: A 58-year-old man with a mitral valve prosthesis inserted two years ago has six days of fever, a new murmur and a tender nodule on a finger pulp. Three blood culture sets are positive with Gram positive cocci in clusters, speciation pending.

data_table.Echocardiography: 12 mm mobile vegetation on the mitral prosthetic ring
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 92 mg/L, white cell count 12.6 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic combination?

options.text: Vancomycin with rifampicin 600 mg 12-hourly and gentamicin
Flucloxacillin 2 g four-hourly as intravenous monotherapy
Benzylpenicillin 1.8 g four-hourly with once daily gentamicin
Ceftriaxone 2 g daily with oral doxycycline 100 mg
Meropenem 1 g eight-hourly until sensitivities return

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in intercurrent illness
stem: A 42-year-old man with Addison disease is admitted with pneumonia. He has vomited everything since yesterday and has taken no hydrocortisone. Despite 1 L of sodium chloride he is confused with severe abdominal pain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 /min, BP 88/56 mmHg supine, 72/44 sitting
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.8 mmol/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, cortisol sample sent

lead_in: What is the most important next intervention?

options.text: Give a 500 mL sodium chloride bolus and await the cortisol
Give intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg now with fluid resuscitation
Give intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg to avoid cortisol assay interference
Give oral hydrocortisone 40 mg with intravenous ondansetron 4 mg
Give a 500 mL dextrose bolus and a fludrocortisone infusion

subtopic_detail: Diabetic foot osteomyelitis diagnostic pathway and antibiotic duration
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 20 years and peripheral neuropathy. He presents with a plantar ulcer over the fifth metatarsal head that has been present for eight weeks. He has attended community wound care but the ulcer has not healed. He has never had osteomyelitis.

On examination the ulcer is 2 cm across with granulating base; a sterile probe passes freely to bone at the base of the ulcer. He is systemically well with normal observations. There is no cellulitis and no fluctuance.

Plain radiograph shows subtle cortical erosion under the fifth metatarsal head; ESR is 96 mm/h and CRP 42 mg/L. HbA1c is 79 mmol/mol.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: 2 cm plantar ulcer over fifth metatarsal head with clean granulating base, probe-to-bone positive, no cellulitis, no fluctuance, reduced monofilament sensation to ankle
data_table.Investigations: ESR 96 mm/h (<15), CRP 42 mg/L (<5), HbA1c 79 mmol/mol, creatinine 92 micromol/L, white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L, foot X-ray: subtle cortical erosion at fifth metatarsal head

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral flucloxacillin 500 mg 6 hourly for 14 days empirically without any further investigation now
Send superficial swab of the ulcer surface for microbiology and start amoxicillin-clavulanate empirically
Arrange MRI foot to define bone involvement plus bone biopsy for targeted antibiotics for at least 6 weeks
Refer directly for below-knee amputation because chronic diabetic osteomyelitis has universally poor healing
Request nuclear medicine bone scan and treat with amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily while awaiting results

subtopic_detail: Massive haemoptysis - lateral positioning and bronchial arteriography
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department when a 54-year-old man with long-standing bronchiectasis is brought in by ambulance. He has coughed up around 350 mL of fresh red blood over the last 40 minutes in three episodes at home. His observations on arrival: pulse 128, BP 96/60, SpO2 92% on 10 L via non-rebreather. Chest X-ray shows dense right upper zone consolidation.

You know from previous imaging that his major cavity is right upper lobe, and multiple prior CT reports have suggested his bleeding is right-sided.

He has continued to spit bright red blood into the emesis bag during the initial assessment; the anaesthetic and interventional radiology teams have been paged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 /min, SpO2 92% on 10 L non-rebreather, temperature 37.2 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, coughing bright red blood, chest crackles bilaterally worse right upper zone, fresh blood on lips, no obvious epistaxis
data_table.Investigations: Bedside haemoglobin 96 g/L (baseline 128), INR 1.1, platelets 168 x10^9/L, chest X-ray: dense right upper zone opacity with air bronchograms

lead_in: What is the single best immediate management step (before definitive bronchial artery embolisation)?

options.text: Perform emergency CT pulmonary angiogram before any positioning change or airway intervention or transfer
Position supine with head-up tilt, intubate, and start intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes now
Start non-invasive ventilation and give nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 solution as first-line control
Right lateral decubitus positioning (bleeding-side down), activate massive transfusion, expedite embolisation
Refer directly to thoracic surgery for emergency lobectomy without prior imaging or bronchial artery embolisation

subtopic_detail: Ischaemic stroke thrombolysis contraindications with recent surgery
stem:
You are the stroke registrar in a comprehensive stroke centre reviewing a 68-year-old woman brought in by ambulance with left facial droop and left arm weakness noted by her husband on waking 90 minutes ago. She was last known well when she went to bed at 22:00 the previous night. Non-contrast CT brain excludes haemorrhage and shows a subtle hyperdense right middle cerebral artery sign; CT angiogram confirms right M1 occlusion; CT perfusion shows a small ischaemic core with a large penumbra.

Her history includes an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy nine days ago. She is otherwise on aspirin 100 mg only. There is no history of intracerebral haemorrhage, no recent significant head trauma, and no active bleeding.

Her blood pressure is 172/94, glucose 6.8 mmol/L, INR 1.0, and platelets 260 x10^9/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 172/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: NIHSS 12: left facial droop, left arm 2/5, left leg 4/5, dysarthria, left homonymous hemianopia; laparoscopic port sites healing
data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT: hyperdense right MCA sign, no haemorrhage. CT angiogram: right M1 occlusion. CT perfusion: core 12 mL, penumbra 88 mL, mismatch ratio 8. INR 1.0, platelets 260, glucose 6.8

lead_in: What is the single best next step in reperfusion management?

options.text: Give intravenous tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg then transfer immediately for endovascular thrombectomy on M1 lesion
Await MRI diffusion-weighted imaging before deciding on any reperfusion strategy including thrombectomy today
Manage with intravenous aspirin 300 mg and admission to the stroke unit without any reperfusion intervention
Give reduced-dose alteplase 0.6 mg/kg and defer endovascular thrombectomy for 24 hours awaiting stability
Proceed directly to endovascular thrombectomy without intravenous thrombolysis given the recent 9-day surgery

subtopic_detail: Unprovoked PE anticoagulation duration
stem: A 58-year-old man is reviewed three months after a first unprovoked segmental pulmonary embolism. He has taken apixaban 5 mg twice daily with no bleeding. He has no thrombophilia, no family history of venous thromboembolism and no malignancy on age-appropriate screening.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73 m2, HAS-BLED score 1

lead_in: What anticoagulation plan is most appropriate from now?

options.text: Switch to warfarin for nine further months, then cease
Cease apixaban after three further months at full dose
Continue apixaban indefinitely at 2.5 mg twice daily
Cease apixaban and start aspirin 100 mg daily instead
Insert an inferior vena cava filter and cease apixaban

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis empirical therapy
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar admitting a 42-year-old woman with two days of right sided loin pain, fever and dysuria. She reports vomiting twice this morning and cannot tolerate oral fluids. She has no history of urological surgery, renal stones or recurrent UTI. She is not pregnant and has no known drug allergies.

On examination she is warm and flushed with tender right renal angle percussion. Abdomen is soft with mild suprapubic tenderness. Chest is clear. She has no rigors currently but had one this morning.

Urinalysis: leukocytes 3+, nitrites positive, blood 1+. Midstream urine sample sent. Blood cultures drawn from a peripheral cannula. She has not received any antibiotics in the past three months. She has no history of recent overseas travel or antibiotic resistance.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Right renal angle tenderness, mild suprapubic tenderness, no peritonism, no vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: White cells 16.8 x10^9/L, CRP 168 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L (baseline 70), urinalysis leucocytes 3+ nitrites positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for seven days at the current outpatient dosing regimen from home
Intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily with intravenous amoxicillin 2 g every 6 hours empirically
Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for ten days at outpatient dosing on discharge from hospital
Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily as inpatient therapy
Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg four times daily for seven days at outpatient dosing on ward discharge

subtopic_detail: DKA fluid choice in adult
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 34-year-old man with a two day history of vomiting, polyuria and polydipsia. He has established type 1 diabetes on twice daily insulin who has been unwell with viral gastroenteritis and reduced his insulin doses. He is drowsy but orientated on arrival.

Capillary blood glucose is 26.4 mmol/L. Venous pH 7.14, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, ketones 5.6 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), chloride 100 mmol/L. Creatinine 132 micromol/L (baseline 78 six months ago). His weight is 78 kg. Urinalysis: ketones 3+, glucose 3+.

He has no cardiac or renal comorbidity and no chest pain. Chest x-ray is clear. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 118 with peaked T waves in the precordial leads.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 /min with Kussmaul pattern, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, capillary refill 3 s, drowsy GCS 14, Kussmaul respiration, acetone breath
data_table.Investigations: As above; POC glucose 26.4 mmol/L, venous pH 7.14, bicarbonate 8, ketones 5.6, sodium 132, potassium 5.6, creatinine 132

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid regimen?

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol infusion over 2 hours to correct the venous pH before insulin
Intravenous 5% dextrose 1 L over 1 hour to protect against hypoglycaemia during insulin infusion start
Intravenous 0.45% sodium chloride 1 L over 1 hour to avoid hyperchloraemia and correct free water deficit
Intravenous 0.9% saline 1 L over 1 hour, reassess potassium, then start fixed rate insulin infusion
Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L with 40 mmol/L potassium chloride over 1 hour with insulin start

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis hydrocortisone dosing
stem: A 46-year-old man with Addison disease has 24 hours of vomiting, abdominal pain and light headedness. He has kept no hydrocortisone down and stopped all medication yesterday.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, BP 84/56 mmHg lying, systolic 68 on standing
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.4 mmol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L (baseline 82), cortisol and ACTH sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 40 mg now, observing for oral tolerance
Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg with 1 L of sodium chloride
Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg, awaiting the synacthen result
Intravenous fludrocortisone 100 microgram, observing the response
Hypertonic saline 3 percent, 100 mL, deferring steroid

subtopic_detail: SJS/TEN immediate management
stem: A 58-year-old woman has two days of fever and a painful rash that began on her chest and blistered overnight. She started allopurinol 300 mg for gout three weeks ago.

data_table.Examination: Flaccid bullae and desquamation over 12 per cent of body surface, positive Nikolsky sign, erosions of lips, conjunctivae and genitalia
data_table.Investigations: White cells 14.2 x10^9/L, creatinine 148 micromol/L (baseline 118), T 38.4 degrees C

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue allopurinol, add prednisolone 50 mg daily
Cease allopurinol, transfer to a burns unit, supportive care
Skin biopsy today with empirical amoxicillin clavulanate
Topical steroid at home with dermatology review
Restart allopurinol at 100 mg and add azathioprine

subtopic_detail: Myasthenic crisis management
stem: A 52-year-old woman with antibody positive myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine and prednisolone has two weeks of worsening bulbar and limb weakness. Azithromycin was started two days ago for a chest infection. She is now breathless at rest with nasal regurgitation of liquids.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis, weak neck flexion, single breath count 15
data_table.Investigations: Vital capacity 780 mL (12 mL/kg), negative inspiratory force -18 cmH2O, pCO2 47 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intensive care, cease azithromycin, start plasma exchange
Increase pyridostigmine to 90 mg six times daily
Pulse intravenous methylprednisolone on the ward
Urgent oesophagoscopy to assess her swallowing difficulty
Intravenous edrophonium 10 mg as a diagnostic test

subtopic_detail: Warfarin ICH reversal and BP
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 78-year-old woman brought in by ambulance with sudden onset right sided weakness and dysphasia one hour ago. She is on warfarin for atrial fibrillation, target INR 2-3. She takes no other anticoagulant or antiplatelet.

On arrival she is drowsy but rousable, GCS 12 (E3 V3 M6), has a dense right hemiparesis (0/5 arm, 1/5 leg) and expressive dysphasia. Vital signs show blood pressure 218/118 mmHg and heart rate 98 irregular. Non contrast CT head shows a 32 mL left basal ganglia haematoma with no intraventricular extension, midline shift 3 mm. There is no evidence of a large vessel occlusion on CT angiogram.

Urgent bloods return INR 3.4, haemoglobin 128 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L. She is otherwise haemodynamically stable and there is no external bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98 /min irregular, blood pressure 218/118 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: GCS 12, dense right hemiparesis, expressive dysphasia, no external bleeding, no signs of trauma
data_table.Investigations: INR 3.4, haemoglobin 128, platelets 240, creatinine 92, CT head 32 mL left basal ganglia haematoma with 3 mm midline shift

lead_in: What is the most appropriate combination of interventions in the first hour?

options.text: IV vitamin K 10 mg plus PCC 50 units/kg now, and IV labetalol titrated to systolic 130 to 140 in 1 hour
Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg without prothrombin complex concentrate and permissive hypertension
Intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg for suspected stroke and hold blood pressure treatment pending review
Vitamin K 10 mg intravenous alone and monitor INR every 6 hours without prothrombin complex concentrate
Idarucizumab 5 g intravenous for anticoagulant reversal with blood pressure target 180 over 100 mmHg

subtopic_detail: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis thresholds in newly diagnosed HIV
stem:
You are the infectious diseases registrar reviewing a 32-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV. He presented with 2 weeks of dry cough, exertional dyspnoea and 4 kg weight loss. He is now hospitalised. His viral load is 380,000 copies/mL and his CD4 count returned this afternoon. Chest X ray shows bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates. He has been started on treatment doses of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for suspected Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia after bronchoalveolar lavage. Toxoplasma IgG is positive. Cytomegalovirus IgG positive.

He has never taken antiretroviral therapy. The infectious diseases consultant is planning to start dolutegravir plus tenofovir alafenamide and emtricitabine after 2 weeks. He asks what other prophylactic antimicrobials to start now given the CD4 result.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106 /min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 92% on 2 L nasal prongs, temperature 38.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, mucosal candidiasis, fine crackles bilaterally, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: CD4 count 42 cells/microL, viral load 380,000 copies/mL, toxoplasma IgG positive, cytomegalovirus IgG positive, cryptococcal antigen negative

lead_in: Which opportunistic infection prophylaxis regimen best matches ASHM guidance for this CD4 count?

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength daily for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis only at this point in his HIV care
Fluconazole 200 mg daily for oral candidiasis treatment and primary cryptococcosis prevention at this point in his HIV care today
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength daily (covers Pneumocystis and toxoplasmosis) plus azithromycin 1200 mg weekly for MAC prophylaxis
Isoniazid 300 mg daily for 9 months regardless of tuberculosis screening result, given the low CD4 count at this presentation today
Valganciclovir 900 mg daily for primary cytomegalovirus prophylaxis given the positive cytomegalovirus IgG serology reported today

subtopic_detail: Hour-1 bundle in septic shock
stem: A 68-year-old woman with pneumonia is confused and hypotensive 30 minutes into her sepsis screen. Cultures, lactate and imaging are done, intravenous access is in, and she has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, BP 84/48 mmHg, mean arterial pressure 60 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 145 micromol/L, right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: Which combination best matches the hour-1 sepsis bundle?

options.text: Antibiotics within 3 hours, 500 mL fluid, lactate at 6 hours
Ceftriaxone alone, no fluid until vasopressor, target 65 mmHg
Amoxicillin and gentamicin, 10 mL/kg fluid, await lactate fall
Ceftriaxone with azithromycin within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid
Meropenem alone, 20 mL/kg saline, noradrenaline to 75 mmHg

subtopic_detail: Tension pneumothorax vs primary spontaneous pneumothorax management pathway
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar attending a 22-year-old tall thin man who presented with sudden left sided pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea while sitting studying. He is not hypoxic, tolerating conversation and haemodynamically stable. There is no trauma. His symptoms started 2 hours ago and are worse on deep inspiration. He has no prior lung disease. He is a light social smoker. Chest X ray done 30 minutes ago shows a left sided pneumothorax with an intrapleural distance of 2 cm at the level of the hilum, no mediastinal shift, no surgical emphysema.

He is comfortable now. There is no clinical evidence of tension. His observations have been stable for 30 minutes on room air.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Reduced breath sounds left upper zone, resonant to percussion, no tracheal deviation, no jugular venous distension
data_table.Investigations: Chest X ray left pneumothorax with 2 cm intrapleural distance at hilum, no mediastinal shift, no other lung pathology; blood gases not done

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate needle thoracostomy at the second intercostal space midclavicular line with a 14 gauge cannula on the affected side
Insert an intercostal catheter 28 French to underwater seal drain in the fifth intercostal space anterior axillary line
Discharge home with paracetamol as needed and no imaging follow up because he is now clinically asymptomatic at rest
Commence high flow nasal cannula at 40 L/min to accelerate pleural air reabsorption over the next 24 hours on ward
Admit for observation with supplemental oxygen; if breathless or the pneumothorax progresses use needle aspiration first

subtopic_detail: First line biochemical test for suspected Cushing syndrome
stem: A 46-year-old woman has 12 months of central weight gain, easy bruising, proximal weakness, a dorsocervical fat pad and purple abdominal striae. Her blood pressure is 168/98 mmHg on ramipril and amlodipine, and type 2 diabetes was diagnosed 8 months ago. She has never taken corticosteroids.

data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.4 mmol/L, haemoglobin A1c 9.8 percent, 8 am serum cortisol 720 nmol/L (140-690)

lead_in: Which first line screening test is most appropriate?

options.text: Two separate 24 hour urinary free cortisol collections
A single random daytime serum cortisol from clinic
A single 8 am serum adrenocorticotropic hormone level
Contrast enhanced computed tomography of the pituitary
A high dose 8 mg dexamethasone suppression test

subtopic_detail: Multiple sclerosis: dissemination in time and space criteria
stem: A 28-year-old woman has 4 days of right visual blurring with pain on eye movement. Eight months ago she had right hand clumsiness for 10 days that resolved untreated. She has a right relative afferent pupillary defect.

data_table.Magnetic resonance imaging: Two periventricular T2 lesions, one enhancing; a juxtacortical lesion and a C4 cord lesion, neither enhancing

lead_in: Do these findings meet the 2017 McDonald criteria?

options.text: No, a third attack in a new location is required
Yes, two attacks with dissemination in space and time
No, cord lesions do not count for dissemination
No, the attacks must be within 30 days of each other
No, aquaporin 4 antibody must be negative

subtopic_detail: Pattern recognition in antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody vasculitis
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 62-year-old woman with 3 months of sinusitis, epistaxis, saddle nose deformity noted on physical examination, migratory joint pains, and a new 2 week history of haemoptysis with breathlessness. On admission today she has developed rising creatinine and 4 red cell casts on urine microscopy consistent with active glomerulonephritis. She has no fever. Her chest computed tomography demonstrates multiple bilateral nodules with cavitation and patchy alveolar haemorrhage.

Her autoimmune serology returns positive for c-antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody with anti proteinase 3 (PR3) specificity on enzyme linked immunosorbent assay, negative anti myeloperoxidase (MPO), negative anti glomerular basement membrane, negative antinuclear antibody. She has no personal or family history of asthma or eosinophilic disease. She has never smoked.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Saddle nose deformity, crusted nasal mucosa, no rash, bilateral crackles on auscultation, no peripheral neuropathy documented
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 220 micromol/L (baseline 78), urine microscopy 4 red cell casts, c-ANCA/PR3 positive, MPO negative, anti glomerular basement membrane negative, complement C3 and C4 normal, eosinophil count 0.2 x10^9/L

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Microscopic polyangiitis with pulmonary renal syndrome, based on the current serological and clinical pattern findings
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss) based on the current clinical and serological pattern findings
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener granulomatosis) based on the current clinical and serological pattern findings
Anti glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture syndrome) based on the current clinical and serological pattern findings
Systemic lupus erythematosus with pulmonary renal syndrome, based on the current serological and clinical pattern findings

subtopic_detail: Warfarin reversal in ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm needing massive transfusion
stem: A 72-year-old man on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve is shocked with a ruptured 7 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm on ultrasound. Massive transfusion has begun and theatre is being arranged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132 /min, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg, temperature 35.6 degrees C

lead_in: Which haemostatic strategy is most appropriate now?

options.text: Intravenous vitamin K 10 mg alone, delaying theatre until reversal
Fresh frozen plasma 4 units alone, withholding vitamin K
Recombinant activated factor VII 90 microg/kg bolus alone
Vitamin K 5 to 10 mg with Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg and plasma
Andexanet alfa 800 mg bolus then infusion before theatre

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in Addison disease with concurrent sepsis and vomiting inability to take oral steroid
stem: A 45-year-old woman with Addison disease on hydrocortisone 20 mg, 10 mg and 5 mg daily and fludrocortisone has vomited for 8 hours with gastroenteritis and kept down no hydrocortisone today. She is drowsy. Saline and ceftriaxone have been given.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132 /min, blood pressure 78/48 mmHg, temperature 38.6 degrees C

lead_in: Which steroid strategy is most appropriate now?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg with an antiemetic, repeated hourly
Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg alone until endocrinology review
Intramuscular hydrocortisone 20 mg as a single dose
Continue her usual oral maintenance hydrocortisone only
Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg now, then 200 mg over 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Acute pericarditis diagnosis and first line management in an outpatient adult
stem: A 32-year-old man has 3 days of sharp pleuritic chest pain, worse supine and relieved by leaning forward, two weeks after a viral illness. He has no cardiovascular risk factors.

data_table.Examination: Triphasic pericardial rub at the left sternal edge
data_table.Investigations: ECG diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, troponin normal, CRP 68 mg/L, no pericardial effusion

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Ibuprofen 600 mg 8-hourly tapered, with colchicine for 3 months
Aspirin 300 mg 6-hourly tapered, with colchicine for 3 months
Prednisolone 30 mg daily tapered, with colchicine for 3 months
Paracetamol 1 g 4- to 6-hourly alone with activity restriction
Intravenous heparin bolus then infusion titrated to the APTT

subtopic_detail: Adult male iron deficiency anaemia requires evaluation for occult gastrointestinal blood loss
stem: A 55-year-old man has new iron deficiency anaemia with mild exertional dyspnoea. He has no overt bleeding, no dysphagia, no anti-inflammatory use and no family history of bowel cancer.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 72 fL, ferritin 8 microg/L, transferrin saturation 4 per cent, coeliac serology negative

lead_in: Which investigation will best identify the source of iron loss?

options.text: Contrast computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis first
Faecal occult blood testing, endoscoping only if positive
Capsule endoscopy first to examine the small bowel
Twelve weeks of oral iron, then rescreen the haemoglobin
Urgent bidirectional endoscopy, gastroscopy and colonoscopy

subtopic_detail: Differentiating Graves disease from subacute thyroiditis at initial assessment
stem: A 32-year-old woman has five weeks of palpitations, tremor and 4 kg weight loss, with no recent viral illness or iodine exposure.

data_table.Examination: Diffuse smooth non-tender goitre with an audible bruit
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mU/L, free thyroxine 45 pmol/L, thyroid receptor antibodies positive, C-reactive protein normal

lead_in: Which feature most strongly favours Graves disease over subacute thyroiditis?

options.text: A free thyroxine of 45 pmol/L, well above the reference range
Positive thyroid receptor antibodies with an audible thyroid bruit
Weight loss of 4 kg over five weeks with heat intolerance
A diffusely enlarged, smooth, non-tender goitre on palpation
A thyroid stimulating hormone suppressed below 0.01 mU/L

subtopic_detail: Transient ischaemic attack risk stratification and initiation of dual antiplatelet therapy
stem: A 68-year-old man had a 20-minute episode of right face and arm weakness with expressive dysphasia six hours ago, now fully resolved. He has hypertension and diabetes and takes no antithrombotic.

data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography brain normal; angiogram shows 40 per cent left internal carotid stenosis; electrocardiogram sinus rhythm; blood pressure 178/98 mmHg

lead_in: Which secondary prevention regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily alone, with stroke clinic referral
Aspirin and clopidogrel for 21 days, then single agent, plus a statin
Warfarin to an international normalised ratio of 2 to 3
Left carotid endarterectomy within 14 days as first line
Intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg within the 4.5 hour window

subtopic_detail: Hepatic encephalopathy escalation to rifaximin after lactulose in cirrhosis
stem: A 62-year-old man with Child-Pugh C cirrhosis has a third episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy in 4 months despite lactulose 30 mL three times daily titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools, taken reliably. No bleeding or infection.

data_table.Examination: West Haven grade 2 with asterixis

lead_in: Which addition is most appropriate to prevent recurrence?

options.text: Cease lactulose, switch to sodium benzoate 5 g twice daily
Add neomycin 500 mg 6-hourly instead of rifaximin
Add oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily instead of rifaximin
Add rifaximin 550 mg twice daily alongside lactulose
Restrict dietary protein to 0.5 g/kg daily to reduce ammonia

subtopic_detail: Discriminating primary biliary cholangitis from primary sclerosing cholangitis in cholestatic derangement
stem: A 52-year-old woman has six months of fatigue and pruritus without jaundice. She takes no medication, drinks no alcohol and has no inflammatory bowel disease.

data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 480 U/L, GGT 380 U/L, ALT 65 U/L, antimitochondrial antibody positive at high titre, IgM raised; cholangiopancreatography normal

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis and first line therapy?

options.text: Primary biliary cholangitis, treated with ursodeoxycholic acid 13 to 15 mg/kg daily
Primary sclerosing cholangitis, with ursodeoxycholic acid and colonoscopic surveillance
Autoimmune hepatitis, treated with a prednisolone taper plus azathioprine
Fatty liver disease, managed with a 10 per cent weight loss target
IgG4 related sclerosing cholangitis, treated with prednisolone 40 mg

subtopic_detail: Amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis type 1 versus type 2 differentiation and management
stem: A 68-year-old man on amiodarone 200 mg daily for 3 years has 6 weeks of palpitations, weight loss and heat intolerance. His ejection fraction is 38%.

data_table.Examination: No goitre or eye signs, pulse 122 /min irregularly irregular
data_table.Investigations: TSH below 0.01 mU/L, free thyroxine 62 pmol/L, receptor antibodies negative, interleukin 6 elevated
data_table.Imaging: Normal sized thyroid, absent Doppler flow

lead_in: Which subtype and first-line treatment are most appropriate?

options.text: Type 2 disease; prednisolone 40 mg daily tapered over 3 months
Type 1 disease; carbimazole 40 mg daily with potassium perchlorate
Mixed disease; carbimazole with prednisolone and lithium 800 mg
Subacute thyroiditis; ibuprofen 400 mg 6-hourly, continue amiodarone
Factitious thyrotoxicosis; cease all exogenous thyroid hormone

subtopic_detail: Serotonin toxicity grading and management after tramadol plus escitalopram co-prescription
stem: A 64-year-old woman on escitalopram 20 mg daily started tramadol 50 mg six-hourly twelve hours ago. She is agitated and diaphoretic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 178/108 mmHg, temperature 39.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Sustained inducible ankle clonus, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, lower limb hypertonia
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 3200 U/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Dantrolene 1 to 2.5 mg/kg, continuing both current medications
Continue both drugs, give paracetamol and admit for observation
Cease escitalopram only and give intravenous haloperidol for agitation
Cease both drugs, cool and sedate, and give cyproheptadine 12 mg
Ceftriaxone and dexamethasone for meningitis, continuing both drugs

subtopic_detail: Rule out chest pain pathway in a low risk patient with a normal initial high sensitivity troponin
stem: A 54-year-old man had 90 minutes of central chest heaviness at rest, now resolved. He has hypertension on amlodipine and stopped smoking 5 years ago.

data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm, no ST or T wave change, no bundle branch block
data_table.Troponin: High sensitivity troponin I 6 ng/L at 2 hours after pain onset (99th centile 26 ng/L)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge now; one normal troponin at 2 hours excludes infarction
Admit for telemetry with six-hourly troponins for 24 hours
Repeat troponin at 1 hour, then outpatient stress testing within 72 hours
Load aspirin and ticagrelor now, angiography within 24 hours
Outpatient computed tomography coronary angiography within 7 days

subtopic_detail: Addition of a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor to established guideline therapy in symptomatic HFrEF without diabetes
stem: A 68-year-old man with ischaemic heart failure, ejection fraction 32 per cent, remains New York Heart Association class II on maximally tolerated sacubitril valsartan, bisoprolol 10 mg and spironolactone 25 mg. He has no diabetes.

data_table.Observations: Blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, pulse 68 /min in sinus rhythm, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Renal: Creatinine 108 micromol/L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 62, potassium 4.5 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add ivabradine 5 mg twice daily for rate lowering
Add digoxin 125 microg daily as fourth line therapy
Add oral furosemide 40 mg daily for his breathlessness
Add dapagliflozin 10 mg daily and recheck renal function
Switch bisoprolol to metoprolol succinate 190 mg daily

subtopic_detail: Timing of N acetylcysteine administration after acute single ingestion paracetamol overdose
stem: A 22-year-old woman weighing 60 kg took thirty 500 mg paracetamol tablets five hours ago. She is alert with mild nausea and no co-ingestion.

data_table.Laboratory: Paracetamol 195 mg/L at 4 hours, above the nomogram treatment line; ALT 22 U/L, international normalised ratio 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Start intravenous N-acetylcysteine now on the 21 hour regimen
Give activated charcoal 50 g and repeat the paracetamol at 8 hours
Give oral methionine 2.5 g four hourly for four doses
Give a single 5 g N-acetylcysteine bolus and repeat the level
Observe, starting N-acetylcysteine only if the ALT rises

subtopic_detail: Choice of pharmacological venous thromboembolism prophylaxis on admission with community acquired pneumonia
stem: A 76-year-old woman is admitted with severe community-acquired pneumonia needing oxygen and intravenous antibiotics. Her mobility is limited and she is expected to stay 5 to 7 days. She takes aspirin 100 mg for a previous transient ischaemic attack.

data_table.Laboratory: eGFR 58 mL/min/1.73 m2, platelets 220 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 122 g/L, INR 1.0
data_table.Risk: No active bleeding, no epidural, no planned surgery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate venous thromboembolism prophylaxis?

options.text: Continue aspirin 100 mg daily as sole prophylaxis
Subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg daily with compression stockings
Apixaban 2.5 mg orally twice daily while inpatient
Graduated compression stockings alone with daily reassessment
Subcutaneous unfractionated heparin 5000 units three times daily

subtopic_detail: Immediate management sequence for hyperkalaemia with electrocardiogram changes in a chronic kidney disease patient
stem: A 74-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease feels weak and lightheaded. He takes ramipril and spironolactone, and his general practitioner started trimethoprim 300 mg daily last week.

data_table.Laboratory: Potassium 7.2 mmol/L on repeat, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, creatinine 320 micromol/L
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Peaked T waves V2 to V4, PR interval mildly prolonged, no widened QRS

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral polystyrene sulfonate 15 g four times daily, recheck in 4 hours
Nebulised salbutamol 10 mg over 10 minutes as first line
Calcium gluconate, then insulin with dextrose, and stop the culprit drugs
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mL over 30 minutes first
Urgent haemodialysis without any prior medical therapy today

subtopic_detail: Selection of intravenous fluid transition in adult diabetic ketoacidosis with falling blood glucose
stem: An 80 kg man with type 1 diabetes is four hours into treatment for ketoacidosis. He has had 2 L of 0.9 per cent saline, now running at 250 mL/hour, with fixed rate insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour.

data_table.Biochemistry: Glucose 12 mmol/L (26 at presentation), ketones 3.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What change to fluid and insulin is most appropriate?

options.text: Stop the infusion and switch to subcutaneous glargine and aspart
Reduce insulin to 0.03 units/kg/hour, continuing saline alone
Change the saline to Hartmann solution, insulin unchanged
Add 10 per cent dextrose at 125 mL/hour, insulin unchanged
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 30 minutes

subtopic_detail: Choice of vasopressor and access in septic shock with fluid unresponsive hypotension in emergency
stem: A 68-year-old man with 2 days of cough, fever and rigors has had 30 mL/kg Hartmann over 90 minutes and piperacillin-tazobactam after blood cultures. Lactate has fallen from 4.6 to 3.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg (MAP 60), SpO2 93% on 6 L/min
data_table.Access: Peripheral 18 gauge cannula, no central line
data_table.Imaging: Right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Adrenaline 1 mg intravenously and intubate before any vasopressor

Start peripheral noradrenaline targeting mean arterial pressure 65

subtopic_detail: First line antibiotic choice for uncomplicated acute cystitis in a non pregnant woman with no antibiotic history and normal renal function
stem: A 34-year-old non-pregnant woman has 24 hours of dysuria, frequency and suprapubic discomfort. She has no fever or flank pain, no recent antibiotics and normal renal function.

Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic and disposition decision for community acquired pneumonia with SMART COP score 3 in a previously well adult
stem: A previously well 58-year-old man has 3 days of productive cough, right pleuritic chest pain and fever. He is not confused.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 108 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 92% on room air

subtopic_detail: Choice and initiation of first line disease modifying antirheumatic drug in early seropositive rheumatoid arthritis
stem: A 46-year-old woman has 10 weeks of 2-hour morning stiffness with symmetrical synovitis of 8 metacarpophalangeal, proximal interphalangeal and wrist joints. She is not pregnant and uses effective contraception.

data_table.Serology: Rheumatoid factor 92 IU/mL (below 15), anti-CCP 180 U (below 20), CRP 42 mg/L, ESR 46 mm/hr

Oral methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid and prednisolone bridging

subtopic_detail: Duration of anticoagulation for a first unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis in a 55 year old with no additional bleeding risk factors
stem: A 55-year-old man completed 3 months of apixaban for a first unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis and has no residual symptoms. There was no surgery, immobilisation, cancer or oestrogen use, and antiphospholipid screening was negative. He has had no bleeding; HAS-BLED is 1.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing plan?

options.text: Continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely with annual review
Stop apixaban now and review clinically every 3 months

Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely at full dose
Switch to warfarin indefinitely targeting an INR of 2.0 to 3.0

subtopic_detail: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis thresholds and drug choice in a newly diagnosed patient with advanced HIV and CD4 count 90 cells per microlitre
stem: A 42-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV. He is asymptomatic and starts bictegravir, tenofovir alafenamide and emtricitabine this week. He has no sulfa allergy and normal renal and liver function.

subtopic_detail: Perioperative hydrocortisone stress dosing for a woman with primary adrenal insufficiency undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy
stem: A 52-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency takes hydrocortisone 15 mg, 5 mg and 5 mg daily with fludrocortisone 100 microgram. She is well, with no infection or vomiting, and has elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy tomorrow.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg sitting, 112/72 mmHg standing

subtopic_detail: Reversal strategy for an incidental INR of 8 in a patient on warfarin for mechanical mitral valve without any bleeding

subtopic_detail: Correction rate and monitoring plan to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome in chronic severe hyponatraemia of 108 mmol/L due to thiazide use

subtopic_detail: Adult sepsis hour-1 bundle in a patient with urinary source
stem: A 72-year-old woman has 8 hours of fever, rigors, confusion and dark offensive urine. Her abdomen is soft with suprapubic tenderness. She has had 30 mL/kg of intravenous crystalloid, cultures, oxygen and empirical antibiotics, and her blood pressure has not improved.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, temperature 38.9 degrees C

options.text: Empirical intravenous fluconazole added to the antibiotics

subtopic_detail: Adult meningitis empirical antibiotic and adjunctive dexamethasone
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 46-year-old previously well woman presents with 12 hours of severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and one episode of vomiting. She has no rash. She has no immunosuppression, no recent travel, no contact with meningitis, and no penicillin allergy.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable. Vital signs are pulse 108, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius. Kernig's sign is positive and she has photophobia. There are no focal neurological signs, no papilloedema and no seizures. Capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.7).

Blood cultures have been drawn, IV access is established, and a CT head has been requested because of the reduced level of consciousness before lumbar puncture. The CT is expected within 30 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 132/78 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, positive Kernig's sign, photophobia, no focal neurology, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.7); CT head requested

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Benzylpenicillin 2.4 g intravenous alone as monotherapy for suspected meningococcal disease
Wait for CT head then perform LP before giving any antibiotic or dexamethasone
Dexamethasone 10 mg intravenous plus ceftriaxone 2 g intravenous without waiting for CT or LP
Ceftriaxone 2 g intravenous alone with dexamethasone deferred until CSF Gram stain returns
Aciclovir 10 mg/kg intravenous 8 hourly alone for suspected HSV encephalitis

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection recognition with LRINEC scoring
stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has 24 hours of severe left calf pain after a gardening scratch. The pain is out of proportion to the findings.

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in a patient on chronic prednisolone
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on prednisolone 7.5 mg orally daily for 3 years is brought in with 24 hours of vomiting, diarrhoea and lethargy. She was hospitalised 2 days ago for a similar gastroenteritis episode and discharged after clinical improvement, but at that time she was unable to keep her prednisolone down for 48 hours and her general practitioner did not adjust her dose.

On examination she is drowsy and looks unwell. Vital signs are pulse 128, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg lying and unrecordable standing, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius. She is warm and mildly hyperpigmented in the palmar creases. Bloods: sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), creatinine 128 micromol/L (45-90), venous pH 7.30 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22-32), lactate 2.2 mmol/L (under 2).

Her other medications are methotrexate 15 mg weekly and folic acid, and she has no known adrenal disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 88/52 mmHg lying and unrecordable standing, RR 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, unwell, warm, mild palmar crease hyperpigmentation
data_table.Investigations: Na 128 mmol/L (135-145), K 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), creatinine 128 micromol/L (45-90), venous pH 7.30 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22-32), lactate 2.2 mmol/L (<2)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Vasopressin infusion at 0.03 units/min to correct hypotension without steroid therapy
Dexamethasone 8 mg intravenous while awaiting a short synacthen test for definitive diagnosis
Increase her regular oral prednisolone dose to 15 mg daily and observe for improvement
Fludrocortisone 200 micrograms intramuscular alone for mineralocorticoid replacement
Hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous bolus and intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride resuscitation

subtopic_detail: Massive transfusion protocol activation and initial component ratio
stem:
You are the trauma team leader in a metropolitan emergency department. A 34-year-old man is brought in by ambulance after being struck by a car at high speed. He is on the trauma trolley and reports severe abdominal pain.

He has a distended tender abdomen with pelvic tenderness. Vital signs on arrival are pulse 142, blood pressure 78/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 96 percent on 15 L/min oxygen non-rebreather, temperature 35.2 degrees Celsius. A rapid FAST scan is positive with free fluid in Morison's pouch and the pouch of Douglas. Blood tests are pending but the initial venous blood gas shows lactate 6.8 mmol/L (under 2), base deficit -12 mmol/L, haemoglobin 82 g/L (135-175). The initial 500 mL crystalloid bolus has produced no improvement in blood pressure. Two 14 gauge intravenous cannulae are in situ and the operating theatre is being prepared for immediate laparotomy.

The consultant surgeon requests the massive transfusion protocol be activated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 142, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 96% on 15 L/min O2, temperature 35.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Distended tender abdomen with pelvic tenderness; positive FAST in Morison's pouch and pouch of Douglas
data_table.Investigations: VBG lactate 6.8 mmol/L (<2), base deficit -12 mmol/L, haemoglobin 82 g/L (135-175); initial 500 mL crystalloid ineffective

lead_in: Which single initial blood component ratio is delivered on massive transfusion activation under Australian trauma guidance?

options.text: Whole blood exclusively as first line without component therapy
Packed red cells and fresh frozen plasma in a 2:1 unit ratio without platelets
Packed red cells with cryoprecipitate as first pack without platelets or plasma
Packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma and platelets in a 1:1:1 unit ratio
Packed red cells alone with prothrombin complex concentrate at 25 units/kg

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic decision in an infective COPD exacerbation using Anthonisen criteria
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 67-year-old ex-smoker with GOLD stage 3 chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. His usual FEV1 is 42 percent predicted and he is on tiotropium 18 microgram inhaled once daily and salmeterol/fluticasone 25/250 microgram inhaled twice daily. He presents with 4 days of increased breathlessness above baseline, increased sputum volume, and a change of sputum colour from clear to yellow-green.

His pulse is 96, blood pressure is 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate is 24, SpO2 is 90 percent on room air (his baseline is 93 percent), and temperature is 37.4 degrees Celsius. Chest auscultation reveals bilateral polyphonic wheeze and mild crackles at the right base. Chest radiograph shows hyperinflation and no consolidation. Arterial blood gas on room air is pH 7.36, PaCO2 46 mmHg, PaO2 62 mmHg, and bicarbonate 26 mmol/L.

Sodium is 140 mmol/L (135 to 145), CRP is 46 mg/L (below 5), white cell count is 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), and eosinophils are 0.16 x10^9/L. He has commenced back-up prednisolone 50 mg orally once daily.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 128/74 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 90% on room air (baseline 93%), temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Symptom triad: Increased dyspnoea, increased sputum volume, sputum colour change clear to yellow-green
data_table.Investigations: ABG pH 7.36, PaCO2 46 mmHg, PaO2 62 mmHg, HCO3 26 mmol/L; CXR hyperinflation without consolidation; CRP 46 mg/L (below 5); WCC 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0)

options.text: Add ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily for 5 days
Add doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days
Add amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for 5 days
Add azithromycin 500 mg orally daily for 3 days
Withhold antibiotics and rely on the prednisolone alone

subtopic_detail: Antihypertensive choice in type 2 diabetes with albuminuria
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 58-year-old carpenter with type 2 diabetes mellitus of 8 years standing, on metformin 1 g orally twice daily. His HbA1c is 7.1 percent (below 7.0), his lipids are within target on rosuvastatin 20 mg orally each night, and his weight is 92 kg. He does not smoke and drinks 4 standard drinks a week.

Today's blood pressure over three separate visits in the last month is averaging 152/94 mmHg. A urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) sent last week is 12 mg/mmol (below 2.5), confirmed on a repeat first-morning sample. Serum creatinine is 88 micromol/L (60 to 110), eGFR is over 90 mL/min/1.73m2, potassium is 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), and sodium is 140 mmol/L (135 to 145).

He is not on any antihypertensive currently, has no known ischaemic heart disease, has no history of angioedema, and is willing to start a new medication. Retinal examination six months ago showed background diabetic retinopathy.

data_table.Ambulatory blood pressure: Average 152/94 mmHg over three visits in the last month
data_table.Renal and metabolic: eGFR over 90, creatinine 88 micromol/L, potassium 4.2, sodium 140, HbA1c 7.1% (below 7.0)
data_table.Albuminuria: uACR 12 mg/mmol (below 2.5) confirmed on repeat first-morning sample

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial antihypertensive?

options.text: Hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg orally each morning titrated to blood pressure control
Amlodipine 5 mg orally each morning titrated to blood pressure control

Bisoprolol 2.5 mg orally each morning titrated to blood pressure control
Spironolactone 25 mg orally each morning as initial monotherapy

subtopic_detail: Adult DKA fluid initiation
stem:
You are the acute medicine registrar. A 27-year-old man with type 1 diabetes on multiple daily insulin injections presents with 24 hours of vomiting, deep breathing, and abdominal pain. He ran out of his rapid acting insulin 2 days ago.

On assessment he is alert but drowsy. Peripheries are cool with capillary refill of 3 seconds centrally. Mucous membranes are dry.

Vital signs: pulse 122, blood pressure 106/64, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.4. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.10, HCO3 8 mmol/L, glucose 26 mmol/L, ketones 5.4 mmol/L. Sodium 134, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, chloride 100, urea 9, creatinine 118 micromol/L. He weighs 80 kg.

data_table.Electrolytes: Sodium 134, potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), chloride 100, urea 9, creatinine 118 micromol/L

subtopic_detail: DOAC dose in non valvular AF with renal impairment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 78-year-old woman with non valvular atrial fibrillation attends for review. She was commenced on apixaban 5 mg twice daily 4 weeks ago at her cardiology appointment.

She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and stage 3b chronic kidney disease. Repeat urea and electrolytes today show creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-100) and eGFR 34 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her serum potassium is 4.2 mmol/L. She weighs 62 kg. She has no active bleeding.

She takes perindopril 4 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, and empagliflozin 10 mg daily. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 5.

data_table.Current dose: Apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily for 4 weeks

data_table.Other conditions: Hypertension; type 2 diabetes; stage 3b CKD; CHA2DS2-VA 5
data_table.Other medications: Perindopril 4 mg daily; metformin 1 g twice daily; atorvastatin 40 mg daily; empagliflozin 10 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate adjustment to her apixaban dose?

options.text: Cease anticoagulation because CHA2DS2-VA 5 is offset by bleeding risk at this age
Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg orally twice daily because her creatinine is at or above 133 micromol/L

stem:

subtopic_detail: Rapid TIA workup and secondary prevention
stem: A 68-year-old man presents 3 hours after a 25 minute episode of right arm weakness and aphasia that has fully resolved. He takes perindopril and atorvastatin, no antiplatelet, and has had no previous stroke or bleeding.

subtopic_detail: Suspected giant cell arteritis workup
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar. A 74-year-old woman presents with 6 days of new right sided temporal headache and 2 days of jaw claudication when chewing steak. She denies visual loss, diplopia, or scalp tenderness.

She has a background of osteoporosis on denosumab and hypertension on amlodipine. She takes no anticoagulants and has no allergies.

On examination the right temporal artery is prominent and tender but pulsatile. Visual acuity is 6/6 bilaterally. Fundoscopy shows a normal disc bilaterally with no pallor. Cranial nerves are otherwise intact.

Vital signs are within normal limits. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 84 mm/hour (0-30), C reactive protein 92 mg/L (0-5), platelets 445, ALP 148 U/L (30-120).

data_table.Symptoms: 6 days right temporal headache; 2 days jaw claudication on chewing; no visual loss or diplopia; no scalp tenderness reported
data_table.Examination: Right temporal artery prominent and tender but pulsatile; visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally; fundoscopy normal discs
data_table.Inflammatory markers: ESR 84 mm/hour (0-30); CRP 92 mg/L (0-5); platelets 445 x10^9/L
data_table.Liver panel: ALP 148 U/L (30-120); other LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days for anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy prophylaxis
Await temporal artery biopsy results before starting corticosteroids to avoid masking pathology
Commence oral prednisolone 60 mg orally daily immediately and arrange a temporal artery biopsy within 14 days
Commence tocilizumab 162 mg subcutaneous weekly as monotherapy for steroid sparing induction
Commence naproxen 500 mg twice daily and reassess in 48 hours after inflammatory markers repeat

subtopic_detail: Cancer associated VTE anticoagulant choice
stem:
You are the oncology inpatient registrar. A 61-year-old woman with locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma on cycle 3 of FLOT chemotherapy is admitted with new left leg swelling. Compression ultrasound confirms an occlusive left femoral vein deep venous thrombosis without extension into the iliac veins. She is haemodynamically stable and has no chest symptoms.

She has no history of bleeding, no varices, and no active peptic ulceration on recent gastroscopy. Recent bloods: haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-165), platelets 168, creatinine 68 micromol/L. Her medications include ondansetron 8 mg TDS during chemotherapy cycles and pantoprazole 40 mg daily.

There is no mucosal bleeding on examination. She is fully oriented and mobilising.

data_table.Imaging: Left femoral vein occlusive DVT on compression ultrasound; no iliac extension; no PE symptoms
data_table.Malignancy: Locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma; cycle 3 FLOT chemotherapy
data_table.Bleeding history: No prior bleeding; no varices; no active peptic ulceration on recent gastroscopy
data_table.Bloods: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-165); platelets 168 x10^9/L; creatinine 68 micromol/L
data_table.Medications: Ondansetron 8 mg TDS; pantoprazole 40 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulant regimen?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally daily and knee high compression stockings for at least 3 months without anticoagulant
Rivaroxaban 15 mg orally twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily for at least 6 months of active cancer
Warfarin bridging with enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily until INR 2 to 3 for a minimum of 3 months
Apixaban 10 mg orally twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for at least 6 months of active cancer
Retrievable inferior vena cava filter alone instead of anticoagulation because of chemotherapy bleeding risk

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in steroid dependent patient
stem:
You are the medical registrar on for after hours. A 54-year-old woman with long standing rheumatoid arthritis on prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for 6 years presents with 24 hours of fever, watery diarrhoea, and vomiting.

She has not taken any prednisolone today because she cannot keep tablets down. She has no other medications and no allergies.

On assessment she is drowsy and cool peripherally. Peripheries are cool with capillary refill of 4 seconds centrally.

Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 82/54, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 39.0. Point-of-care glucose 3.1 mmol/L. Bloods: sodium 128, potassium 5.4 mmol/L, urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 132 micromol/L. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.30, HCO3 18, lactate 3.0 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 82/54, RR 24, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.0
data_table.Examination: Drowsy; cool peripheries; capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Electrolytes: Sodium 128 mmol/L; potassium 5.4 mmol/L; urea 12; creatinine 132 micromol/L
data_table.Medication history: Prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for 6 years; missed today because of vomiting

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Commence noradrenaline infusion targeted to a MAP of 65 mmHg and defer corticosteroid until inotrope is titrated
Restart oral prednisolone at double her usual daily dose once she stops vomiting and rehydrate her with oral fluids
Give intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg once alongside 0.9% saline resuscitation and await the results of a short synacthen test
Give intravenous fludrocortisone 100 microgram alone with 0.9% saline resuscitation and reassess in 4 hours
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately then 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion, plus 0.9% saline and 10% dextrose

subtopic_detail: Progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids with a normal endoscopy
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 46-year-old woman with two years of food sticking in the chest. She says liquids have been just as difficult as solids from the beginning and that she often has to stand up and stretch her neck to make things go down.

She regurgitates undigested food onto her pillow at night and has lost 6 kg. She was treated with a proton pump inhibitor for eighteen months for presumed reflux without benefit. Upper endoscopy performed last month was reported as normal to the level of the stomach, with no stricture, no ring, no oesophagitis and no mucosal abnormality, and biopsies taken from the proximal and distal oesophagus showed no eosinophilic infiltrate. She has never lived outside Australia and takes no other medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg per square metre, no cervical lymphadenopathy, chest clear, abdomen soft with no mass
data_table.Investigations: Upper endoscopy normal with no stricture or mucosal lesion, oesophageal biopsies with no eosinophilic infiltrate, haemoglobin 132 g/L (115-155), C-reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: High resolution oesophageal manometry to characterise peristalsis and relaxation of the lower sphincter
Repeat upper endoscopy with careful retroflexed views and further biopsies of the distal oesophagus
Twenty four hour ambulatory oesophageal pH monitoring to quantify acid exposure and symptom correlation
Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen to look for a malignancy infiltrating the gastric cardia
Videofluoroscopic swallow assessment with a speech pathologist to evaluate the oropharyngeal phase

subtopic_detail: Food impaction requiring endoscopic disimpaction in a young man with atopy
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar attending a 23-year-old man who presented last night unable to swallow his own saliva after eating steak. The impacted bolus has just been removed endoscopically and he is comfortable in recovery.

He tells you he has been cutting food into small pieces and drinking water with every mouthful for the past three years, and that this is his second impaction. He has asthma treated with an inhaled corticosteroid, hay fever and a childhood history of eczema. At endoscopy the operator described concentric rings along the oesophagus with linear furrows and scattered white exudate, and no stricture or ulceration. He has taken a proton pump inhibitor intermittently for what he was told was reflux, with no clear benefit.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Comfortable in recovery, chest clear, no surgical emphysema in the neck, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Endoscopy showing concentric oesophageal rings, linear furrows and white exudate with no stricture or ulceration, bolus removed intact, eosinophil count 0.7 x10^9/L (less than 0.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry to exclude a primary disorder of oesophageal motility
Take multiple oesophageal biopsies from proximal and distal sites and count eosinophils per high power field
Arrange serum specific immunoglobulin E testing to a broad food panel and eliminate every positive food
Arrange endoscopic dilatation at a second procedure to widen the oesophagus and prevent further impaction
Increase the dose of his inhaled corticosteroid on the basis that his asthma control is driving symptoms

subtopic_detail: Unilateral facial weakness including the forehead developing over a day
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 41-year-old man who woke twenty hours ago unable to close his right eye and with the right side of his mouth drooping. He is frightened that he has had a stroke.

He describes an ache behind the right ear that began the day before the weakness, and says sounds seem uncomfortably loud on that side. On examination he cannot raise the right eyebrow or wrinkle the right forehead, cannot bury the right eyelashes, and the right nasolabial fold is flattened. Eye movements are full, pupils are equal and reactive, there is no limb weakness, no sensory loss and no ataxia, and speech is clear with normal tongue and palatal movement. There is no vesicular rash in or around the ear or on the palate, and the tympanic membranes are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, BP 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Complete right sided facial weakness including frontalis, incomplete eye closure with Bell phenomenon, hyperacusis on the right, normal extraocular movements, no limb or sensory deficit, no rash in the ear canal or on the palate
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 5.4 mmol/L (4.0-7.8)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Referral for facial nerve electrophysiological studies within the next week to establish the prognosis
Reassurance with facial exercises and review in two weeks if the weakness has not begun to improve
Oral prednisolone started today with lubricating eye drops and an eye pad for overnight protection
Urgent computed tomography of the brain with consideration of thrombolysis for an acute stroke syndrome
Oral valaciclovir alone for seven days on the basis of probable herpes simplex reactivation in the nerve

subtopic_detail: Brief positional spinning on rolling over in bed with a normal neurological examination
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 64-year-old woman with four days of spinning that comes on when she rolls over in bed or tips her head back to hang washing. Each episode lasts under a minute and settles if she keeps still.

She is completely well between episodes and has no symptoms while sitting still. She has no hearing loss, no tinnitus, no ear fullness and no headache. Neurological examination shows normal eye movements with no gaze evoked nystagmus, normal finger nose and heel shin testing, normal gait with a negative Romberg test, and intact cranial nerves. There is no spontaneous nystagmus when she looks straight ahead. Her blood pressure shows no postural drop and her heart rhythm is regular.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min regular, BP 134/80 mmHg lying and 130/78 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No spontaneous nystagmus, full smooth pursuit without gaze evoked nystagmus, normal coordination and gait, negative Romberg, hearing normal to whispered voice bilaterally, tympanic membranes normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and posterior fossa to exclude a central cause of vertigo
Start betahistine and a low salt diet with a trial of fluid restriction to reduce endolymphatic pressure
Refer for formal vestibular rehabilitation therapy as the initial management of her positional symptoms
Perform the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre and proceed to a repositioning manoeuvre if it is positive
Prescribe prochlorperazine regularly for two weeks to suppress the vestibular symptoms she describes

subtopic_detail: Acute monoarthritis of the knee in an older patient with chondrocalcinosis on radiograph
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 76-year-old woman with a hot swollen left knee that came on over twelve hours. She has been admitted for four days with a community-acquired pneumonia and has been improving on antibiotics.

She has osteoarthritis of both knees and takes no regular anti inflammatory medication. She has never had gout and has no tophi. The knee is warm, swollen with a tense effusion and painful through the last thirty degrees of flexion. There is no break in the skin over the joint, no cellulitis and no ulceration. A radiograph of the knee shows linear calcification within the meniscal cartilage of both knees. She is on no diuretic and her renal function has been stable throughout the admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 37.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Warm swollen left knee with tense effusion, restricted terminal flexion, intact overlying skin with no cellulitis, no tophi, other joints unaffected
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5), serum urate 0.34 mmol/L (0.15-0.45), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90), knee radiograph showing linear meniscal calcification bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral colchicine on the basis that the cartilage calcification confirms a crystal induced arthritis
Start intravenous flucloxacillin empirically for septic arthritis and arrange orthopaedic review tomorrow
Commence allopurinol at low dose with colchicine cover and titrate to a target serum urate concentration
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the knee to assess for osteomyelitis of the distal femur or tibia
Aspirate the joint and send fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture and polarised light microscopy

subtopic_detail: Nocturnal hand paraesthesiae relieved by shaking with normal strength on examination
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 52-year-old woman who wakes most nights with pins and needles in her right hand and has to hang it over the side of the bed and shake it for relief.

The tingling affects the thumb, index and middle fingers and she has begun dropping her coffee cup in the mornings. She works as a hairdresser. Sensation to light touch is reduced over the palmar aspect of the radial three digits with normal sensation over the thenar eminence itself. Abductor pollicis brevis power is full and there is no visible wasting. Neck movements are full and painless and do not reproduce the symptoms, and reflexes in both arms are normal and symmetrical. Her thyroid function and glycated haemoglobin measured last month were normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Reduced light touch over palmar thumb, index and middle fingers with preserved sensation over the thenar eminence, abductor pollicis brevis power 5 out of 5, no thenar wasting, full painless neck range, biceps and triceps reflexes normal and symmetrical
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), glycated haemoglobin 5.4 percent (less than 6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Provide a neutral position wrist splint to be worn overnight and review her symptoms in six weeks
Refer for nerve conduction studies before offering any treatment for her hand symptoms at this stage
Refer for urgent surgical decompression of the nerve to prevent irreversible loss of thenar muscle bulk
Arrange cervical spine imaging to investigate a C6 radiculopathy as the cause of her arm symptoms
Commence oral pregabalin titrated over two weeks to control the neuropathic symptoms in the hand

subtopic_detail: Deranged liver enzymes with a new movement disorder in a young adult
