stem: A 22-year-old man has abnormal liver enzymes. Over the past year his handwriting has deteriorated, his speech is intermittently slurred, and he is failing subjects for the first time.

data_table.Examination: Coarse postural tremor, mild dysarthria, dysdiadochokinesis, liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 118 U/L, caeruloplasmin 0.19 g/L (0.20-0.60), viral and autoimmune liver serology negative

lead_in: Which combination of investigations best confirms the diagnosis?

options.text: Genetic sequencing of the gene with parental carrier testing
Twenty four hour urinary copper with slit lamp examination
Repeat serum caeruloplasmin and serum copper in three months
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and basal ganglia
Liver biopsy with quantitative hepatic copper measurement

subtopic_detail: Chronic watery diarrhoea with a macroscopically normal colonoscopy in an older woman
stem: A 67-year-old woman has eight months of watery diarrhoea, six to nine times daily including at night, with 4 kg weight loss and no blood. She takes a proton pump inhibitor and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory.

data_table.Investigations: Faecal calprotectin 96 micrograms/g (less than 50), coeliac serology negative with normal immunoglobulin A, colonoscopy macroscopically normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen for a neuroendocrine tumour
Start a gluten free diet despite the negative coeliac serology
Take random biopsies from the right and left colon for histology
Trial loperamide titrated to stool frequency, reviewing in eight weeks
Arrange a selenium homocholic acid taurine scan for bile acid diarrhoea

subtopic_detail: New persistent unilateral parotid enlargement in a woman with established sicca symptoms
stem:
You are the rheumatology registrar reviewing a 58-year-old woman with a nine year history of dry eyes and dry mouth, positive anti-Ro antibodies and a previously positive labial gland biopsy. She has been stable on hydroxychloroquine and artificial tears.

She attends because her left parotid gland has been firm and enlarged for three months and has not fluctuated with meals. She has no fever, no toothache and no purulent discharge from the duct. Her complement C4 has fallen from 0.22 to 0.09 g/L over the past year and a serum protein electrophoresis performed six months ago showed a small immunoglobulin M kappa paraprotein. She has palpable non-tender lymph nodes in the left cervical chain and reports drenching night sweats twice weekly.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 126/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Firm non-tender enlarged left parotid gland, two palpable left cervical lymph nodes each about 2 cm, no skin purpura, no splenomegaly, dry buccal mucosa
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), lymphocytes 0.9 x10^9/L (1.0-4.0), lactate dehydrogenase 310 U/L (120-250), complement C4 0.09 g/L (0.15-0.55), serum protein electrophoresis showing a small immunoglobulin M kappa paraprotein, anti-Ro antibody positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for two weeks to treat bacterial infection of the parotid gland
Arrange sialography with a course of gland massage and sialogogues for a presumed obstructing duct stone
Repeat the anti-Ro and anti-La antibody titres with a rheumatoid factor to reassess disease activity now
Arrange biopsy of the enlarged gland with imaging of the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging
Increase the hydroxychloroquine dose and add pilocarpine to improve her glandular secretion and comfort

subtopic_detail: Persistent daytime sleepiness with sudden knee buckling during laughter
stem:
You are the respiratory and sleep registrar reviewing a 26-year-old man referred with three years of overwhelming daytime sleepiness. He falls asleep in lectures and in the passenger seat and takes two naps most days, waking refreshed for an hour or two.

He describes his knees buckling and his jaw sagging for a few seconds whenever he laughs hard or is startled, remaining fully aware throughout. He also describes vivid frightening images as he falls asleep and occasional inability to move for a minute on waking. His body mass index is 23 kg per square metre, he has a Mallampati class 1 airway, and his partner reports no snoring and no witnessed pauses in breathing. His Epworth sleepiness score is 19. A polysomnogram performed last week showed an apnoea hypopnoea index of 2 per hour with normal oxygenation and reduced sleep latency.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg per square metre, Mallampati class 1, no tonsillar hypertrophy, no retrognathia, normal neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: Epworth sleepiness scale 19 out of 24, polysomnogram apnoea hypopnoea index 2 per hour with normal nocturnal oxygenation, ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30-300), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat polysomnography with oesophageal pressure monitoring to detect upper airway resistance events
Electroencephalography with sleep deprivation to investigate the episodes as atonic epileptic seizures
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast to exclude a hypothalamic structural lesion present
Actigraphy over two weeks with a sleep diary to assess for chronic insufficient sleep as the explanation
Multiple sleep latency testing performed on the day immediately following the overnight sleep study

subtopic_detail: Persistent organism after a first line eradication regimen confirmed by breath testing
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 54-year-old man who had a duodenal ulcer found at endoscopy four months ago with biopsy confirmed Helicobacter pylori. He completed a seven day course of esomeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin, taking every dose.

He returns because his epigastric pain has recurred. A urea breath test performed eight weeks after treatment, with his proton pump inhibitor withheld for two weeks beforehand, is positive. He has no penicillin allergy, has never taken a macrolide before that course, and has no alarm features with no weight loss, no vomiting, no dysphagia and no melaena. He does not smoke and takes no non-steroidal anti inflammatory medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness, no mass, no lymphadenopathy, no signs of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: Urea breath test positive eight weeks after treatment with proton pump inhibitor withheld two weeks, haemoglobin 146 g/L (130-170), previous endoscopy showing a duodenal ulcer with biopsy confirmed Helicobacter pylori

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: A second line regimen that avoids clarithromycin, using different antibiotics for a longer treatment course
Repeat the identical seven day regimen for a further fourteen days to overcome incomplete organism clearance
Long term proton pump inhibitor treatment alone with a plan to reassess his symptoms after six months
Repeat gastroscopy with gastric biopsies for culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing before treating
Repeat the urea breath test in a further three months since the earlier result may reflect residual organism

subtopic_detail: Burning upper abdominal discomfort partly controlled by six weeks of self prescribed acid suppression at forty two
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 42-year-old truck dispatcher with three months of burning discomfort high in the abdomen, worse after meals and sometimes waking him at night. Six weeks ago he bought esomeprazole from the pharmacy and has taken it every morning since.

He says he is about sixty per cent better on it but that the burning returns within two days whenever he forgets. He has no difficulty or pain on swallowing, has not vomited, has lost no weight, and has seen no blood or black material in his stool. He takes no anti-inflammatory drugs, drinks four standard drinks a week and has never smoked. His parents were born in Vietnam and no relative has had stomach cancer.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg/m2, mild epigastric tenderness without guarding, no mass, no hepatosplenomegaly, no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, conjunctivae not pale
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-175), mean cell volume 89 fL (80-100), ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30-300), liver function and lipase within normal limits, faecal occult blood negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for gastroscopy while he continues the proton pump inhibitor
Stop the proton pump inhibitor for two weeks then arrange a urea breath test
Arrange a urea breath test now while he continues his current treatment
Double the proton pump inhibitor dose and review his symptoms in eight weeks
Arrange serology for Helicobacter pylori and treat him if the result is positive

subtopic_detail: Negative coeliac serology in a woman who began a strict gluten free diet two months before the blood test
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 32-year-old woman who has had twelve months of bloating, loose stools and fatigue. Two months ago, after reading about it online, she cut out all gluten and says her bowels settled within a fortnight and her energy improved.

The locum ordered tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A antibodies before her last appointment and the result is negative, with a normal total immunoglobulin A. She has a younger sister with type 1 diabetes. She and her partner are planning a pregnancy next year and she wants to know whether she actually has to avoid gluten for life or whether she can stop bothering.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg/m2, pale conjunctivae, no mouth ulcers, no rash over the elbows or knees, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A antibodies negative with normal total immunoglobulin A, haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 76 fL (80-100), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (30-300), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.0 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Accept the negative result and manage her as having irritable bowel syndrome
Arrange duodenal biopsy now while she continues her gluten free diet
Arrange faecal calprotectin and refer for colonoscopy if it is raised
Advise a gluten challenge for six weeks and then repeat the serology
Arrange coeliac associated genetic typing and stop testing if it is positive

subtopic_detail: Progressive oedema with 6 g of daily proteinuria and albumin 24 g/L in a previously well man of forty
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 40-year-old warehouse supervisor referred with three weeks of leg swelling that now reaches his thighs, and puffiness around his eyes that is worst when he wakes. He mentions that the toilet bowl is full of froth in the mornings.

He has never been unwell, takes no regular medication and no anti-inflammatory drugs, and has no rash, joint pain or recent infection. Urine microscopy shows no red cells, no red cell casts and no dysmorphic cells. His blood pressure is 142/88 mmHg on repeated measurement.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 142/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pitting oedema to the mid thigh bilaterally, periorbital puffiness, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, jugular venous pressure not elevated, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein to creatinine ratio 620 mg/mmol (less than 30), serum albumin 24 g/L (35-50), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), total cholesterol 8.4 mmol/L, hepatitis B and C and human immunodeficiency virus serology negative, antinuclear antibody negative, fasting glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for renal biopsy and start an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor
Start high dose prednisolone and review his proteinuria in four weeks
Start a loop diuretic alone and review his proteinuria in four weeks
Start prophylactic anticoagulation and review his proteinuria in four weeks
Arrange computed tomography of chest abdomen and pelvis to seek a malignancy

subtopic_detail: Preparing a patient on three antihypertensives for an aldosterone to renin ratio with potassium 3.2
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 46-year-old teacher whose blood pressure remains 168/102 mmHg despite perindopril 10 mg, amlodipine 10 mg and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. Her pharmacy dispensing record and her home readings both confirm she is taking them.

She takes no potassium supplement, no liquorice and no anti-inflammatory drugs. She does not snore and has no daytime sleepiness, and there is no abdominal bruit. Her renal function is normal and her renal ultrasound showed two normal sized kidneys. You decide to screen her for an excess of mineralocorticoid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 168/102 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg/m2, no Cushingoid features, no abdominal bruit, no radiofemoral delay, fundi with arteriovenous nipping only
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 143 mmol/L (135-145), bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22-32), creatinine 72 micromol/L (45-90), urine albumin to creatinine ratio 4.2 mg/mmol (less than 3.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate preparation before the blood test?

options.text: Stop the amlodipine for four weeks and replace it with spironolactone cover
Stop all three of her agents for four weeks with no antihypertensive cover
Correct the potassium, stop the thiazide for four weeks and use prazosin cover
Proceed with the test now because none of her current drugs affect the ratio
Stop the perindopril for four weeks and continue her other two drugs unchanged

subtopic_detail: A low density lipoprotein of 4.4 in a well woman of fifty eight whose calculated five year risk is four per cent
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old librarian who has come for the results of a routine check. She feels completely well, walks the dog twice a day and has no chest symptoms.

She has never smoked, has no diabetes, and no relative has had a heart attack or stroke before the age of sixty; her father had a myocardial infarction at seventy four. She has no tendon thickening at the Achilles or over the knuckles and no arcus. Her blood pressure has been averaged over three separate visits. Using the Australian risk calculator, her estimated five year risk of a cardiovascular event is four per cent. She has read that her cholesterol is high and expects a prescription.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg averaged over three visits, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg/m2, waist circumference 84 cm, no tendon xanthomata, no corneal arcus, no xanthelasma, normal heart sounds with no bruits
data_table.Investigations: Total cholesterol 6.8 mmol/L, low density lipoprotein cholesterol 4.4 mmol/L, high density lipoprotein cholesterol 1.7 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.3 mmol/L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 88 mL/min/1.73m2, urine albumin to creatinine ratio 1.2 mg/mmol (less than 3.5), glycated haemoglobin 36 mmol/mol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start atorvastatin 20 mg daily and recheck her lipids in three months
Start a statin and an antihypertensive and recheck both in three months
Refer her to a specialist lipid clinic for assessment of familial hypercholesterolaemia
Advise dietary and physical activity change and recalculate her risk in two years
Arrange a coronary artery calcium score and decide on treatment from it

subtopic_detail: Lichenified flexural dermatitis in an adult unchanged after four weeks of a low potency topical corticosteroid
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 38-year-old accountant with six weeks of intensely itchy rash in both elbow creases, both knee creases and across the sides of her neck. She scratches in her sleep and wakes her partner most nights.

She had asthma and hay fever as a child. She has used hydrocortisone 1 per cent cream for four weeks, applying what she describes as a small dab on the worst patches when the itch becomes unbearable, and stopping as soon as it eases, because she has read that steroids thin the skin. There is no weeping, crusting or pustulation, no ring shaped scaly edge with central clearing, and she has not changed soap, laundry powder, jewellery or cosmetics.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Poorly demarcated erythematous plaques with thickened skin and accentuated skin markings in both antecubital and popliteal fossae and on the lateral neck, excoriations, no pustules or golden crust, no scaly annular border, nails normal
data_table.Investigations: Bacterial swab of the neck grew no significant growth, skin scraping for fungal microscopy negative, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Change to a potent topical corticosteroid ointment applied daily with emollient
Add oral cefalexin for seven days and continue the current topical treatment
Refer for patch testing and continue the current topical treatment meanwhile
Start oral prednisolone for two weeks and continue the current topical treatment
Change to a topical antifungal cream applied twice daily with emollient

subtopic_detail: Hepatitis B surface antigen positive with repeatedly normal transaminases and a very high viral load at twenty four
stem:
You are the general practitioner following up a 24-year-old woman who was born in Vietnam, came to Australia at the age of six, and was found to be hepatitis B surface antigen positive on a new patient screen. She feels entirely well and drinks no alcohol.

Her mother is also surface antigen positive. Nobody in the family has had liver cancer. She is not pregnant, is not planning a pregnancy this year, and takes no medication. Her transaminases have now been measured twice, six months apart, and both were normal, and her transient elastography and ultrasound were both unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No jaundice, no spider naevi, no palmar erythema, liver edge not palpable, no splenomegaly, no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis B e antigen positive, hepatitis B viral load 8.2 log10 IU/mL, alanine aminotransferase 22 units/L (5-35) on two occasions six months apart, transient elastography 4.2 kPa, hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis D serology negative, alpha fetoprotein within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start tenofovir disoproxil and review her viral load in three months
Start pegylated interferon alfa and review her viral load in three months
Refer for liver biopsy to decide whether antiviral treatment is needed
Discharge her from follow up as her liver function tests are normal
Monitor her transaminases and viral load six monthly without treatment

subtopic_detail: Post bronchodilator ratio of 0.64 with a 210 mL improvement in a fifty eight year old current smoker
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 58-year-old woman with a forty pack year smoking history who has had two years of breathlessness walking up the hill to her house and a productive morning cough on most days through the winter months.

She does not wake at night with wheeze or cough, and her symptoms do not vary much from day to day or with the seasons. She had no childhood asthma, has no hay fever and keeps no pets. You have arranged spirometry before and after 400 micrograms of inhaled salbutamol, and the technician reports three reproducible efforts with acceptable flow volume loops.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 134/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, reduced breath sounds throughout with prolonged expiration, no wheeze at rest, no clubbing, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Pre bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in one second 1.52 L with forced vital capacity 2.66 L, post bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in one second 1.73 L which is 65 per cent of predicted, post bronchodilator forced vital capacity 2.70 L, post bronchodilator ratio 0.64

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation of this spirometry?

options.text: Normal spirometry because the post bronchodilator volumes are within predicted
Persistent airflow obstruction with a significant bronchodilator response
A restrictive pattern requiring measurement of static lung volumes
Reversible airflow obstruction that excludes chronic obstructive disease
A poor quality test that should be repeated after four weeks of steroid

subtopic_detail: A single prostate specific antigen of 5.5 in an asymptomatic man of fifty eight with a normal examination
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old bus driver who asked for a prostate check after a workmate was diagnosed with prostate cancer last month. He has no urinary symptoms at all: no hesitancy, no poor stream, no nocturia and no haematuria.

No relative has had prostate or breast cancer. He has not had a urinary infection, has not cycled or ejaculated in the preceding forty eight hours, and takes no medication. You discussed the benefits and harms of testing at his last visit and he chose to proceed. His prostate specific antigen has come back at 5.5 micrograms/L and his digital rectal examination today is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Digital rectal examination reveals a smooth symmetrical prostate of about 30 mL with no nodule, no induration and no tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Total prostate specific antigen 5.5 micrograms/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110), midstream urine microscopy shows no pyuria and no organisms, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer him directly for transrectal ultrasound guided prostate biopsy now
Repeat the test in twelve months and refer only if it has risen further
Repeat the test within one to three months before arranging any referral
Reassure him that the result is normal for his age and repeat in two years
Start a five alpha reductase inhibitor and repeat the test in six months

subtopic_detail: Positional pleuritic chest pain with widespread concave ST elevation and PR segment depression at thirty four
stem: A 34-year-old man has two days of central chest pain, worse lying flat, eased by leaning forward, following a sore throat last week. Echocardiography is normal with no pericardial fluid.

data_table.Examination: Scratching sound at the left sternal edge
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression, PR elevation in aVR. High sensitivity troponin 8 ng/L on serial testing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate transfer for percutaneous coronary intervention
Start prednisolone 50 mg daily with a taper over four weeks
High dose ibuprofen with colchicine for three months and reduced exertion
Therapeutic low molecular weight heparin and computed tomography
High dose ibuprofen alone for two weeks with outpatient review

subtopic_detail: Drowsiness with pH 7.28 after high concentration oxygen during transport for an exacerbation of airways disease
stem:
You are the emergency registrar receiving a 71-year-old woman with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease who has had three days of increasing breathlessness with green sputum. The paramedics found her saturating at 84 per cent on room air and applied oxygen at 10 L per minute through a reservoir mask for the twenty five minute journey.

On arrival she is rousable but drowsy and cannot complete a sentence when she does speak. Her husband says she was talking normally when the ambulance arrived. She has had two admissions this year and uses home oxygen for sixteen hours a day. An arterial blood gas has been taken on the reservoir mask.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 142/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on 10 L per minute by reservoir mask, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable to voice, coarse tremor of the outstretched hands, widespread expiratory wheeze with poor air entry, no focal chest signs, warm peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Arterial pH 7.28 (7.35-7.45), arterial carbon dioxide tension 78 mmHg (35-45), arterial oxygen tension 145 mmHg (80-100), bicarbonate 34 mmol/L (22-32), chest radiograph shows hyperinflation with no consolidation or pneumothorax

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intubate her immediately and commence invasive mechanical ventilation in the department
Continue the current oxygen and start non-invasive ventilation immediately at the bedside
Stop all oxygen therapy and reassess her arterial blood gases after twenty minutes
Give intravenous doxapram and reassess her arterial blood gases after twenty minutes
Titrate oxygen to a saturation of 88 to 92 per cent and repeat the gas in twenty minutes

subtopic_detail: Ferritin 140 with transferrin saturation 12 per cent in a man with heart failure limited by fatigue
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 68-year-old retired carpenter in the heart failure clinic. His ejection fraction is 32 per cent and he is established on a beta blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, an angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor and a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor at target doses.

He has not been admitted for twelve months and is clinically euvolaemic today, with no rise in weight and no orthopnoea. What limits him is fatigue and breathlessness on the flat after about a hundred metres, which has not improved despite the last two dose increases. He has no rectal bleeding, no melaena and no dyspepsia, and gastroscopy and colonoscopy performed a year ago for a previous episode of anaemia were both normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 66 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure not elevated, no ankle oedema, chest clear, apex displaced, no hepatomegaly, no pallor of the conjunctivae
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (130-175), mean cell volume 88 fL (80-100), ferritin 140 micrograms/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 12 per cent (16-45), C reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 110 micromol/L (60-110), faecal occult blood negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral ferrous sulfate daily and recheck his iron studies in three months
Give intravenous ferric carboxymaltose and recheck his iron studies in three months
Transfuse two units of packed red cells and recheck his haemoglobin in three months
Start an erythropoiesis stimulating agent and recheck his haemoglobin in three months
Take no action as his ferritin is within the laboratory reference range for iron stores

subtopic_detail: A firm pink dome shaped nodule that has grown over eight weeks on the shoulder of a roof plumber
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62-year-old roof plumber who has noticed a lump on his left shoulder that was not there when he started a job eight weeks ago. It now catches on his shirt and has bled twice.

It is 9 mm across, firm, dome shaped and uniformly pink with no brown or black in it. He has no other new or changing spots that he is aware of, and he checked against a photograph his wife took in January. He had a basal cell carcinoma excised from his back four years ago. On dermatoscopy there is no pigment network, and you see polymorphous vessels and milky red globular areas across the surface.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: A 9 mm firm elevated pink nodule on the left shoulder with a small central crust, no surrounding pigment, no satellite lesions, no axillary or cervical lymphadenopathy, widespread solar keratoses over the forearms and scalp
data_table.Investigations: Dermatoscopy shows absent pigment network with polymorphous vessels and milky red areas, full blood count and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a punch biopsy of the centre of the lesion and review with the report
Arrange a shave biopsy of the lesion and review the histology with the report
Apply liquid nitrogen cryotherapy and review the shoulder again in eight weeks
Excise the whole lesion with a 2 mm margin down to subcutaneous fat for histology
Photograph the lesion for comparison and review the shoulder again in eight weeks

subtopic_detail: Eighteen months of widespread pain with normal inflammatory markers and a proposed diagnostic steroid trial
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 55-year-old childcare worker referred with eighteen months of pain in her neck, both shoulders, both hips, both hands and both feet. The referral asks whether a trial of prednisolone 15 mg daily would settle the question, on the basis that polymyalgia responds within forty eight hours.

She wakes unrefreshed however long she sleeps, describes her concentration as foggy, and has had alternating constipation and loose stools for years. Her stiffness is present all day rather than easing after the first hour, and it is no worse in the morning than the evening. She has no headache, no scalp tenderness, no jaw pain on chewing and no visual symptoms. There is tenderness over most muscle groups on light pressure, and no joint swelling anywhere.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Full range of movement at both shoulders and hips with pain reported throughout, no synovitis in any joint, tenderness on light palpation over the trapezius, gluteal and lateral epicondylar regions, normal power, temporal arteries non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 8 mm/h (less than 20), C reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), creatine kinase 92 units/L (30-180), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), vitamin D 62 nmol/L (50-150), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the diagnosis and start graded exercise with sleep focused therapy
Start prednisolone 15 mg daily and reassess her pain after forty eight hours
Start prednisolone 15 mg daily and arrange temporal artery ultrasound as well
Start a slow release opioid at night and reassess her pain in four weeks' time
Refer for whole body magnetic resonance imaging to look for an inflammatory cause

subtopic_detail: Creatinine 212 after three days of vomiting in a man taking a diuretic, a blocker of the renin system and ibuprofen
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 74-year-old retired fitter who has had three days of vomiting and watery diarrhoea since a family barbecue. He has kept almost nothing down and feels faint when he stands.

His regular medications are perindopril, indapamide, empagliflozin, metformin and atorvastatin, and he has been buying ibuprofen for his knee for the past month. He has taken all of them every day through the illness because, as he puts it, he was told never to miss a dose. He has passed only a small amount of dark urine since yesterday. He has no abdominal pain, no urinary symptoms and no history of prostatic obstruction.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/64 mmHg standing from 150/80 mmHg lying, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, jugular venous pressure not visible, abdomen soft with no palpable bladder, no flank tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 212 micromol/L (60-110) from a baseline of 92, potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urea 18.2 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22-32), glucose 9.2 mmol/L, blood ketones 0.6 mmol/L (less than 0.6), urinalysis negative for blood and protein, bladder scan shows 20 mL

lead_in: Alongside intravenous rehydration, which of his medications should be withheld today?

options.text: Perindopril, indapamide, ibuprofen, metformin and empagliflozin
Perindopril, indapamide and ibuprofen, continuing the other three
Metformin and empagliflozin only, continuing the other four
Ibuprofen only, continuing his five other regular medications
All six of his regular medications including the atorvastatin

subtopic_detail: Blood pressure 232/128 with flash pulmonary oedema and a plan to bring the pressure to normal within the hour
stem:
You are the emergency registrar called to a 58-year-old delivery driver who became severely breathless two hours ago and cannot lie flat. He is sitting bolt upright, speaking in single words, and coughing up frothy pink sputum.

He ran out of his blood pressure tablets three weeks ago and has not been back to his general practitioner. He has no chest pain, no tearing interscapular pain, no headache and no visual disturbance, and his radial and femoral pulses are symmetrical. The intern has drawn up a large dose of furosemide and asks whether the aim is to get the blood pressure back to normal before the next set of observations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 232/128 mmHg in both arms, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, SpO2 86 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Sitting forward and using accessory muscles, sweating, crackles to both mid zones, third heart sound, no murmur, calves soft, no focal neurological signs, fundi show flame haemorrhages without papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with left ventricular hypertrophy and lateral repolarisation change and no ST elevation, high sensitivity troponin 45 ng/L (less than 16), creatinine 108 micromol/L (60-110), chest radiograph shows bilateral perihilar alveolar shadowing with a normal mediastinal contour

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous furosemide alone and aim for normal blood pressure within the hour
Give intravenous metoprolol and aim to reduce the mean pressure by a quarter
Start a glyceryl trinitrate infusion and aim to reduce the mean pressure by a quarter
Give sublingual nifedipine and aim for normal blood pressure within the first hour
Start an oral antihypertensive and aim for normal blood pressure over twenty four hours

subtopic_detail: Sequencing blood cultures and antimicrobials in an indolent presentation with a new regurgitant murmur
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar admitting a 58-year-old man with six weeks of fevers, night sweats, fatigue and 5 kg of weight loss. He had a dental extraction two months ago and has a known bicuspid aortic valve.

He is comfortable at rest, his pulse is 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air and temperature 37.9 degrees Celsius. There is a new early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge and three splinter haemorrhages. His chest is clear, his venous pressure is not raised and there are no signs of heart failure. Haemoglobin is 108 g/L, C reactive protein 84 mg/L, and creatinine is normal. He has received no antibiotics.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: New early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, three splinter haemorrhages, chest clear, jugular venous pressure not raised
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (130-170), C reactive protein 84 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), urinalysis showing microscopic haematuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Take one set of blood cultures and start empirical intravenous antibiotics immediately after that sample
Take three sets of blood cultures and start intravenous vancomycin with gentamicin while the results are awaited
Take three sets of blood cultures from separate venepuncture sites over an hour before starting antibiotics
Start oral amoxicillin as empirical cover for oral streptococci and arrange outpatient cultures and echocardiography
Arrange transoesophageal echocardiography first and start antibiotics once a vegetation has been demonstrated

subtopic_detail: Positive interferon gamma release assay found during screening before a biologic is started
stem:
You are the rheumatology registrar reviewing a 44-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis whose disease has not responded to methotrexate and leflunomide, and for whom a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor has been recommended.

She was born in Vietnam and moved to Australia at 19. She has no cough, no fever, no night sweats and no weight loss. Her screening interferon gamma release assay is positive, her chest radiograph is normal with no apical scarring or calcification, and her liver function tests and full blood count are normal. She has no known contact with active tuberculosis and no previous treatment for it, and she takes no other immunosuppressive medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Synovitis of both wrists and several metacarpophalangeal joints, chest clear, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Interferon gamma release assay positive, chest radiograph normal, alanine aminotransferase 24 units/L (5-35), white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), human immunodeficiency virus serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start a standard four drug antituberculous regimen and begin the biologic after the intensive phase is complete
Repeat the interferon gamma release assay and proceed with the biologic if the second result is negative
Start treatment for latent infection and begin the biologic after at least four weeks of that treatment
Start the biologic now and treat for latent infection only if symptoms or radiographic changes develop later
Attribute the result to previous bacille Calmette Guerin vaccination and proceed with the biologic without treatment

subtopic_detail: Vomiting for twelve hours in a patient on replacement steroid who cannot keep tablets down
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 42-year-old man with twelve hours of vomiting and watery diarrhoea after a family barbecue, with two other family members similarly unwell.

He has primary adrenal insufficiency diagnosed eight years ago and takes hydrocortisone 20 mg in the morning and 10 mg at midday, with fludrocortisone daily. He doubled his morning dose today but vomited within twenty minutes of taking it and has kept nothing down since. His pulse is 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 94/58 mmHg lying and 78/50 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air and temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius. His sodium is 129 mmol/L, potassium 5.3 mmol/L, glucose 3.8 mmol/L and creatinine 104 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 94/58 mmHg lying and 78/50 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, abdomen soft with generalised mild tenderness, no guarding
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 129 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), glucose 3.8 mmol/L (4.0-7.8), creatinine 104 micromol/L (60-110), venous bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22-32)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Parenteral hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately with intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 percent and glucose
Oral hydrocortisone 40 mg with an antiemetic and oral rehydration solution, reassessing him in two hours
Parenteral dexamethasone 4 mg immediately with intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 percent and glucose
Intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 percent with a random cortisol and short synacthen test before any steroid
Intravenous calcium gluconate with insulin and glucose for the potassium, then parenteral hydrocortisone

subtopic_detail: Vertebral fracture from a trivial mechanism when bone density has not been measured
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 68-year-old woman who developed sudden mid thoracic back pain while lifting a full kettle. Her menopause was at 51 and she has taken no hormone therapy.

Thoracic spine radiographs show a new wedge compression fracture at the ninth thoracic vertebra with 30 percent anterior height loss, and no lytic lesion. Her pain is severe on movement and settles at rest. Serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, renal function, thyroid function, vitamin D, serum protein electrophoresis and full blood count are all normal. She has never had a bone density scan, takes no corticosteroids, does not smoke and drinks two standard drinks weekly. She walks daily and has had no previous fracture.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Focal tenderness over the ninth thoracic spinous process, no neurological deficit, normal gait
data_table.Investigations: Radiograph showing a new wedge compression fracture at the ninth thoracic vertebra with 30 percent height loss, corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), alkaline phosphatase 78 units/L (30-110), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (50-150), serum protein electrophoresis normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her bone health?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine and defer bone treatment until malignancy is excluded
Prescribe calcium and vitamin D with a graded exercise program, and reassess her fracture risk in twelve months
Arrange bone densitometry and start an antiresorptive agent only if the T score is minus 2.5 or lower
Refer for vertebroplasty of the fractured level, with pharmacological treatment considered after the procedure
Start an antiresorptive agent now with calcium and vitamin D, and arrange bone densitometry as a baseline

subtopic_detail: Reversal strategy for a factor Xa inhibitor during torrential upper gastrointestinal bleeding
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to a 76-year-old man who has vomited a large volume of fresh blood twice in the emergency department. He takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation and took his last dose four hours ago.

His pulse is 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 86/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on 6 litres per minute by mask and temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius. He is pale and clammy with melaena on rectal examination. Haemoglobin is 74 g/L, platelets 188 x10^9/L, international normalised ratio 1.3, creatinine 132 micromol/L and lactate 3.4 mmol/L. Two units of red cells and the massive haemorrhage protocol have been activated, and the gastroenterology team is preparing for endoscopy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 86/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on 6 litres per minute, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale and clammy, melaena on rectal examination, abdomen soft, no signs of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 74 g/L (130-170), platelets 188 x10^9/L (150-400), international normalised ratio 1.3, creatinine 132 micromol/L (60-110), lactate 3.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.0)

lead_in: Which haemostatic treatment is most appropriate alongside resuscitation?

options.text: Haemodialysis arranged urgently to clear the drug once the bleeding source is being addressed and blood is running
Fresh frozen plasma at four units given rapidly once the bleeding source is being addressed and blood is running
Intravenous vitamin K 10 mg given slowly once the bleeding source is being addressed and blood is running
Prothrombin complex concentrate given as a single weight based dose once the bleeding source is being addressed
Idarucizumab given as two sequential vials once the bleeding source is being addressed and blood is running

subtopic_detail: Order of antihypertensive agents when imaging shows a tear extending from the ascending aorta
stem: A 63-year-old man has two hours of tearing interscapular pain maximal at onset. Computed tomography angiography shows an intimal flap from the ascending aorta extending beyond the left subclavian artery. Cardiothoracic surgery has been contacted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, BP 198/104 mmHg right arm, 164/88 mmHg left

lead_in: Which pharmacological management is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous nitroprusside to a systolic below 120 mmHg, then a beta blocker
Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate titrated to pain relief, with morphine
Intravenous esmolol to a heart rate below 60 /min, then a vasodilator
Treatment dose intravenous heparin with aspirin pending coronary angiography
Intravenous hydralazine to a systolic below 120 mmHg with analgesia

subtopic_detail: Pleural fluid that meets exudative criteria in a patient already treated with a loop diuretic
stem: A 74-year-old man with an ejection fraction of 30 percent has had four days of intravenous furosemide 80 mg twice daily for bilateral pleural effusions, losing 4.5 kg. The right effusion is aspirated.

data_table.Pleural fluid: Straw coloured. Protein 32 g/L with serum protein 62 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase ratio 0.62, albumin 20 g/L with serum albumin 34 g/L

lead_in: How should this fluid be interpreted?

options.text: An exudate, since the protein ratio exceeds the 0.5 threshold
A parapneumonic effusion requiring intercostal drainage
An indeterminate result requiring thoracoscopic pleural biopsy
A transudate, shown by a serum to pleural albumin gradient above 12 g/L
A malignant effusion pending cytology, given the bilateral distribution

subtopic_detail: Numb feet and unsteadiness when the vitamin assay sits inside the reference interval
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 66-year-old man with four months of numbness and tingling in both feet, now reaching the mid calf, and increasing unsteadiness in the dark. He has taken metformin for twelve years and a proton pump inhibitor for eight.

On examination he has reduced vibration sense to the knees, absent ankle reflexes with extensor plantar responses, and a positive Romberg test. His full blood count shows a haemoglobin of 141 g/L with a mean corpuscular volume of 94 fL and no hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum vitamin B12 is 168 picomol/L, folate is normal, thyroid function is normal, and glycated haemoglobin is 52 mmol/mol. Methylmalonic acid is markedly elevated and homocysteine is elevated.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Reduced vibration sense to the knees, absent ankle reflexes, extensor plantar responses, positive Romberg test, normal power
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 141 g/L (130-170), mean corpuscular volume 94 fL (80-100), vitamin B12 168 picomol/L (150-700), folate normal, methylmalonic acid markedly elevated, homocysteine elevated, glycated haemoglobin 52 mmol/mol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin on an alternate day loading schedule, then continue three monthly maintenance
Withhold replacement and repeat the serum vitamin level in three months, as the result lies within the reference interval
Attribute the signs to diabetic peripheral neuropathy and start duloxetine with podiatry referral and glycaemic review
Start oral folic acid at 5 mg daily and recheck the neurological examination and blood film in three months
Start oral cyanocobalamin at high dose daily and recheck the serum vitamin level and symptoms in three months

subtopic_detail: Choosing the next inhaled agent using the blood eosinophil count after repeated exacerbations
stem: A 69-year-old ex-smoker has had three community-treated exacerbations and one admission this year. She uses a combined long-acting muscarinic antagonist and beta agonist with good technique and adherence, and has completed pulmonary rehabilitation. She has no asthma or atopy.

data_table.Investigations: Post bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.58, FEV1 48 per cent predicted, blood eosinophils 0.42 x10^9/L twice, CT emphysema without bronchiectasis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her inhaled treatment?

options.text: Replace the muscarinic antagonist with an inhaled corticosteroid
Switch to a different long-acting muscarinic antagonist
Add long term oral azithromycin three times weekly
Add low dose maintenance oral prednisolone daily
Add an inhaled corticosteroid, moving to triple therapy

subtopic_detail: Limb pain disproportionate to skin findings when the risk score reads low
stem: A 57-year-old man with diabetes, admitted eight hours ago with a red left calf on flucloxacillin, needs hourly morphine for pain far worse than the leg looks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 104/58 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Erythema advanced 6 cm in four hours; tense dusky skin, reduced sensation
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.6 x10^9/L, lactate 3.1 mmol/L; soft tissue risk score low

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate theatre for exploration with broad spectrum antibiotics
Contrast computed tomography of the leg before operating
Escalate to vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam, review in four hours
Continue antibiotics and repeat the risk score in six hours
Bedside incision of the dusky area under local anaesthesia

subtopic_detail: Deciding on airway support using bedside respiratory mechanics rather than oximetry in neuromuscular weakness
stem: A 48-year-old woman admitted with worsening generalised myasthenia gravis has developed nasal speech over six hours and cannot lift her head from the pillow. She takes pyridostigmine and prednisolone.

data_table.Examination: Single breath count 12, weak cough, no retained secretions, respiratory rate 28 /min
data_table.Investigations: Forced vital capacity fallen from 2.4 to 1.1 litres over six hours, pH 7.44, pCO2 38 mmHg, SpO2 97 per cent on air

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ward non-invasive ventilation, reassess in two hours
Intensive care intubation, then plasma exchange
Edrophonium test to exclude cholinergic crisis
Ward observation with hourly oximetry and gases
Substantially increase the pyridostigmine dose

subtopic_detail: A negative early polymerase chain reaction in a febrile confusional state with temporal lobe changes
stem: A 39-year-old man was admitted two days ago with fever, headache, progressive confusion and a generalised seizure, and started on intravenous aciclovir and ceftriaxone. He remains febrile and disorientated.

data_table.Investigations: Lumbar puncture at 12 hours: 34 lymphocytes per microlitre, protein 0.62 g/L, herpes simplex polymerase chain reaction negative, cultures sterile. Magnetic resonance imaging: right medial temporal signal change. Electroencephalogram: right temporal periodic discharges

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue aciclovir and add intravenous ganciclovir empirically
Continue aciclovir and arrange a temporal lobe brain biopsy
Continue aciclovir and repeat the lumbar puncture for testing
Cease aciclovir and start high dose methylprednisolone
Cease aciclovir and investigate for an alternative cause

subtopic_detail: Rash with fever and organ involvement six weeks after a new urate lowering drug
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar admitting a 62-year-old man with a widespread rash, fever and malaise. He was started on allopurinol six weeks ago for recurrent gout and takes no other new medication.

He has a confluent morbilliform eruption over more than half his body surface with facial swelling, and there are no mucosal erosions and no skin detachment. His temperature is 38.7 degrees Celsius, pulse 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and SpO2 97 percent on room air. His white cell count is 16.8 x10^9/L with eosinophils 1.9 x10^9/L and atypical lymphocytes on the film, alanine aminotransferase is 312 units/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L and thyroid function is normal. He is of Han Chinese background.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform eruption over more than half the body surface, marked facial oedema, cervical lymphadenopathy, no mucosal erosions, no skin detachment
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with eosinophils 1.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), atypical lymphocytes on film, alanine aminotransferase 312 units/L (5-35), creatinine 128 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the allopurinol at a reduced dose and start systemic corticosteroid, with weekly monitoring of organ function
Cease the allopurinol and transfer him urgently to a burns unit for management of an epidermal necrolysis spectrum reaction
Cease the allopurinol and give supportive care with emollients and antihistamines, avoiding systemic corticosteroid
Cease the allopurinol and start systemic corticosteroid, with weekly monitoring of liver and renal function
Cease the allopurinol and start intravenous immunoglobulin, with weekly monitoring of liver and renal function

subtopic_detail: Ketoacidosis after surgery in a patient whose glucose never rises above the usual diagnostic threshold
stem: A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes on metformin and empagliflozin is nauseated and breathing deeply on the second day after laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She took her usual medications on the morning of surgery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 /min, respiratory rate 28 /min
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 9.4 mmol/L, pH 7.21, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Attribute the acidosis to metformin and give bicarbonate
Treat postoperative pain and nausea and repeat the gas
Measure blood ketones and start insulin with glucose and saline
Attribute the acidosis to sepsis and start antibiotics
Restart her oral agents with fluid and recheck the gas

subtopic_detail: Repeated explosive headaches in the weeks after childbirth with normal initial investigation
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman who is eleven days after an uncomplicated vaginal birth. She has had four separate headaches over six days, each reaching maximum intensity within a minute and each lasting about two hours, two of them triggered by coughing and one by showering.

Her pulse is 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air and temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Non contrast computed tomography on day two of the headaches was normal, and lumbar puncture performed that day showed no xanthochromia and a normal cell count. Neurological examination is normal, the headache is not postural, and she has had no seizures. She has been using pseudoephedrine for nasal congestion and has no history of migraine.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Normal fundi, no neck stiffness, no focal neurological deficit, normal visual fields to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Non contrast computed tomography of the brain normal, cerebrospinal fluid with no xanthochromia and normal cell count, platelets 268 x10^9/L (150-400), urate and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation and management?

options.text: Magnetic resonance venography with therapeutic anticoagulation started for a presumed cerebral venous thrombosis
Cerebral angiographic imaging with nimodipine started and the pseudoephedrine stopped
Repeat computed tomography angiography with an epidural blood patch arranged for a presumed low pressure headache
Catheter digital subtraction angiography with sumatriptan prescribed for the recurrent severe headaches
Repeat lumbar puncture with measurement of the opening pressure and acetazolamide started for raised pressure

subtopic_detail: Choosing an anticoagulant class when the thrombosis accompanies an intact luminal bowel tumour
stem: A 68-year-old man has a segmental pulmonary embolism found on staging computed tomography for an untreated locally advanced rectal adenocarcinoma, starting chemoradiotherapy next week. Colonoscopy showed a friable circumferential tumour that bled on contact, and he has passed fresh rectal blood for two months.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (130-170), platelets 212 x10^9/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, haemodynamically stable

lead_in: Which anticoagulation strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Warfarin to an international normalised ratio of 2 to 3
A retrievable inferior vena cava filter without anticoagulation
Therapeutic low molecular weight heparin for at least six months
Therapeutic rivaroxaban, continued for at least six months
Observation with serial imaging and no anticoagulation

subtopic_detail: Proximal weakness that improves briefly with sustained effort in a long term smoker
stem:
You are the neurology registrar seeing a 64-year-old man with five months of difficulty rising from low chairs and climbing stairs. He has smoked 45 pack years.

He describes a dry mouth, constipation and erectile difficulty over the same period. On examination proximal lower limb power is 4 out of 5, knee reflexes are absent at rest but become detectable after ten seconds of sustained quadriceps contraction, and grip strength improves briefly after repeated effort. There is no ptosis, no diplopia and no bulbar weakness. Creatine kinase is normal, inflammatory markers are normal, thyroid function is normal, and acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative. A chest radiograph is reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Proximal lower limb power 4 out of 5, absent knee reflexes that reappear after sustained contraction, dry mouth, no ptosis or diplopia, normal sensation
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 118 units/L (30-200), C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, acetylcholine receptor antibodies negative, chest radiograph reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis with myositis specific antibody testing for an inflammatory myopathy
Vitamin D and parathyroid hormone measurement with a trial of exercise for osteomalacic myopathy
A therapeutic trial of pyridostigmine with repeat acetylcholine receptor antibody testing in three months
Computed tomography of the chest together with voltage gated calcium channel antibody testing
Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine with nerve conduction studies for a proximal radiculopathy

subtopic_detail: Recurrent falls in an older person whose medication list carries a heavy anticholinergic and sedative load
stem: An 82-year-old woman has had a third fall in four months, now fracturing her wrist. She takes oxybutynin, temazepam nightly, amitriptyline 25 mg, perindopril, atorvastatin and pantoprazole.

data_table.Observations: Blood pressure 136/78 mmHg lying, 112/64 mmHg standing without symptoms
data_table.Examination: Slow wide-based gait, dry mouth, impaired attention and recall
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, thyroid function and electrocardiogram normal

lead_in: Which intervention will most reduce further falls?

options.text: Withdraw oxybutynin, amitriptyline and temazepam with a balance program
Start a bisphosphonate with calcium and refer to fracture liaison
Start a cholinesterase inhibitor and refer for occupational therapy
Reduce perindopril and add fludrocortisone for the postural drop
Substitute a shorter half life benzodiazepine and assess hazards

subtopic_detail: Biopsy technique for a pigmented skin lesion where melanoma is the clinical concern
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 52-year-old man who has noticed that a mole on his upper back has darkened and enlarged over the past five months. His wife says it looks different from his others.

He has fair skin that burns easily, worked outdoors for two decades and had a basal cell carcinoma excised from his nose four years ago. The lesion is 9 mm across with an irregular notched border, two shades of brown and a small black area at one edge. Dermoscopy shows an atypical pigment network with irregular streaks at the periphery. There is no ulceration and no palpable axillary lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: 9 mm pigmented lesion on the upper back with border irregularity and colour variegation, no ulceration, no satellite lesions, no palpable axillary or cervical lymphadenopathy, numerous solar keratoses on the forearms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate way to obtain a tissue diagnosis?

options.text: Serial dermoscopic photography of the lesion with planned review in three months' time
Shave biopsy of the raised component with diathermy to the base of the pigmented lesion
Partial punch biopsy taken from the most darkly pigmented area of the pigmented lesion
Complete excision biopsy of the whole lesion with a two millimetre peripheral margin
Wide local excision with a one centimetre margin performed at the initial operation today

subtopic_detail: Imaging the sacroiliac joints when pelvic radiographs are normal in suspected axial inflammatory back disease
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 26-year-old man with 14 months of lower back and buttock pain that wakes him in the second half of the night and forces him to get up and move around. He has more than an hour of stiffness each morning that eases with activity and worsens with rest.

His pain has not responded to paracetamol but improved noticeably during a two week course of a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug. He had an episode of a painful red eye with photophobia treated by an optometrist last year. Examination shows reduced lumbar flexion on the modified Schober test and tenderness over both buttocks with no neurological deficit and a negative straight leg raise. An anteroposterior pelvic radiograph is reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Modified Schober test 3.5 cm, chest expansion 4 cm, tenderness over both sacroiliac regions, no neurological deficit in the lower limbs, straight leg raise negative bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 14 mg/L (<5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 28 mm/h (<15), full blood count within normal limits, anteroposterior pelvic radiograph reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat plain radiography of the sacroiliac joints with dedicated oblique views in two years
Human leucocyte antigen B27 testing used on its own to confirm or exclude the diagnosis
Computed tomography of the sacroiliac joints to assess for erosion and joint space narrowing
Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints including fat suppressed sequences
Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine to look for disc protrusion and nerve root compression

subtopic_detail: Medical rather than surgical first line therapy for a large prolactin secreting pituitary tumour
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar seeing a 38-year-old man referred with two years of reduced libido and erectile dysfunction, and six months of bumping into door frames on his left side.

He takes no medication, has no chest pain and has never had a head injury. Formal perimetry confirms a bitemporal hemianopia denser superiorly. Serum prolactin measured on two occasions is 8400 milliunits/L and 8100 milliunits/L (85-500), with testosterone low, luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone low, and thyroid function and early morning cortisol within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a 24 mm pituitary lesion with suprasellar extension abutting the optic chiasm and no haemorrhage.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bitemporal hemianopia on confrontation and formal perimetry, no ophthalmoplegia, visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally, no galactorrhoea, reduced body hair
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 8400 and 8100 milliunits/L (85-500), testosterone low, luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone low, thyroid function and 8 am cortisol within normal limits, magnetic resonance imaging shows a 24 mm sellar mass with suprasellar extension

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Oral cabergoline titrated with serial prolactin measurement and repeat visual field testing
Testosterone replacement therapy to correct his hypogonadal symptoms while monitoring the tumour
Urgent transsphenoidal surgical debulking of the tumour to decompress the optic chiasm
Stereotactic radiotherapy to the pituitary fossa with endocrine review every three months
Observation with repeat imaging and prolactin measurement in six months before any treatment

subtopic_detail: Choosing a topical regimen for stable chronic plaque disease on extensor surfaces
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 41-year-old woman with a two year history of scaly patches on both elbows and knees that itch mildly and flake onto her clothes. She has tried an over the counter moisturiser and 1% hydrocortisone with minimal improvement.

She has no joint pain, no nail changes and no scalp involvement, and she takes no regular medication. Examination shows four well demarcated salmon pink plaques with thick silvery scale over both elbows and both knees, together involving around 4% of her body surface area. There are no plaques in the flexures, on the face or in the genital region, and the rest of her skin is clear.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Four well demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on both elbows and knees, approximately 4% body surface area, no nail pitting or onycholysis, no scalp or flexural involvement, no joint swelling or tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Narrowband ultraviolet B phototherapy attending a dermatology unit three times each week
A further trial of a mild topical corticosteroid applied twice daily for six to eight weeks
Oral methotrexate commenced weekly with folic acid and regular blood test monitoring
Topical coal tar preparation applied nightly under occlusion with emollient during the day
A potent topical corticosteroid combined with calcipotriol applied to the affected plaques

subtopic_detail: Initial management of chronic widespread pain once inflammatory disease has been excluded
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 45-year-old woman with four years of aching in her neck, shoulders, lower back and both thighs, present most days. She wakes unrefreshed after eight hours in bed and describes difficulty concentrating and finding words.

Her symptoms worsen with stress and cold weather. There is no joint swelling, no morning stiffness beyond 15 minutes and no rash, weight loss or fever. Examination shows a full range of movement in all joints with no synovitis, normal power and normal reflexes, but widespread tenderness to light palpation over the trapezius, gluteal and thigh muscles. Full blood count, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, creatine kinase, thyroid function and vitamin D are all within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No synovitis in any joint, full range of movement, normal power and reflexes, widespread soft tissue tenderness to light palpation, no rash, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, creatine kinase, thyroid function and vitamin D all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: A graded aerobic exercise program with education about the condition and sleep strategies
A slow release opioid analgesic titrated to effect with review of her pain scores monthly
An antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor panel with rheumatology referral if abnormal
A regular non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug with a proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection
Referral for magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical and lumbar spine before treatment starts

subtopic_detail: Immediate priority for rapidly progressive epidermal detachment after a recently started anticonvulsant
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 34-year-old woman with a three day history of fever, sore throat and painful eyes, followed today by a spreading rash that began on her trunk. She started lamotrigine 18 days ago for bipolar disorder.

She describes her skin as feeling like it is burning. Examination shows dusky macules with central blistering across her chest, back and proximal limbs, and gentle lateral pressure on unblistered skin at the edge of a lesion causes the epidermis to shear away. There are erosions on her lips, buccal mucosa and conjunctivae, and she cannot open her eyes fully. Around 12% of her body surface area is detached or detachable. She is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112/min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.7 C
data_table.Examination: Dusky targetoid macules with central blistering over trunk and proximal limbs, positive epidermal shearing on lateral pressure, erosions of lips, buccal mucosa and conjunctivae, approximately 12% body surface area involved
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), eosinophils 0.2 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22-32), liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most important immediate action?

options.text: Commence broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics prophylactically and admit under the medical team
Cease the causative drug immediately and transfer her urgently to a specialist burns unit
Reduce the anticonvulsant dose and observe for 24 hours to see whether the rash stabilises
Commence high dose intravenous corticosteroid therapy and continue the anticonvulsant meanwhile
Arrange urgent skin biopsy for direct immunofluorescence before making any treatment decision

subtopic_detail: Eosinophilic drug hypersensitivity with hepatic involvement six weeks after starting urate lowering therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 61-year-old man with a widespread rash and fever for five days. He started allopurinol six weeks ago after a third episode of gout and takes perindopril for hypertension, unchanged for three years.

Examination shows a confluent morbilliform eruption covering around 60% of his body surface with marked facial oedema, particularly periorbitally. There is no epidermal detachment and no mucosal erosion, though his lips look dry. He has tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. His creatinine has risen from a baseline of 88 to 174 micromol/L (60-110), alanine aminotransferase is 310 U/L (<40) and his eosinophil count is 2.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.9 C
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform eruption over approximately 60% body surface area, marked facial and periorbital oedema, tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, no epidermal detachment, no mucosal erosions
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 2.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), white cell count 14.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), alanine aminotransferase 310 U/L (<40), creatinine 174 micromol/L (60-110, baseline 88), atypical lymphocytes seen on blood film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the causative drug and transfer him urgently to a specialist burns unit for wound care
Cease the causative drug and manage with topical corticosteroid and oral antihistamine only
Cease the causative drug and commence systemic corticosteroid with prolonged tapering
Continue the causative drug at a reduced dose and add intravenous fluids for the kidney injury
Cease the antihypertensive as the likely cause and continue urate lowering therapy unchanged

subtopic_detail: First biochemical test when growth hormone excess is suspected from acral and facial change
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 47-year-old woman who has had three rings resized in two years and has gone up two shoe sizes. She mentions that her dentist commented her teeth have become more widely spaced.

She has been treated for carpal tunnel syndrome in both wrists, snores heavily and was diagnosed with hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance last year. She has noticed increased sweating and headaches. Examination shows a prominent brow and jaw, large fleshy hands, an enlarged tongue and skin tags on the neck. Her old photographs from ten years ago show visibly different facial contours. Visual fields are full to confrontation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 154/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Frontal bossing, prognathism with interdental separation, macroglossia, spade-like hands, multiple skin tags, visual fields full to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.6 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), HbA1c 45 mmol/mol (<42), electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: Which investigation should be requested first?

options.text: Overnight dexamethasone suppression testing with a morning cortisol measured the next day
Random serum growth hormone level measured at the time of the consultation today
Serum insulin-like growth factor 1 compared against an age and sex matched reference range
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary with dedicated thin slices through the sella
Oral glucose tolerance test with serial growth hormone sampling over the following two hours

subtopic_detail: Escalation after non-steroidal failure in purely axial disease without peripheral involvement
stem:
You are the rheumatology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old man with magnetic resonance imaging confirmed active sacroiliitis and 18 months of inflammatory back pain. He has completed sequential four week trials of two different non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs at maximum tolerated dose, with only partial relief.

He attends a structured physiotherapy program twice weekly and has done so for six months. He has no peripheral joint swelling, no dactylitis, no enthesitis and no psoriasis or bowel symptoms. His Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index remains high and he has reduced his work hours. C-reactive protein is 32 mg/L (<5) and screening for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Restricted lumbar flexion, tenderness over both sacroiliac joints, no peripheral synovitis, no dactylitis, no enthesitis, no skin or nail psoriasis
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 32 mg/L (<5), magnetic resonance imaging shows bilateral active sacroiliitis with bone marrow oedema, interferon gamma release assay negative, hepatitis B and C serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next treatment?

options.text: Commence oral methotrexate weekly with folic acid supplementation and monthly blood monitoring
Commence long term oral prednisolone at low dose with bone protection and gastric prophylaxis
Commence sulfasalazine titrated gradually with regular full blood count and liver function testing
Continue the physiotherapy program alone and reassess his disease activity in six months
Commence a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor after completing the required screening process

subtopic_detail: Reversing a factor Xa inhibitor for intracranial bleeding when the timing of the last dose is unknown
stem: An 81-year-old woman on apixaban was found confused; the time of her last dose is unknown. Glasgow Coma Scale is 13 with new left hemiparesis. The hospital does not stock andexanet alfa.

data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography brain: 32 mL right basal ganglia haematoma. Prothrombin time 15 s (11-14), activated partial thromboplastin time 34 s (25-35), weight 58 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate haemostatic management?

options.text: Withhold haemostatic therapy since the coagulation tests are normal
Give intravenous idarucizumab as a specific reversal agent
Give intravenous vitamin K with weight based fresh frozen plasma
Give activated charcoal and arrange urgent haemodialysis for clearance
Give prothrombin complex concentrate at a weight based dose

subtopic_detail: Urinary calcium excretion measurement before parathyroid surgery for familial hypercalcaemia
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar seeing a 34-year-old man referred for parathyroidectomy. He was found to have a raised calcium on a routine check two years ago and repeat testing has shown persistently similar values since.

He has no bone pain, no renal colic, no polyuria, no constipation and no fractures, and he plays competitive squash. He takes no supplements, no thiazide and no lithium. A dual energy X-ray absorptiometry scan shows normal bone mineral density for age, and renal tract ultrasound shows no calculi and no nephrocalcinosis. His mother and one of his two sisters have also been told they have a high calcium and neither has had symptoms. A sestamibi scan reported no definite parathyroid adenoma.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
